News.title: ‘I thought I was going to die’… Minute-by-minute how Lewes derailment unfolded from buckled track to flipped carriages
News.content:
PASSENGERS screamed and were hurled from their seats as three carriages of a busy commuter train derailed.

Home-bound commuters felt the carriages “rocking” moments before the 300-ton train bucked off the tracks just as it was approaching the historic market town of Lewes, East Sussex.



Disaster struck the packed 2.24pm service from London Victoria to Eastbourne when the train’s rear three carriages left the track at around 90 minutes later at around 3.50pm.

The service was already running around 20 minutes late – having been subject to speed restrictions before disaster struck.



Passengers were tossed around inside the train with commuters describing people “dropping from the sky” as the rear three carriages of the eight coach train were thrown down a dusty embankment.

The derailment left 40 of the train’s 150 terrified passengers trapped on one of the hottest days of the year – with two people being left seriously injured.

Investigators from the Rail Accident Investigation Board will now be studying the train’s black box as they aim to get to the bottom of what caused Britain’s second rail disaster in two months.

When the train set off from London Victoria – it was a journey like any other, with commuters heading home back into the Sussex countryside.



However, the train crawled towards disaster – with tracking data showing it lost around 20 minutes as it travelled from East Croydon to Gatwick Airport.

It then passed through Haywards Heath, Wivelsfield and Cooksbridge – before beginning its fateful two-mile journey to Lewes.

People aboard the crashed train told of the terrifying moment the carriages were thrown from the tracks.

Passenger Rachel Heath said it was “terrifying” she thought she was going to die.

She told the BBC: “I just remember thinking to myself that I was going to die.



“Here was about two seconds where I genuinely thought this was it, and so I went on my phone, immediately called my partner as the train was still flipping.

“[That] was just kind of in my mind as I made that call—calling to say goodbye.”

Nathan Cole, 30, told The Sun: “I was at the very back carriage. Even before it derailed it wobbled and I saw a woman kind of grab onto her seat. I’m even a bit worried myself.



“Then after I heard the suspension go into full force.

“The train carried on going, and then within a minute, it’s done it again, and then it’s just gone straight off the track.

“I’m facing backwards, I’m travelling backwards, but the window is to my right side.

“One woman almost fell on me.

“The woman who was holding onto the chair, when the train came to a stop I had to pick her up because she couldn’t really move.



“At that time, I didn’t really feel any pain. I think it was the adrenaline. I just wanted to get out of the train.

“I was worried that the train was going to catch on fire, to be honest.”

Rob Bradley, who was travelling with his six-year-old daughter Mabel, described his horror at seeing the carriage he was in jump “vertically upwards” – and said the train was “rocking” before the crash.

He told The Times his and his daughter’s bags, as well as his laptop and AirPods, were thrown forward by the sudden jerk of the derailment.

After the train derailed at 3.45pm twenty people in total were rushed to hospital after being triaged next to the tracks by emergency responders.



Two suffered serious injuries and were sent to a major trauma centre for treatment.

Terrifying pictures from the scene show the carriages lying on their sides, with passengers standing on top of the train as they were helped to safety.

One bloodied passenger described the moment everything went “topsy-turvy” as the train suddenly picked up speed and rolled over.



Susan Lees told The Sun: “I’m just happy to be alive and that there were no fatalities on the train.

“Some people were injured quite badly I understand, we’ve all been looked after so wonderfully.”

And Cole, told The Times that he watched as dirt flew by the window just inches from his face.

He said: “I’m thinking, I hope this window doesn’t burst, because if the window will break that goes right in my face.”

Pictures of the crash scene revealed the devastation.



And immediately questions were asked about the visibly buckled track and crumbled embankment

Experts have told how the short journey time meant the train was likely travelling at just 40mph – which thankfully meant passengers were saved from the horror of a high-speed crash.

As the RAIB probes the disaster, experts believe they will be looking at one likely cause – warped tracks.

Cameras on the train will show the state of the track before the carriages passed over it – and images from the scene reportedly support the buckled rail theory.



The former chairman of the Strategic Rail Authority said investigators should be able to see “what the track looked like as the train arrived” at the section of rail where it was thrown from the track.

Richard Bowker told BBC Radio 4’s Today Programme that the Rail Accident Investigation Branch will “be looking at things like the condition of the track.”

He added: “We’ve seen images of damaged track – was that caused by the derailment, or did it cause it, or a bit of both?”

Bowker said: “The train itself I would expect to be fitted with forward-facing CCTV cameras, so it will be possible to see, I would suspect, what the track looked like as the train arrived.”



He added that the train’s black box will show investigators what speed it was going and whether the driver applied the breaks.

Investigators will likely focus on the section of track known as the ballast and will also probe the nearby embankment.

Yesterday, local MP James MacClearly told The Times: “I had a meeting literally last week with Greater Thameslink Railway, who are the parent company of Southern Rail.

“We did discuss the track and the fact that it has been a bit bumpier in recent months.”

The exact cause of the derailment will remain a mystery until the RAIB publishes its findings.

News.title: Daughter slams killer dad for refusing to reveal where her mum’s body is – as top judges rule he will STAY in prison
News.content:
'NO PEACE' Daughter slams killer dad for refusing to reveal where her mum’s body is – as top judges rule he will STAY in prison

THE DAUGHTER of a woman murdered by her husband has slammed the monster for still refusing to reveal where her body is 24 years later.

Glyn Razzell was jailed for life with a minimum of almost 16 years in 2003 for killing mum-of-four Linda Razzell.



Linda had disappeared on her way to work at Swindon College, Wiltshire, during the couple’s divorce proceedings.

Razzell has never revealed where his wife’s body is despite multiple pleas from her devastated family.



The Parole Board previously ruled Razzell could be released on licence but the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) referred the decision to the High Court.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb today quashed the initial decision, stating that she was “not satisfied that it is no longer necessary for the protection of the public that Glyn Razzell be confined”.

She continued she found Razzell to be “fundamentally dishonest” and said she was “satisfied that he continues to withhold information he could deliver up”.

Razzell, now aged 66, has always denied being responsible for the 2002 killing.

Linda’s family had urged the court to block the release, with her cousin Julie Westmore “all hope of ever finding [her] remains will be lost” if the killer is freed.

Razzell and Linda’s daughter Catherine today said her dad’s decision not to reveal the location of her mum’s body meant there was “no peace” for the family.



She also slammed Razzell for “continuing to do our family harm” and was “actively choosing to be controlling and abusive from within prison”.

Catherine, who was 13 at the time of her mum’s disappearance, said today’s ruling was a “relief” but her dad’s continuing decision not to disclose the location of the remains was “cruel”.

She added: “By choosing to withhold the only information that could provide us with some comfort and closure, and preventing us from being able to hold a funeral for our much-loved mother, he is clearly demonstrating he is still abusive – retaining power over the situation and prioritising his narrative, where he can deny killing her, despite being found guilty and given a life sentence.



“To our knowledge, he is of sound mind and knows what he is doing, so there is no reason for him to be released while he is still actively choosing to be controlling and abusive from within prison.

“However, it is important to recognise that while we welcome the decision made today, part of my father’s abuse is that, as a family, we have to go through this process.

“As well as experiencing the most devastating loss of my mother, 24 years later we are still in court trying to keep the rest of our family safe from a man who is continuing to do our family harm.

“None of us want my father to die in prison; what we want is for him to acknowledge what he has done, show remorse and tell us where our mother’s body is so that we can finally lay her to rest.

“There is no peace for us until that happens.”



Linda, who was 41 when she vanished, was last seen parking her car while on her way to work in March 2002.

She had been in the middle of a divorce battle with Razzell and had visited a bank with a court order to freeze her husband’s bank accounts the week before she vanished.

Following her disappearance, shameless Razzell appealed for her return but was later arrested and charged with murder.

It came after officers discovered a significant amount of Linda’s blood in the boot in his car.

During the trial, jurors heard Linda was due to receive the marital home in Highworth and a £30,000 lump sum.



A month before Linda vanished, Razzell had been acquitted of a charge of wounding after allegedly repeatedly hitting her head against a window in the home they shared.

He had also made chilling comments to a pal about disposing of a body in quicksand near Cotswold Water Park.

Razzell had been refused release on three separate occasions and in 2021, became the first prisoner to be denied parole under Helen’s Law.

Named after Helen McCourt, who was murdered in 1988 and whose killer never revealed where her body was, Helen’s Law compels the Parole Board to consider a prisoner’s refusal to reveal the victim’s remains when assessing their suitability for release.

Despite previously being denied release, in January this year Razzell was granted parole as he went before the board yet again.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In her ruling, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said Linda’s loved ones had “described their suffering with remarkable moral clarity”.

She added: “The on-going agony of not being able to lay their beloved mother to rest and the regular pain of having to write down how they are coping with the hurt that invades so much of their lives should have rung in the defendant’s ears. Perhaps it does?”

News.title: Moment drink driving mum ploughs into parked car before smashing into house on her way to pick up kids
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a drink driving mum ploughs into a parked car before smashing into a house while on her way to pick up her kids.

Tamara Bowen, 44, has avoided jail after she drove into Jill Robinson’s bungalow in Strood, Kent, last October.



Footage shows Bowen’s silver Vauxhall Astra ramming into a parked Volkswagen Polo, pushing it a short distance, driving into the front of the home.

Jill described how she was in her kitchen when she heard a “bang” and “crash”, but thought a picture might have fallen off the wall – only to discover part of the bumper of a car was now inside her bedroom.



The mum-of-two pleaded guilty to being twice the drink-drive limit when she smashed into the house, knocking down the walls and leaving it too “structurally insecure” to live in.

Jill, who is 84 and has terminal leukaemia, was forced to live in a Premier Inn until May 1 when it was finally safe to return.



At Maidstone Magistrates’ Court, police bodycam footage was played and showed officers checking on Bowen and asking her what had happened.

She responds from between the seats and the airbags, saying “I don’t know”, before telling the officer she doesn’t need an ambulance.

Leaving the vehicle with paramedics, Bowen can be seen wearing a jumper and joggers and later told them she had been drinking at home before the 8pm incident.

Prosecutor Lucie Fish said: “She [Bowen] was going to collect her children. If it had been 10 minutes earlier, Jill would have been in her room. She could have been seriously hurt.”



In her victim impact statement, Jill said: “This incident has completely turned my life upside down. I have terminal leukaemia… living in this hotel has made everything so much worse.”

Helgaardt Strydom, defending, told the court that Bowen was of previous good character and had entered a guilty plea at the earliest opportunity.

He said: “She tried to move or fix the carpet in the footwell while she was driving and that was the main reason the accident took place.”



Mr Strydom explained Bowen had come out of an abusive relationship and drinking had become a “coping mechanism”.

He told the court she had since recognised the drinking problem and engaged with The Forward Trust, a charity that helps people with drug and alcohol dependence.

As the defence solicitor explained that Bowen risked losing her own house because her husband had not been paying the mortgage, she began to cry.

Bowen was given a 12-month custodial sentence, suspended for 18 months, and an alcohol abstinence and monitoring requirement for 120 days, which uses an electronic ankle tag that tests sweat.



She has also been disqualified from driving for 28 months and must carry out 15 rehabilitation activity requirement sessions.

Bowen was ordered to pay a £187 victim surcharge and a contribution to prosecution costs of £85, which she will repay at a rate of £20 a month.

Reacting to the sentencing, Jill said it felt like Bowen was “getting off lightly”, but after the proceedings she described feeling “content”, adding: “She deserves every bit of it.”

Now back home, the mum-of-three is happy justice has been served, but she’s still dealing with the effects of the crash.

“I’m still not sleeping at night,” she added. “I don’t think she’s sorry; she doesn’t show any remorse or regrets at all.



“How can a person do that when they’re going to pick up their children? You don’t do that sort of thing.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Jill says she broke down twice while living out of a hotel room, but she expressed her gratitude for the team who kept her spirits up.

“If it wasn’t for the staff, I don’t think I’d have survived it. Those staff and guests were what got me through it.”

News.title: Nearly 30 sharks suddenly wash up along popular beach as expert warns there may be ‘something in the water’
News.content:
NEARLY 30 dead sharks have mysteriously washed up on a popular beach as an expert warns there may be “something in the water” killing the beasts.

Dozens of the dangerous predators suddenly appeared along the shore overnight confusing locals and scientists with no one knowing what’s behind the shocking deaths.



Alarms were first raised by local Michelle Greening who went for a morning walk and noticed dozens of sharks had washed up on the beach.

Growing concerned, Michelle carried on walking and counted 29 of the animals lying dead on the shore in Sea Isle City, New Jersey.



The appearance of the sharks, believed to be dogfish or Squalidae, sparked fears among locals that there could be a toxic substance in the sea.

Michelle told CBS News: “All of a sudden, you start seeing a concentration of small sand sharks, and I thought, ‘well, this is odd’.

Read more in US news ONCE BITTEN Fears over shark attacks after internet trend draws predators closer to shore



“The first couple weren’t too surprising, but when I saw three and four and five, I knew something was up.”

Michelle also noted several of the animals had worrying red markings on the underside of their stomachs.

Despite the toxins theory, no other fish or humans who entered the water fell sick or died.



Marine science professor Stephen Nagiewicz told 6ABC: “One theory is that there’s something in the water, and they got sick and died.

“That’s probably unlikely since people haven’t been affected.”

The reason behind the tragic shark deaths still remain a mystery.

Professor Nagiewicz says he would bet it’s likely the sharks were accidentally caught up in fishing nets before being chucked over the side of boats.



He added: “They dumped them over the side or lost a net with all the things in there by accident, and all those sharks just floated up on the beach with the tides.”

Dogfish sharks can grow to be 5ft in length.

The predators swim in huge schools of hundreds or even thousands, Nagiewicz said.

Fishermen often call the predators “junk fish” because they gobble up bait that they use to reel in tastier sea animals.

The sharks have seen a decline in numbers as they are frequently caught in nets.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Dogfish and other small sharks can also come close to the shore to search for food before being trapped by changing tides, according to the New Jersey Division of Fish and Wildlife.

An investigation into the mysterious mass shark deaths is underway.

News.title: Kids want to ban homework and let animals visit them in school
News.content:
HAPPY LIFE Kids want to ban homework and let animals visit them in school

THE top things children would do to make the world a better place include banning homework, helping those in need more, and taking better care of the planet.

A poll of 1,000 six to 16-year-olds found 42 per cent would introduce longer playtimes, build more parks and playgrounds (43 per cent), and make everyone happier by giving them more time to rest (37 per cent).

While 83 per cent think more time for drawing, making and inventing things would make people happier.



More than eight in 10 (83 per cent) would make it their mission to help others more if they were in charge instead of grown-ups.



And 92 per cent feel it’s important to make sure nobody feels left out or alone – so would include everyone in games (31 per cent) and sit with people who are lonely (34 per cent).

A spokesperson for the creative play and stationery experts, Maped Helix UK, which commissioned the research, said: “Kids have the most fascinating imaginations, filled with care and compassion, but also plenty of honesty.

“What’s so heartwarming from this research is just how instinctively children want to look after each other – whether that’s helping someone in need, making sure nobody feels left out, or simply putting more time aside for play and creativity.

“It really shows that, at their core, children aren’t thinking about big, complicated fixes – they just want a kinder, happier world where everyone feels included.”

The study also showed if children saw someone being picked on, they’d tell a teacher or grown-up (46 per cent), help them or stand by them (37 per cent) or ask someone else to help (10 per cent).



When asked what is the nicest thing to do when someone feels sad or lonely, 31 per cent said talk to them, 28 per cent would make them laugh and 19 per cent would ask them to join in.

While just 14 per cent of the kids polled via OnePoll.com thought grown-ups always listen to children’s good ideas, 75 per cent admitted adults did listen – sometimes.

However, nearly one in 10 (eight per cent) of the youngsters said adults never listened at all.

Playing with friends (66 per cent), doing something fun with family (61 per cent) and getting a treat or something special (55 per cent) were the top three things to make their day really great.

But laughter was not far behind since nearly half (49 per cent) said this would make their day.



When it comes to who can make the world better 43 per cent said children were best for the job although the most popular answer (70 per cent) was ‘everyone working together’.

Whereas the ‘people who make the rules’ only came in at 34 per cent, indicating kids think they’d do a better job of it.

Of the 1,000 parents also polled 85 per cent said their child’s outlook on the world was positive.

While 88 per cent agreed kids today care about improving the world, 42 per cent said their child often talks about the positive things they’d do and 78 per cent reckon their improvements would be better and are more imaginative than those of adults.

Mostly, they said kids just want to make everyone happier (44 per cent).



Nearly nine in 10 parents (88 per cent) said their child is creative and 94 per cent said free time is important for their happiness.

The top three things they felt would make the biggest difference to their young one’s happiness would be less academic pressure (39 per cent), more outdoor time and more opportunities to get creative.

The spokesperson for Maped Helix said: “The findings highlight just how positive and thoughtful children are about the future.

“It’s a powerful reminder that when children are given the space to share their ideas and get hands on, their creative minds and outlook is not only optimistic, but genuinely inspiring.”

News.title: Orphaned triplet loses her parents and both sisters in horror Colombia earthquake: ‘They were inseparable from birth’
News.content:
A TRIPLET has had her life ripped apart after losing both her twin sisters and parents in Colombia’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

Ana María Saavedra, 23, was pulled alive from the rubble of her destroyed four-storey home in Cali, the worst-hit city.



A sturdy wooden table had saved her after hiding underneath it as the building came tumbling down.

Tragically her parents Jairo Hernán Saavedra, 63, and Victoria Caicedo, 61, were found dead in each other’s arms.



Sister Sofía died trapped under a ruined staircase, while the body of the third triplet, Isabella, was recovered late last night.

Their uncle was also found dead in the ruins of the apartment block – with Ana María the only person found alive from the building so far.

Cousin Carlos Augusto Saavedra said about the rescue of Ana María: “The neighbours say they started to hear her cries and immediately came to her aid (…) and took her to the clinic.”

After suffering a fractured pelvis and multiple arm injuries, she had to undergo an operation.



Doctors are hopeful and expect her to walk again within a few weeks.

Her cousin added: “She is conscious, perfectly lucid, she speaks.”

He described the three sisters as “very joyful” and “very happy” people who “loved spending time with their families, loved music, and adored salsa.”

“They had records, organised parties with friends, and got together to listen to music,” he added.

The sisters studied marketing together, spent a final university term in France and worked side by side.



Friends described them as the best of friends.

Their parents were known locally for their festive spirit, and as big fans of salsa.

More than 281 people have been killed – many in Cali and Pereira – and nearly 4,000 wounded in the earthquake, according to the latest official figures.



The data indicated 379 people were still reported to be missing.

But hopes of finding more survivors are fading after the disaster response surpassed the crucial first 72 hours.

David Tamayo, head of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management, said late last night: “Unfortunately, we are reaching a point where the likelihood of finding survivors is dwindling, but our mission is to keep searching and find all those people who are reported missing.”



This comes as a 4.2 magnitude aftershock struck San José del Palmar, in the Chocó region – the epicentre of the earthquake – yesterday.

More than 160 aftershocks have rocked Colombia, according to the Geological Survey.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We’re pretty shaken up, but we’re in good spirits,” volunteer helper Jairo Galán said in Cali, where food and donation centres were set up.

“We can see everyone working hard to get through this very complex situation.”

News.title: Man arrested for ‘attempted abduction after approaching girl under 10 on the street’
News.content:
SNATCH FEARS Man arrested for ‘attempted abduction after approaching girl under 10 on the street’

A MAN has been arrested for “attempted child abduction” after a girl aged under 10 was approached on the street, police said.

Cops scrambled to a quiet town on the edge of the Lake District after reports of a man approaching a child at 7.45pm on Wednesday.

Officers said there was no physical contact with the girl at Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria, but that they “take such reports seriously”.

The man has since been bailed, having come forward following reports circulating online.





Detectives conducted house-to-house enquiries in the area after the incident and said they’ve increased local patrols since.

Police warned locals to be vigilant, but urged against online speculation and asked for ‘time to carry out their work and establish the factual circumstances’.

Anyone with information which may assist has been urged to contact Cumbria Police, referencing incident 264 of 12 August 2026.

People can also report online at www.cumbria.police.uk/report-it quoting the incident number, or phone 101.

News.title: Temperatures to hit 34C today after hottest day of the year – before mercury dips as thunderstorms to hit
News.content:
HOT STREAK Temperatures to hit 34C today after hottest day of the year – before mercury dips as thunderstorms to hit

TEMPERATURES will hit a balmy 34C today following the hottest day of the year – with thunderstorms on the horizon.

It comes as the UK saw astonishing highs of 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London yesterday, beating the previous record of 38C in Norfolk in June.



The Met Office has said temperatures will reach highs of 34C in the south east on Friday, dropping to 30C over the weekend.

Light rain is forecast for central and southeastern parts of England on Friday and Saturday, bringing in fresher, less humid air and possible thunderstorms.



The north of England could also see rain moving into Monday and Tuesday, but the majority will fall over Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Any meaningful rainfall across drought-ridden parts of the UK may not be seen until the end of next week, however.





Deputy Chief Forecaster, Steven Keates, said: “Many people are desperate for some rain to alleviate the impacts of the prolonged dry spell.

“There is a chance of some thunderstorms developing in central and southeastern parts of England later on Friday into Saturday, however these are very uncertain.”

Brits will no doubt be welcoming in the cooler front over the weekend, after Thursday smashed the record for the hottest day of the year yet.

Sunseekers across the country flocked to beaches as temperatures soared, with a staggering 38.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.

But while the 2026 record was broken, the highest temperature ever logged in the UK remains 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire, in 2022.



The August record similarly remains untouched, at 38.5C in Kent back in 2003.

Nonetheless, 2026 has seen countless extreme heat records broken, including this week’s four day streak which saw the mercury consistently hit 36C or above.

Chief Forecaster Neil Armstrong, said: “This current spell of extreme heat is the latest in a remarkable summer.

“Numerous temperature records have been broken and we’ve seen an exceptionally dry season across much of England and Wales too.”

Nearly 75 per cent of England and Wales is now officially in drought, with July and August experiencing record-breaking dry conditions.



Some 1,017 wildfires were recorded across England and Wales, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council.

An “apocalyptic” wildfire in Stourbridge, near Birmingham, broke out yesterday, leaving grasslands scorched and nearby homes completely destroyed.

Shocking aerial shots show rooftops ravaged by flames as the fast-moving blaze scorched 40 acres of residential land.

News.title: Farage's by-election victory won't stop questions about finances
News.content:
Nigel Farage did not turn up to savour his victory in the by-election he triggered himself.

Overnight he told a rally of Reform UK supporters he had been advised there was an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" and wanted to avoid being "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".

When the official result did come in hours later, it confirmed the Reform UK leader had indeed won this by-election convincingly with 22,239 votes, but without any serious opposition after the other main parties did not put up candidates.

Farage's allies say he has been both emboldened and re-energised by this race, and it is not difficult to work out why.

He is clearly popular in the constituency, his party has had a commanding lead in national opinion polls for much of the past 18 months, and he has achieved something remarkable in turning his upstart organisation into a mass-membership movement with a serious chance of getting into government.

But today's result won't stop the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to Reform UK, questions about Farage's friendship with a convicted fraudster, or the parliamentary investigation into why he did not register a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

And given Farage triggered this race and the result was entirely predictable, what was the point of it all?

News.title: Eurovision proposes new rules to tackle mass voting
News.content:
Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest are proposing major rule changes to discourage voting campaigns that aim to influence the results.

Under the current system, viewers can vote up to 10 times for their favourite act by phone, text message or online.

In a letter to participating broadcasters, the EBU reportedly suggested moving the vote entirely online and forcing the public to select their top three acts - instead of being able to vote multiple times for one contestant.

The EBU said politically motivated voting had become "persistent" and was seen by many as "deeply worrying". The voting rules have been under scrutiny since the Israeli government encouraged fans to register multiple votes for the country's contestant in 2025.

Yuval Raphael's song, New Day Will Rise, placed 15th with the contest's juries - but outperformed every other participant in the public vote, scoring 297 points. In the end, Raphael finished as the overall runner-up.

A number of broadcasters subsequently queried how Israel placed so highly. They pointed to the fact that official social media accounts linked to Israel's government, including that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, had asked people to vote for Raphael 20 times, the maximum allowed.

News.title: The Office's Lucy Davis 'overwhelmed' by kindness after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
The Office actress Lucy Davis has thanked fans for their "kindness and support" after revealing she has incurable breast cancer.

The 53-year-old, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom, announced on Tuesday she is "trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can".

A flood of friends, family and followers - including her comedian father Jasper Carrott, former co-star Ricky Gervais and her Office US counterpart Jenna Fischer - left public messages of support.

"Ok, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," Davis wrote on Instagram on Thursday, external.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

News.title: Mother jailed for killing baby by burning her with a hairdryer
News.content:
A mother who killed her baby daughter by burning her with a hairdryer has been jailed for six years.

Courtney Gartshore, 28, used the appliance to subject three-month-old Dahlia-Rose to "significant and sustained heat" on her head and body.

Emergency services were called to the scene at a property in Peterhead, Aberdeenshire, in September 2023, but the child had died.

Gartshore was convicted of culpable homicide - the closest equivalent to manslaughter in Scots Law - following a trial at the High Court in Aberdeen in July.

Sentencing Gartshore at the High Court in Edinburgh, judge Simon Collins KC described the case as "uniquely disturbing and distressing".

He said it was "tragic as well as terrible".

Gartshore appeared via videolink at the 25-minute hearing, during which she sobbed and wiped away tears.

The judge said Gartshore would have to live for the rest of her life knowing she was responsible for her daughter's death.

"This was a gross breach of the most basic duty as a parent," he added.

Judge Collins said her likely cause of death was hyperthermia and heat stroke.

News.title: Watch: What happens if Luigi Mangione pleads guilty?
News.content:
The case of Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York, is back in the spotlight.

His lawyers are preparing to meet federal prosecutors for a potential plea agreement, according to reports in US media.

Mangione faces two federal charges of stalking resulting in death, each carrying a maximum sentence of life in prison. It was not immediately clear which charges are under discussion.

He also faces a separate state trial over Thompson's death. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases.

News.title: NHS service admits data breach due to pager use
News.content:
The sensitive medical data of transplant patients from across the UK was routinely sent over an unencrypted pager network, an NHS service has admitted.

A BBC investigation found NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) sent the names, dates of birth and types of organs being offered or needed to members of hospital transplant teams who were using pagers, unaware they were not encrypted.

In 2019, then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock announced the NHS in England should stop using pagers by 2021, but some parts of the organisation have continued doing so.

NHSBT said it was "deeply sorry" and has reported the data breach to the Information Commissioner. It added it has now stopped sending patient data in this way.

Pagers are small battery operated radio receivers - popular in the 1980s and 1990s - that can receive short text messages, numbers to call, or alerts.

They are a one-way communication system and only able to receive messages, not send them, which was why they largely fell out of public use as more and more people started carrying mobile phones.

News.title: BBC Verify speaks to woman who filmed ICE agent pointing gun at her
News.content:
A video showing a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent pointing his gun at a woman has been viewed by millions after she shared the moment on Instagram.

Carolina Molina says she was out delivering business cards in Falls Church, Virginia, when she saw ICE agents, who then surrounded her car.

The US Department of Homeland Security said she "attempted to harm officers by weaponising her vehicle". Molina denies this.

BBC Verify assesses the dashcam footage shared by Molina. Jake Horton reports.

Produced by Tom Joyner. Graphics by Mark Edwards.

News.title: Final day of heatwave for many before weekend cooldown
News.content:
Kew Gardens in London reached 38.1C on Thursday, making it the UK's hottest day of 2026 so far, and the fifth hottest UK day on record.

It is also the second time this year that the temperature has reached 38C, after Lingwood, Norfolk recorded 38.0C on 26 June.

This is only the second time that 38C has been reached twice in the same year - the previous occasion being 2022.

Though the Met Office amber warning for extreme heat that covered large swathes of England on Thursday expired at midnight, high temperatures will linger in central and eastern parts of England on Friday.

Long spells of sunshine will lift temperatures to 29-34C (84-93F) across large parts of the Midlands, Lincolnshire, East Anglia and the south-east.

For many places it will mark a third consecutive day above official heatwave thresholds.

The heat will ease elsewhere.

Somewhat cooler conditions will begin to move into northern and western parts of the UK, although temperatures will generally remain above the norm for the time of year - widely reaching the low to mid-20s Celsius.

Many places will be dry with a mix of cloud and sunny spells although a few showers are possible, and these could be heavy and thundery in some places.

News.title: Man died after being 'trampled' by cattle on estate
News.content:
A man injured in the grounds of a National Trust estate died from "severe chest injuries" after being trampled by cattle, an inquest has heard.

John Orton, 78, a retired telecommunications engineer, died at Felbrigg Hall, near Cromer in Norfolk on 13 July.

Assistant coroner for Norfolk, Maeve Sykes, opened an inquest into his death at Norfolk Coroner's Court on Friday and said a post-mortem examination gave a provisional cause of death as "severe chest injuries".

A National Trust spokesperson said: "We have been left shocked and deeply saddened by the death of a visitor who was seriously injured while walking at Felbrigg last month."

On 13 July, Norfolk Police were called to the estate at about 11:45 BST and said despite efforts to save him, Orton died at the scene.

Following the incident, the estate was closed while inquiries were carried out.

News.title: Brothers injured by 'exploding' steam room door
News.content:
Two children from Harrogate were hurt after a steam room door shattered while they were in Turkey on a package holiday.

The brothers, who were 11 and 16 at the time of the incident, were staying at the Green Nature Diamond Hotel with their parents. CCTV footage sourced from the hotel by their father shows the moment the glass door shattered, leaving them with cuts to various parts of their bodies.

Jet2Holidays initially denied liability, but later agreed to pay Â£7,000 compensation to the family.

The travel company said: "We would like to reiterate how sorry we are about this incident."

News.title: Killer who hid wife's body refused prison release
News.content:
A man who killed his wife and refuses to reveal where her body is cannot be freed from prison, after the High Court overturned the Parole Board's decision to release him.

Glyn Razzell, 66, was jailed for life in 2003 after being convicted of murdering his estranged wife Linda, who disappeared in Swindon the year before. He has never disclosed what he did with her body.

The Parole Board decided in April that Razzell could be released as his imprisonment was "no longer necessary" to protect the public.

It is the first time the Secretary of State for Justice's power to refer the decision to the High Court has been used to overturn a Parole Board ruling.

Announcing her decision earlier, judge Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said: "I am not persuaded that the risk has diminished to such a level that offender management is capable of keeping the public safe if the defendant is released."

News.title: 'Two out of four, baby' - Hunt wins 200m as she eyes historic quadruple
News.content:
Britain's Amy Hunt charged to 200m glory to secure her second gold medal of the European Championships - but the sprinter has her sights set on a historic quadruple in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old wants to "be iconic" and become the first athlete to win four European gold medals at the same championship.

And after triumphing in the 100m on Monday, she added another gold to her collection with a season's best time of 22.19 seconds in the 200m final on Thursday.

Hunt reeled in rival and compatriot Asher-Smith down the back straight to cross the line first.

"Two out of four, baby!" Hunt told BBC TV.

"This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life."

Hunt is set to compete in the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later and says there will be "no celebrations and no champagne until Sunday night".

"I have got a debt to the ladies," she said.

"We have got to come out here and make sure we show them who the best sprinting nation is in Europe."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

News.title: 'She was just Gaynor from up the road' - villagers ready for emotional Bonnie Tyler goodbye
News.content:
There aren't many villages where you can walk into a jewellers, a hardware shop, or a cafe, and hear stories about one of the world's biggest music icons.

But in Mumbles, Swansea, Bonnie Tyler was never treated like a superstar.

To many local people, she was Gaynor Sullivan, or "Gaynor who lived up the road".

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer, who died in July aged 75, would often be seen doing her shopping or having a drink with friends.

On Wednesday it seemed only fitting that the iconic song could be heard playing throughout the village as the biggest partial solar eclipse in nearly three decades took place, with Spotify streams of it almost doubling.

As locals prepare to say goodbye to Tyler, who split her time between the Mumbles and a home in Portugal, it's ordinary moments that people seem to remember most.

On Saturday, hundreds of people are expected to line the streets of Newton Road to pay their respects, as Tyler's coffin makes its way through the village to her home on Mumbles Road.

A service will then be held in St Mary's Church in Swansea city centre on Monday, for family and invited guests, before the cortege makes its way to her birthplace of Skewen, Neath Port Talbot.

News.title: Ice cream man hit with noise complaint over van's music
News.content:
An ice cream man has been hit with a noise complaint by someone who did not like the loud chimes from his van.

Mark Edwards was contacted by the council after a Tonyrefail resident complained about the van's music being played in the evening.

He said he had been serving the area for more than 20 years without a complaint and was determined "not to let one individual spoil it for everybody else". He has agreed with customers to beep his horn in each street so they know he is there.

Rhondda Cynon Taf council said it received a noise complaint in June relating to music being played after 20:00 BST, which it investigated and found to be valid.

Edwards, from Trebanog, was taken aback when he found a letter from the council on the van's dashboard: "Twenty-odd years and I have never had anything like this at all. It's unbelievable."

He said his employer told him to stop operating in the area because continuing to use the chimes could result in a fine, but he did not want to stop serving customers, so came up with the alternative plan.

"I thought 'I'm not going to let one individual to spoil it for everybody else', so have come to an arrangement with my customers in the area.

"They know roughly what time I'm there and I toot the horn in each street, and they all come out and enjoy it. They're not going to beat me."

The council said the law required a 19:00 cut-off time for ice cream van operators to use their chimes, but it did not "prevent them from trading after this time".

It said Edwards had been sent a letter reminding him of these requirements and that it considers the matter closed.

News.title: It's in my soul - actor brings small town novel to big screen
News.content:
What happens when you bring together a group of friends desperate to escape their small town lives, a ceasefire and 1990s rave culture?

The answer - Skintown, actor and author CiarÃ¡n McMenamin's debut novel which is about to hit the big screen at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.

The Hope Street star's 2017 novel is based on his hometown and will premiere this weekend.

"To get to this stage is a joy really, and the Edinburgh Festival - you couldn't get a better festival for this film," said McMenamin.

He said this will be the first time he will see the entire film "from start to finish".

"It's the best film for that market and it's the coolest festival so we're very excited about it."

McMenamin was born in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, and the title of his novel and film comes from the town's nickname.

Directed by Kieron Walsh, Skintown stars Jack Rowan, Chris Walley, Hope Ikpoku Jnr and Derry Girls' Jamie-Lee O'Donnell.

Nigel Farage has been re-elected as MP for Clacton, comfortably beating Count Binface and 32 other candidates to reclaim the seat he quit two months ago.

But the Reform UK leader was nowhere to be seen when the result was declared, having pulled out of the count at the last minute over what his party called a “credible threat” against him – a claim Essex Police say they never made.

Critics questioned why, after winning “fairly convincingly”, he decided not to face the cameras or his own volunteers.

Within hours of his win, the parliamentary standards investigation into an undeclared £5m donation from the crypto tycoon Christopher Harborne – paused when he resigned – was reopened.

Independent readers had plenty to say about the missing “credible threat”, the £5m question that still won’t go away, and what the numbers actually say about his mandate.

Here’s what you had to say:

An insult to the voters of Clacton

The BBC have confirmed with Essex police that there was no “credible threat”. Not turning up to the count is an insult to the voters of Clacton and to all those who worked through the night to bring him the result.

SallyLunn

A closer look at the turnout numbers

An interesting result, considering the last few elections. I wonder whether, had the other major parties stood, Mr Farage might have been lucky to squeeze in, bearing in mind the proclivities of the Clacton electorate:

2026 turnout 44% (Reform 63%, Binface 27%, Rejoin EU 1%) – 2024 turnout 58% (Reform 46%, Conservative 28%, Labour 16%) – 2019 turnout 61% (Conservative 72%, Labour 16%, Lib Dem 6%)

IndyReader

Demeaned and humiliated by nobodies

‘I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies.’

Is this how Farage sees the people of Clacton who have just re-elected him? You can only feel sorry for those taken in by the guff and propaganda.

Ambigirls

For the best comment, analysis and opinion from across The Independent, 

I know who I believe

He said he was advised by the police not to attend the count because of the risk of significant disruption. The police have stated that they didn’t advise any candidate not to attend. I know who I believe. Perhaps he stayed away in order to sort out his story regarding the £5 million ‘gift’.

GrymSdijk

Farage actually gained votes

Farage actually increased the number of votes and his share of the vote. He got over a thousand extra votes in 2026 – up from 21,225 in 2024 to 22,239.

qball101

Set himself up for the fall

Le Petit Fromage did a runner because he’s having a strop. He was hoping to avoid accountability and scrutiny over his dodgy financial affairs, but has now realised he set himself up for the fall. Facing voters and the media would have exposed him to further embarrassment.

Regardless, the inquiry into his dodgy £5m bung will continue whether he likes it or not. The thing with Farage is he thinks the UK is like the US. He remains just another MP, one out of 650, and all the rules still apply to him.

Tabbers

He threw everything at this by-election

Nigel Farage threw everything at this by-election – he even abandoned the Manchester Mayoralty election, diverting his activists nationally to Clacton. He had no credible opposition party against him, only a satirical bin from outer space. Farage gained just a thousand more votes than in 2024, yet Reform UK are 50 per cent higher in national polls than they were then.

wolfie

The £5m is not going away any time soon

The £5m is not going away any time soon. Farage says the gift was fine because he wasn’t an active politician at the time. That is not how the member’s interest register works for new MPs – they’re all given the same wording, that they had to declare benefits others might reasonably think could influence their votes or actions. It isn’t a matter of proving an MP was influenced, just that they might have been. So do you think £5m might influence someone’s actions?

avidmidlandsreader

What happens if Labour can’t deliver by 2028

“But while he may have won the battle for the constituency of Clacton, he still risks losing the fight for the country,” says Kate Devlin. That might be true today. But if Labour fail to ease people’s material conditions by 2028, I think people will turn to Reform in the hope their radical solutions will help them.

NineyTheObserver

He doesn’t want to be asked questions

The investigation into Farage made him panic enough to resign as an MP to trigger the by-election in Clacton – because if there was no investigation, he wouldn’t have even resigned.

He was not at the count because he wouldn’t feel safe, but he doesn’t want to be asked questions about his dealings with George Cotterell and the £5m donation. Those who voted for Farage do not care that he never visits Clacton, as he’s too busy living the life of a multi-millionaire to really care about his constituents.

Stacey Benoit

He chose not to declare the £5m

Anderson has basically said Essex Police are lying in their statement. No surprise – he’s hardly likely to say Farage didn’t want to thank the council staff, his volunteers or his voters, or that he was scared of the photos of Count Binface and all the other novelty candidates going viral.

Farage got himself into that position by calling a by-election – because it’s reasonable for people to think £5m might influence any given MP.

avidmidlandsreader

The boss of insurer Aviva has urged the new Chancellor not to “fly kites” with prospective policies ahead of the October budget after last year’s speculation around pension changes.

Chief executive Dame Amanda Blanc said widespread rumours that the Government might cut or restrict the 25% tax-free pension lump sum ahead of the autumn budget in 2025 led to a surge in early withdrawals.

She revealed she made the plea to clamp down on pre-budget policy speculation directly with Chancellor John Healey at a recent event to avoid policyholders making rash decisions with long-term consequences.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will present the autumn budget on October 28 (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

Dame Amanda said she wants the Government “to not fly kites” ahead of the Budget on October 28.

She said: “We do not want to see new things every week in the press around what might happen in the run-up to the budget.

“That is not very helpful, because what we do not want is for customers to make decisions that they will regret in the long run when policies are not changed.”

She said the group saw a “significant” amount of money withdrawn from pensions due to the worries over impending tax-free lump sum changes, with former chancellor Rachel Reeves ultimately not altering the rules at least autumn’s fiscal event.

“Customers would have been better to wait and see what the Government was going to do,” said Dame Amanda.

“Once you’ve made the decision to take your tax-free lump sum, you cannot reverse the decision.”

She said Mr Healey had made the commitment in person to her at the recent event not to pre-brief on possible policy changes ahead of the Budget.

She also backed wider industry calls for the Government not to alter the tax-free lump sum allowances.

“We would definitely concur that it’s something that shouldn’t be touched,” she said.

She added the Government should be “encouraging people to save into their pension” and not “double-taxing people”.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities, to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode.

“As has always been the case, the Chancellor will set out decisions at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

Aviva’s budget plea came as the firm reported better than expected half-year earnings and cheered action to “quickly” improve profitability at Direct Line since buying the firm in a £3.7 billion deal.

The group posted a 24% surge in operating profits to £1.33 billion for the six months to June 30.

It said the firm had already started to turn around the performance at Direct Line following the acquisition in July last year, boosting price comparison website sales.

Dame Amanda said: “We are making very good progress with the integration of Direct Line.

“We have quickly improved Direct Line’s profitability, grown price comparison website sales and maintained excellent levels of customer service.

“We are well on track to deliver all the financial benefits of the acquisition.”

Aviva revealed in November last year it was doubling aims for cost savings following the Direct Line deal, having met the £100 million original cost-saving target ahead of plan.

The FTSE 100 firm now expects to strip out £225 million in costs by 2028 following the deal, though it said at the time this was not set to involve further job cuts, with Aviva having already signalled last December that up to 2,300 jobs could go under the cost-cutting plans.

The results showed on a bottom line basis, interim profits nearly halved to £418 million from £819 million a year earlier due to a hit from hedging for interest rate and equity exposures, as well as Direct Line integration and restructuring costs.

Aviva also lowered the outlook for its health division, saying it now expects the division to deliver full-year operating profit of £90 million compared with its previous guidance for around £100 million.

This is due to “slowing market growth” in consumer and small business markets, according to Aviva.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal in talks with England defender and eye Osimhen, Chelsea’s Enzo Fernandez deadline looms
News.content:
Arsenal have reportedly opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over signing England international Jarell Quansah. The Premier League champions have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and the 23-year-old Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.
