“After careful consideration, New Zealand Football has formed the view that decisions and actions within Fifa have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust,” NZF said in a statement.

“NZF believes this point in time represents an opportunity for all Fifa member associations to advocate for stronger governance, accountability and transparency which are fundamental in maintaining confidence of the administration of the global game.”

The NZF chief executive, Andrew Pragnell, said that its decision to withdraw support from Infantino was based on their values. “Everyone who’s connected to the game around the globe deserves to know where we stand,” he said. “New Zealand is a country that’s always led based on its values, and we’re really proud to put those first and put the fans and the football community first, because I think right now there are some pretty strong calls for change.

“There are an incredible group of hard-working professionals at that organisation who’ve been amazing to work with and actually our thoughts are with them at this time, because it’s a difficult time for them to be in this situation as well, and that’s concerning for us.

“So, while we reflect on a lot of positives that have come out of the organisation, ultimately, this type of proposal should never have emerged in the way it did.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 9: Everton
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 10th (NB: this is not necessarily Andy Hunter’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 13th

Prospects

A season stripped of the fear of relegation, featuring more proactive, front-footed football and the return of some hope: had Everton been offered that package before their relocation to Hill Dickinson Stadium last summer it would have been accepted gratefully given the turmoil of the previous four years. For four fifths of last season it was accepted gratefully, but then came a collapse that transformed perceptions of David Moyes’s first full season back in charge. Talk of progress requires more supporting evidence this time around.

Everton were three points off the fifth and final Champions League qualification spot on 21 March having dismantled Chelsea in their finest performance at the club’s new stadium. They did not win another game all season and slumped to 13th on the final day – the same position as the previous campaign under Sean Dyche and Moyes, with only one point more but an inferior goal difference. European football may well have been an ambitious target for a club adjusting to a new home and the loss of 10 players following the expiry of their contracts, loans included. But the opportunity presented itself to Moyes’s team and they blew it.

Without the upheaval of last summer, with midfield resources improved and young players having had the benefit of a year’s experience of the Premier League, European qualification could be a more realistic proposition this season. Provided a few glaring holes in Moyes’s squad are finally filled. An upgrade on the limited centre-forward options of Beto and Thierno Barry is essential, although the latter has shown more promising signs in pre-season. Likewise a successor to Séamus Coleman – one of several big Evertonian losses behind the scenes recently. Everton’s quest for a new right-back is their very own Odyssey, while central defence was another area of concern last season. Genuine progress, the measure of which is not open to debate, rests on the final moves of the window.

Off-field picture

The consequences of Farhad Moshiri’s calamitous ownership are still being felt with Everton ordered to pay almost £40m in compensation to Burnley over the latter’s relegation in 2021-22. Everton are appealing against the can-of-worms verdict by a Premier League independent disciplinary commission, along with the biggest financial penalty ever imposed on a Premier League club, but claim their latest punishment has not affected this summer’s transfer plans. Many season ticket holders have been hit by above-inflation price increases – in some instances of almost 10% – and the club have extended a sponsorship deal with Stake, despite the UK government pledging to crack down on unlicensed gambling operators sponsoring British sports teams.

Owner-fan relationship

The Friedkin Group (TFG) has brought the financial stability that Everton desperately needed but it would be a stretch to suggest fans have connected with a low-key ownership group that rarely attend games. The man they appointed to run the club, chief executive, Angus Kinnear, annoyed supporters at the end of last season by claiming the hierarchy was “happily dissatisfied” with the first campaign at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The comment was portrayed as fresh evidence of Everton accepting mediocrity but in fairness to Kinnear, who was writing about TFG’s determination to banish the threats of financial instability, relegation and regulatory sanction, he did add: “The progress is clear but we have not achieved anything yet.”

The manager

David Moyes turns 64 in April and, while the Premier League’s oldest manager clearly retains the hunger and ambition to rebuild Everton on a stronger footing, it will be interesting to see whether he retains the appetite for a fight with his critics in the event of a poor start. Particularly as the Scotland job remains available and he would appear the ideal candidate to succeed Steve Clarke. Moyes was exceeding his brief until the dismal end to last season cost Everton a shot at Europe and placed his team selections under an unforgiving spotlight. Talk of a contract extension has since gone quiet.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Brennan Johnson struggled at Crystal Palace but could have just the attacking qualities Everton need. Photograph: Everton FC

It has been a sensible window rather than a sexy one from Everton so far – see replacing Idrissa Gana Gueye with the £7m Christian Nørgaard – but they might have delivered in swapping Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. No one would dispute that the Wales’ international’s move from Tottenham to Crystal Palace in January fell flat, least of all Palace who were willing to take a significant hit on their £35m, one-time record investment only seven months later. But if the 25-year-old recaptures the form he showed at Nottingham Forest, or when scoring 18 goals for Spurs in 2024-25, he could prove a steal who addresses several problems in the Everton frontline.

Stat attack

David Moyes loves to keep a settled side. Everton averaged the fewest changes to their starting XI of any team in the 2025-26 Premier League. With the squad looking largely the same as last season, this trend should continue. But what if injuries bite?

Set for a breakthrough

Tyler Dibling would have been a strong candidate for this category last summer following his arrival from Southampton for an initial £35m. It reflects a nonevent of a debut season on Merseyside that he can be nominated 12 months on. Everton invested a lot of time and money into their pursuit of the England Under-21 international, who remains the most expensive signing of Moyes’s second spell in charge, but the return was a huge disappointment. The attacking midfielder started only four league games and was not given a single minute after the 2-0 win over Burnley on 3 March. The manager did not hide his frustration with what he was seeing on the training ground.

World Cup impact

The longest World Cup in history should not have too onerous an impact on Moyes’s squad. Only three of his players were involved and, of those, only Jordan Pickford was in action after 1 July. Pickford came in for familiar criticism following his performances against Ghana and Argentina despite reinforcing his status as England’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper across the tournament. Iliman Ndiaye started once for Senegal and was subbed in the 73rd minute with his country leading Belgium 2-0 in the last-32 tie. They ultimately lost 3-2. Nathan Patterson, whose Everton future is uncertain, featured in all three of Scotland’s forgettable group campaign.

Sports.title: Lincoln trust in double act as second-tier return starts at Middlesbrough
Sports.content:
The last thing the Championship needs is another spying scandal, so when a lorry emblazoned with KGB parked up alongside Lincoln City’s training ground on Tuesday lunchtime there was laughter as staff pondered whether the Soviet Union was examining their set pieces. It shows the relaxed atmosphere at one of the second tier’s newest clubs, one that has had a summer of change yet maintained continuity by appointing joint head coaches.

Tom Shaw and Chris Cohen have replaced Michael Skubala, who led the Imps to 103 points and promotion back to this level after 65 years away before leaving for Bristol City. It was a symbiotic appointment because while the former assistants were devising a sales pitch to the club’s hierarchy, the wheels were already in motion to promote from within. Their plan is to banish English football’s memories of Liverpool’s ill-fated pairing of Roy Evans and Gérard Houllier. The duo are doing final preparations for Saturday’s season opener at the Riverside against Middlesbrough, who have spent more than £20m on summer signings – Lincoln have spent a quarter of that across their 142-year history, indicating the task ahead.

“The difference is that they’re put together by a football club, Evans and Houllier being the prime example, it’s two men just put together and told to go and do the same job,” says Cohen in the office he shares with Shaw. “Me and Tom have formed a relationship over the last few years where the club has seen our relationship as a pair of coaches and blokes evolve. We drive in together, we drive home together, we spend all of our days together, when we’re off, we’ll have a game of golf together.

“They understand that if it is going to work with any two coaches, then this is probably the one with the best chance because we see football the same way, we see life the same way, we see our principles are very, very similar. We obviously have differences in small decisions and nuances within everything, but principally we see the way that a football club should be run and the team should play very, very similarly. That gives us a really good chance.”

Lincoln are a forward-thinking club but the latest major decision is not about experimentation. The duo fit the club’s philosophy, having worked within academies giving them the skills to develop players, as they did with Jack Moylan, who was sold to Cardiff for a record fee. Shaw and Cohen were key members of Skubala’s staff, taking on great responsibility, and Lincoln were keen to reward their progression and give the squad continuity. The players have been told not to call them “gaffer or boss”.

They complement one another, with Cohen’s focus on the defence and Shaw the attack to share the workload. The pair are rarely side-by-side on the training ground, as they seek different perspectives, whether watching a session taken by the other head coach or the former Hull defender Paul McShane, while David Preece oversees goalkeeping.

“We do get to the end of some days and we look at each other and go: ‘Thank God we’ve got each other,’” says Cohen. “Thank God there’s two of us to do that, what we’ve just created on that day on the training pitch or gameplans. I’ve been an assistant for a long time, so I’ve had that relationship with managers where I’ve had their full trust, but there is a different feel about having the final decision and being sure that you’re making the right one. To have two of us to check and challenge each other and then come out with hopefully the best logical decision for the team.” The bickering, they say, is left for golf.

View image in fullscreen Lincoln’s analysts preparing data after a training session. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian

The club have handed out 14 new contracts since promotion, in addition to two permanent signings and three loans to maintain momentum. The 2016-17 run to the FA Cup quarter-finals as a National League side brought prize money which was invested in a purpose-built training ground, having not had one before, which sits between a former RAF base and a potato field. Promotion to the Championship means more income, allowing a £9m upgrade of the ground and training site, with further expansion planned.

One of the few things the pair do apart is holiday, which is when they found out they would be taking over, with Shaw in Greece and Cohen in Spain. Shaw says: “The first two or three days of our holidays were very hectic. We signed the paperwork and then enjoyed the last few days in the swimming pool. There was some emotion in our families,” he adds, looking at a photo of Cohen and him celebrating promotion with their children. “It was just a really nice moment in our journeys and our families know each other and really get on. So just really nice for us to be doing this together and a big moment in our careers.”

The visit to Sincil Bank has been jokingly used to illustrate the impact of relegation on West Ham but Lincoln are far more than a punchline. They are in the Championship on merit, despite being the bookmakers’ favourites to go down. A deserved 2-1 away win over their divisional rivals Derby in the Carabao Cup last weekend further proved their credentials.

Cohen says: “We hope we’re underestimated, we hope the big clubs in the division when they turn up at Sincil Bank underestimate how good our players are, how good our fans are, how good our stadium is to come to. We’re hoping that clubs take us for granted or underestimate us because it just goes back to that group of players in there that we back to the absolute hilt.

“We’re bringing a couple more recruits hopefully to help with the volume of the squad but as I said all along they’re an amazing group – amazing technically, tactically – but the thing they’ve got is heart and passion which wins you games of football.”

The Riverside will be a key test of their credentials. Shaw says: “We will check and challenge each other through the week. We’ll have minor disagreements throughout the week to get to what we think is the right plan. And then by Thursday, Friday we’re super aligned and massively behind whatever decisions we’ve come to, with the support of all the people as well.”

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Arsenal offered Osimhen in exchange deal? Newcastle to make Baleba bid?
Sports.content:
As these glorious pages reported on Thursday, Galatasaray wanted Gabriel Martinelli. In the following 24 hours things changed a bit, creating greater complexity, something we do not approve of. Arsenal have supposedly been offered the chance to involve the Nigeria striker Victor Osimhen in exchange for the Brazilian, which could be temptong for a side looking for a new No 9. To further sweeten any potential, Ethan Nwaneri could be chucked into it too to make it a mega swap.

Tijjani Reijnders may struggle to find a perfect role within Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City. The Dutchman has already been linked with Nottingham Forest, which has stirred some interest in Saudi Arabia from Al Qadsiah, who are managed by Brendan Rodgers and are willing to cough up £51m for the midfielder.

Newcastle are also searching for a central midfielder after losing Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães to Spurs and Arsenal. They did at least get around £175m for the pair, so are eyeing up a deal for Brighton’s Carlos Baleba. Rafik Belghali could head to St James’ Park if the Magpies are willing to stump up £12m for the right back.

Leeds are trying to progress a move for Nico Elvedi from Borussia Mönchengladbach, where the centre-back played under Daniel Farke. The 29-year-old wants out and only has a year remaining on his current contract, so will almost certainly end up at Elland Road.

There is very little like the signing of a third-choice goalkeeper to get fans excited. Nottingham Forest are giving their people what they want by bringing in the former Swansea stopper Steven Benda for nothing. One assumes he will be met at East Midlands Airport by thousands of excited supporters eager to welcome their new hero.

Down at Crystal Palace, getting greater strength in depth is part of the plan. Anan Khalaili is set to help out with that by joining from Union Saint-Gilloise to provide competition for Daniel Munoz at right-back. Palace could be involved in a battle royale for the services of Lecce centre-back Tiago Gabriel, who is valued at £25m. Bournemouth are also tracking the defenders who was previously the subject of a bid from Benfica.

It transpires that Wilfried Zaha is out of work so is back training at Crystal Palace to keep fit. Would he be worth a punt for the Eagles? He came through the ranks at Selhurst Park and returned for a second spell after things did not work out at Manchester United.

Sports.title: How will the three promoted teams fare in the Premier League?
Sports.content:
Coventry

A quarter of a century after their last appearance in the Premier League – following financial ruin, ground-sharing in Northampton and Birmingham and even a spell in League Two – Coventry have finally completed their comeback story. But the bunting has been packed away and they now face the daunting task of proving they belong in the top flight.

Frank Lampard is not starting from scratch. Coventry’s success last season was a collective effort and a product of smart recruitment over the past few years. The result was a side that overwhelmed the Championship with a fearless front-footed approach without relying on a single scorer. Seven Coventry players scored seven or more league goals.

They led the division for shots on target; they ranked second for big chances created, touches in the opposition’s final third and touches in the penalty area; and they produced direct attacking speed and passes-per-sequence numbers comparable to some of the Premier League’s most direct sides, including Brentford and Bournemouth.

The title was wrapped up with three games to spare; they conceded the fewest goals in the division (45 in 46 games), and their 97-goal haul was the fourth highest in a 46-game Championship season, behind only Fulham in 2021–22, Bournemouth in 2014–15 and Reading in 2005–06. Given the success Fulham and Bournemouth have enjoyed in recent years, Coventry will hope that proves a good omen.

Continuity is going to be central to their hopes of survival. They are not following in the footsteps of Sunderland, who spent around £155m last summer. Coventry’s net spend was around £3.5m last summer and just 17% of minutes on the pitch last season went to newcomers. Their best business in the transfer window was holding on to players such as Jack Rudoni and Milan van Ewijk, who were attracting interest from top-flight clubs.

View image in fullscreen Coventry captain Matt Grimes and manager Frank Lampard hold the Championship trophy. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

They have not gone wild this summer but they have invested. Coventry have signed centre-back Aurèle Amenda from Eintracht Frankfurt, winger Loum Tchaouna from Burnley, and midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjaelland while also securing permanent deals for Frank Onyeka and Carl Rushworth, who were both at the club last season. They have also brought back former favourite Gustavo Hamer after his spell at Sheffield United.

Lampard’s biggest challenge will be adapting a style built to dominate in the Championship into one capable of surviving the Premier League. Their direct, attacking approach will be riskier against opponents who possess the pace, quality and tactical sophistication to punish a rushed pass or a risky vertical ball.

Coventry will not have the same territorial control or volume of chances they enjoyed last season either – they need players who can get them up the pitch. Haji Wright’s pace and ability to attack space should be valuable, but Ellis Simms, who tends to thrive attacking the penalty box, will need service.

Hull City

The fact that Hull City are playing in the Premier League this season borders on miraculous. This is a side that survived relegation to League One on goal difference the season before last, entered last season under a transfer embargo, scraped into the playoffs by beating Norwich on the final day of the season, and scored a stoppage time winner in the playoff final. No one backed them in their pre-season predictions, and yet, under the guidance of the relatively unknown Sergej Jakirovic in his first season in charge, they defied the statistics.

If matches in the Championship last season had been decided by expected goals, Hull would have finished second from bottom. The glaringly obvious problem was at the back. They conceded 66 goals, giving them the fourth worst defensive record in the Championship. Looking back at the last 15 teams to be promoted to the Premier League, only Southampton (who conceded 63 goals when they were promoted to the 2023-24 season) have come close to that tally and they went on to concede 86 goals in the top flight, finishing rock bottom with just 12 points.

If that wasn’t bad enough, Hull were lucky to not concede more: opponents failed to convert 10 opportunities where they had at least a 50% chance of scoring according to xG – the most of any side in the league. Hull simply have to improve as fortune does not tend to stick around long when you’re in the Premier League.

There are some reasons for optimism though. Their form against the top teams in away matches was impressive. They conceded just eight goals in their matches at the teams in the top 10; they did not concede in either of their games against Coventry; and they didn’t concede in any of their playoff matches.

View image in fullscreen Hull City players celebrate reaching the Premier League with a victory parade. Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PA

Jakirovic showed an impressive knack of switching tactics depending on who his side faced or how a game was evolving. His switch from their usual 4-2-3-1 formation to a back three with wing-backs in the second leg of their playoff tie against Millwall was perhaps the most telling example of this succeeding as they caught Millwall by surprise, winning 2-0 at the Den. If continuity is the key word in Coventry’s fight for survival then chaos seems to be Hull’s. You don’t really know what to expect from them. Striker Oli McBurnie pointed this out last season: “It’s probably hard to gameplan against us, because we play so many different ways against different teams.”

As well as their unpredictability, this team has heart. They defied all expectations to reach the top, overcoming a relegation battle, a transfer embargo and statistical odds. Jakirovic put their success down to the bond they have forged. “It was like a puzzle,” he said. “Maybe it was the best that it happened like this. This group of players became even closer. They had to stick together and help each other.” As Robert Earnshaw, who played for Derby in their disastrous 2007-08 campaign, has warned: “You can relegate yourself based on how you think. It was almost as if everyone gave up. It was 20 games to go and it was like: ‘We’re never going to do it.’” This Hull side has fight and that should count for something.

Ipswich Town

Two years ago Ipswich entered the Premier League as one of football’s feelgood stories. After 22 years away from the top flight, Kieran McKenna took them back to the top through back-to-back promotions, turning a squad largely built for League One into top-flight contenders. The 2023-24 campaign was fuelled by fearless, attacking football, late goals and a sense of togetherness, with Ipswich finishing second behind Leicester and becoming the first side in 12 years to climb from League One to the Premier League in successive seasons.

McKenna’s side had an established core who had grown together and exceeded expectations but they were small fish in a very big pond, and the Premier League quickly exposed the gulf in quality. Ipswich won just four games, conceded 82 times and finished 19th with 22 points. Their immediate return to the top flight, fuelled by Premier League experience and parachute payments, means this is a very different promotion story – less about underdogs defying expectations and more about a club that is aiming to belong in this league.

Their recruitment in 2024 suggested they had one eye on a return to the Championship. They brought in top Championship players who had potential but were not proven at the top: Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O’Shea and Jacob Greaves. The club’s CEO, Mark Ashton, says they have to be “a bit braver” this time around. Rather than focusing on potential, they want to sign battle-ready, established top-flight performers.

Florentino Luís and Sasa Lukic bring the physicality and ball-winning presence the midfield lacked in 2024-25, while Issa Diop adds Premier League experience at the back. At the other end, with no Ipswich player scoring more than 10 non-penalty goals last season, Emersonn gives them a physically imposing striker, while Daizen Maeda and Abdul Fatawu add running power and intensity. Crucially, a lot of these players have Premier League experience and, with O’Shea, Clarke, Greaves and Jaden Philogene remaining from the season they went down, this is a side that looks more ambitious and ready to compete.

Their defence also looks far more equipped for the top flight. They had the second best defensive record in the Championship last season, keeping 17 clean sheets and conceding just 47 goals (10 fewer goals than when they were promoted in 2023-24). This is not the chaotic and entertaining side that got them to the Premier League two years ago, but a more patient team that knows how to be pragmatic and aggressive.

The biggest negative is the departure of the man who guided them back to the Premier League, with Kieran McKenna stepping away from football to take a break. Gary O’Neil, his replacement, has experienced Premier League relegation battles with Bournemouth and Wolves but it will be difficult to replace the identity, relationships and collective belief McKenna spent five years building through three promotions in four years, and 105 wins in 222 games. O’Neil is inheriting a more expensive and talented side than Ipswich had two years ago, but he will have to hit the ground running and help a host of new players to adapt quickly.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Rangers crash out of Europa League as Derek McInnes’s winless start goes on
Sports.content:
Derek McInnes’s fledgling tenure as Rangers manager is in disarray after his side exited the Europa League qualifiers with a 3-2 aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok after drawing 1-1 at Ibrox.

Rangers had lost 2-1 in the first leg in Poland last week but there was optimism when the captain, Lawrence Shankland, levelled the tie on aggregate with a penalty on 19 minutes.

However, in the 65th minute, the visitors deservedly equalised through the attacker Nik Prelec and the disjointed home side could not get a foothold in the game again despite changes in formation and personnel, with the boos ringing out around the ground at full time from fans frustrated at the dismal start to the season.

McInnes has failed to register a win in four competitive matches since moving from Hearts in the summer and the dispiriting performance means Rangers will take on Jablonec, from Czechia, in the Conference League playoff round.

Hearts, meanwhile, restored some pride in a 1-1 draw with Benfica as they too dropped out of the Europa League.

Tómas Magnússon had the home fans dreaming of a famous win over their illustrious opponents after firing in the opener in the 77th minute. But the Portuguese giants, cruising from a 6-1 first leg win a week earlier, levelled less than a minute later through Dodi Lukébakio to wrap up a 7-2 aggregate triumph.

View image in fullscreen Tómas Magnússon (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring for Hearts against Benfica. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

It was nevertheless an encouraging display from Wouter Vrancken’s side against a team who made seven changes from the first leg.

The consolation for Hearts is a place in the Conference League playoffs, where they will face Rapid Vienna of Austria.

David Gray revealed his Hibernian players had their heads in ice buckets as he lauded them for “an incredible achievement” after closing out a 2-1 aggregate victory over Shkendija to set up a Conference League playoff round showdown with the Belgian side Gent. The two teams played out a tightly contested 0-0 draw in the second leg in the searing heat of the Todor Proeski National Arena.

View image in fullscreen Hibernian fans in the stands at the Todor Proeski National Arena. Photograph: Nikola Krstic/Shutterstock

“I’m delighted for the players,” the Hibs manager told BBC Sport. “It’s a brilliant time to get your first clean sheet of the season.

“I just said to the players, don’t underestimate how big an achievement that is against a really good side who made it to the knockout stages of the competition last season.

“Added to that, the conditions, the heat, we had to deal with all these things. I don’t think it was a brilliant game, but we put our bodies on the line and the attitude was there.”

Sports.title: High-flying Sirius chase shock Allsvenskan title despite losing ‘best player in league’
Sports.content:
For most teams, losing a forward with 15 goals in 15 games midway through the season, amid a historic title chase, might be cause for panic. Sirius, the runaway Allsvenskan leaders, are not most teams.

“I’m actually really confident,” says Henrik Castegren, the club captain, when asked about the team’s ability to adapt after Robbie Ure’s move to Sevilla for a club-record fee, reported to be £5.6m plus add-ons. “I’m really happy for Robbie, but also quite sad because I enjoyed playing with him a lot. I think he was by far the best player in this league for the first six months [of the season] … but, with that being said, I’m feeling quite comfortable with us moving forward.”

It helps that Sirius have been here before. They loaned last season’s top scorer, Leo Walta, to Swansea in February before the deal became permanent this summer for a fee of around £3m. Like Ure, Walta arrived at a young age, developed rapidly, caught the eye of a wealthier club and earned Sirius a significant profit, which they reinvested. That has become the blueprint for their success, allowing a club with no major honours to their name, having spent most of their existence in Sweden’s lower leagues, to compete for a first Allsvenskan title against storied rivals with far greater resources.

“One important part of our strategy is to have a lot of sellable players,” says Jonathan Ederström, Sirius’s sporting director. “We’re not the biggest in Sweden, we’re not the richest in Sweden, we don’t have the fanciest history in Sweden, but we decided that we were going to aim to become the best in terms of development. Having the best development culture, but also building a squad with mostly young players that we saw big potential in.”

In that sense the departure of Ure, a former Scotland youth international who came through Rangers’ academy and Anderlecht’s reserves before moving to Sweden at the start of last season, is a sign that Sirius’s model is working exactly as intended. “It’s such a good thing for all parties,” says Ederström. “It’s a fantastic journey for Robbie, but it’s also fantastic for Sirius.”

As well as allowing for reinvestment in the squad – Sirius have already signed Jesper Uneken, a promising 22-year-old forward from PSV Eindhoven, as Ure’s replacement, along with the Finland Under-21 midfielder Otso Liimatta from Famalicão – the fee will be ploughed back into the club’s infrastructure and facilities. “[The other advantage] is that we become more attractive as a club for other players around the world,” says Ederström. “It can be close by in Sweden but it can also be Belgium, or Netherlands, or Scotland obviously. Hopefully it helps us getting the next Robbie here.”

View image in fullscreen Robbie Ure (left) shrugs off Halmstad’s Gustav Friberg. The forward, who has now moved to Sevilla, scored 31 goals in 50 games for Sirius in all competitions. Photograph: Anders Bjurö/TT/Shutterstock

No one is expecting Uneken to match Ure’s numbers immediately and, if there is a period of adjustment, Sirius have plenty of breathing room. They are 12 points clear of second-placed Hammarby and undefeated in the league with just under half the season to play. Isak Bjerkebo, their left winger, has also been prolific, tallying 14 goals and nine assists in all competitions. They also have one of the tightest defences in the league buttressed by Mohamed Soumah, a goalscoring centre-back brought in with money reinvested from the deal that took Walta to Swansea, and a high-tempo midfield capable of harrying opponents to exhaustion.

Holding it all together is Andreas Engelmark, who was appointed head coach in January last year. The team’s ascent is all the more impressive given that his early days in charge were hard going. Sirius spent a significant portion of last season looking nervously over their shoulders, dropping to 14th, the Allsvenskan’s relegation playoff spot, for several weeks. Engelmark battled on and, despite sustaining the heaviest defeat of the season, an 8-2 loss at Djurgården in September, Sirius ended strongly. In fact, they have not lost in the league since.

“Even though he went tough when the results weren’t there last summer, he stuck to what he thought was the best going forward,” says Castegren. “That, I would say, is his biggest strength, to not give that up and start doing other short-term stuff.

“He really sees you as a player and adjusts small things to get the most out of you, and also how you can complement the team as a collective. I really feel comfortable, in that sense, now Robbie has left us, that we can find ways to get results, to perform well and play well.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Sirius fans display their scarves in the stands with the club’s meteoric rise a source of huge excitement. Photograph: Staffan Claesson/TT/Shutterstock

For people in Uppsala, the city where Sirius are based, the club’s meteoric rise has been a source of huge excitement. Attendances at their ground, Studenternas, have leapt up, while there is a buzz around the place that has energised staff and players alike. “With the results that have come, I think the city has really turned it on,” says Castegren. “You can see blue and black shirts wherever you go … you can tell also by the numbers we have at the games, in the audience. It’s a packed house every game, which you couldn’t even think would be a reality three years ago when I first came here.”

While Sirius winning the title might have seemed unthinkable a few seasons ago, there is an encouraging precedent: last season’s Swedish champions, Mjällby, were also rank outsiders who had never won a major trophy before. All three Scandinavian leagues have been won by dark horses in recent seasons, with Viking, for the first time in 34 years, the reigning champions of Norway, and Aarhus, after a 40-year wait, triumphant in Denmark.

Asked why the Allsvenskan, in particular, has been so unpredictable over the past few years, Ederström gives a concise answer: “Because the big teams underperform.” That has created an opening for insurgent clubs who scout well, recruit smartly and are willing to innovate.

There is still a way to go for Sirius, but they have good reason to believe they can finish the job. “The biggest thing for me this season is what we have created in Uppsala as a city,” adds Ederström. “To have something to believe in, to have something so important in [people’s] life … we really appreciate that.”

Sports.title: Liverpool and Man United denied one of Europe’s hottest talents as contract agreed
Sports.content:
Liverpool and Man United denied one of Europe’s hottest talents as contract agreed

Manchester City starlet Xavier Parker has agreed a new long-term contract with the club, talkSPORT understands.

The 16-year-old is considered one of Europe's top emerging talents, and had been attracting interest from rivals Manchester United and Liverpool.



4 Xavier Parker is set to end speculation over his future Credit: Getty

Parker's previous terms with the Citizens expired this summer, leading to speculation he could be on the move.

However, the highly-rated teenager is now set to commit his long-term future at the Etihad, having recently been given a taste of senior football.

He travelled with the first team on City's pre-season tour of Asia, where he was the youngest player in the squad.



Since Enzo Maresca's side returned to the UK ahead of Sunday's Community Shield meeting with Arsenal, Parker has continued to train with the first team group.

The young midfielder will sign scholarship terms before moving to a full professional contract upon his 17th birthday.



Hard sell

Parker is said to have impressed new City boss Maresca in recent weeks, and appears to have been won over by the Italian.

According to the Athletic, the youngster was taken aback by his head coach's knowledge of him, who was intent on convincing him to stay.



Maresca reportedly oversaw an individual presentation given to Parker in a bid to keep him at the club.

And it might not be long before he gets his chance under the ex-Chelsea boss, with the talented teen expected to feature for City's Under-21 team this campaign and make his senior first-team debut.

Parker starred in the Citizens' youth team last term, playing a key role as they scooped two trophies.

4 Parker played a key role as Man City won back their FA Youth Cup title last term Credit: Getty



4 Enzo Maresca made it clear he sees Parker as one for the future Credit: Getty

He was part of a young City side that retained their Under-18 Premier League North title, alongside winning the FA Youth Cup.

In this success, Parker scored six goals and provided seven assists across 21 appearances.

Next success story?

Born in London, Parker signed for Man City in 2024 after excelling in West Ham's academy.



He was the second starlet to swap the Hammers' famous 'Academy of Football' for the north west that summer, after Divin Mubama made the same move - who recently joined promotion-chasing Southampton on loan in the Championship.

And there are now high hopes that Parker will be yet another success story to come out of City's impressive youth system.

Phil Foden and Cole Palmer are the standout academy graduates to become household names, with Nico O'Reilly the latest star to burst onto the scene.

4 Cole Palmer and Phil Foden have graduated from the City academy to become Premier League stars Credit: Getty



After a breakthrough 2025/25 campaign, versatile left-back O'Reilly was named in Thomas Tuchel's England World Cup squad, going on to feature in seven of their games.

Foden is the biggest success story to emerge from the City youth ranks, becoming one of the most decorated English players after winning 19 major trophies with his boyhood club.

Meanwhile Palmer has established himself as a Premier League star since leaving the Etihad for Chelsea in 2023 for a £40million fee.

With Parker looking to follow in their footsteps, it is not yet known if he will be involved for City's upcoming Community Shield clash.



The Citizens are gearing up for the Community Shield meeting with Arsenal at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.
