World.title: Trump imposes drone tariffs of up to 100% with a lower rate for the EU and UK
World.content:
Imported drones will be taxed at rates reaching 100% under an order the US president approved on Thursday.

 

European producers escaped the harshest tariff bracket. Equipment from the bloc will be charged 15% and British-made models will face a 10% rate. Washington's argument is that the US can no longer afford to depend on foreign factories for a weapon that has reshaped the battlefield and is central to modern warfare.

US President Donald Trump used Section 232 to impose the tariff rate, the national security provision already applied to steel, aluminium, copper, cars and pharmaceuticals.

The 100% rate covers drones weighing more than 25 kilograms at take-off or carrying thermal imaging, plus their docking stations and certain critical components. Smaller, less capable models and other parts face a 25% tariff.

Alongside the EU, the 15% band covers Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Taiwan, with the UK being the only one with the lowest 10% tariff. However, the caveat matters more than the rate.

To qualify for the lower band, all of a drone's hardware, software and technology must substantially originate in those countries or the US. That is a demanding test for European manufacturers, whose motors, batteries, cameras and flight controllers are still often bought from Chinese suppliers that dominate global production.

A drone failing it does not merely lose the discount, it falls back into the 25% or 100% category, depending on size and capability.

The tariffs will take effect 21 days after the signing of the order, or 180 days for less sensitive components, and the US Secretary of Commerce has been told to design a programme rewarding companies that move production onshore.

Who in Europe is exposed

The continent's drone industry is among the fastest-growing corners of European technology, and the US its most coveted export market.

France's Parrot is the most directly exposed listed manufacturer as its ANAFI range is certified under American defence procurement rules and is the default non-Chinese option for Western police and security forces.

Germany's Quantum Systems, valued above €1 billion, sells its reconnaissance aircraft to American customers, while Portugal's Tekever, worth over €1.1 billion, has been expanding into the US.

For some, geography limits the damage.

Quantum Systems already operates production facilities in the US, and several peers have been building American capacity to satisfy procurement rules favouring domestic suppliers. For them, the tariff is an argument for accelerating plans already under way.

FILE. A drone of G-TEKG's Tekever AR5 Evolution Mk.2 is displayed during the Five Country Ministerial meeting at the Honourable Artillery Company in London, Sept. 2025 AP Photo/Kin Cheung

Part of Trump's wider military overhaul

The tariff proclamation is one of several defence measures moving at once.

On the same day, US President Donald Trump signed a memorandum ordering a fifth naval shipyard be built, the first in more than 80 years, to expand submarine and aircraft carrier repair capacity, alongside a new component repair centre and a reorganisation of the Naval Sea Systems Command.

The same order instructs the navy to abandon electromagnetic catapults on its newest carriers and return to steam.

Behind it also lies a supply problem.

US media reported that US President Donald Trump confronted US defense secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David in late July over depleted munitions stocks, after separate reporting suggested the Iran conflict had consumed much of the American inventory.

Those accounts have not been independently verified and the White House denies the exchange took place, with the US president insisting publicly that there is no shortage and calling the coverage false.

The proposed US defence budget for next year is around $1.5 trillion (€1.3bn).

World.title: Amid the Ceuta crisis, how do EU citizens view refugees?
World.content:
Migration is a hot-button issue, especially when displacements peak, such as the recent episode in the Spanish territory of Ceuta, which saw around 80,000 people cross the border from Morocco in just 48 hours at the end of July.

 

Despite the global number of refugees falling by 3% in 2025 compared to the end of 2024, according to the UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, the issue remains firmly on people's minds: Google searches on the topic have increased by 150% in the past five years.

While overall public support for offering refuge remains strong, there are still widespread doubts about whether the people claiming to be refugees are in actual need of protection, according to Ipsos Global Attitudes Towards Refugees 2026.

In general, among EU countries, support for refugees is strongest in Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain, with almost eight in 10 people agreeing that people should be able to seek refuge to escape from war or persecution.

In contrast, those in Hungary and Poland tend to show the least support among EU countries, at 54% each.

Opinions on how countries should deal with refugees vary significantly. For instance, more than half of the Hungarian, Belgian, and German respondents claim that their country should close the borders to refugees entirely and not accept any refugees at this time.

Some countries' positions have shifted over time, however: support for accepting refugees in France has climbed to 68%, up from 43% in 2019.

Do Europeans see most refugees as genuine?

Around 54% of German respondents believe many people claiming to be refugees are not genuine, as they say that these individuals appear to have adequate financial resources already, such as being able to pay smugglers or owning smartphones.

Meanwhile, 46% of Dutch respondents state that genuine refugees would seek asylum in the first safe country they reach, rather than travelling further to other countries.

In addition, more than six in 10 respondents in Germany and Ireland believe that most refugees just want to come to their countries for economic reasons or to take advantage of the country's welfare services, while respondents in Sweden and Italy tend to agree the least with that idea.

A unaccompanied minor who crossed into Spain is escorted by a Spanish soldier to the Spain-Morocco border as the child begs not to be sent back to Morocco. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue

Who do EU citizens think should assist refugees?

Three in 10 German respondents believe the governments of other wealthier nations should contribute more to assist refugees globally.

Meanwhile, the rest of the countries say that international organisations, such as the United Nations and the World Bank, should be the ones contributing more to assist refugees globally.

While not as prevalent, some respondents also support the idea that foundations and non-governmental organisations that fund charitable causes should do more to support refugee funding.

World.title: New Zealand withdraws support for beleaguered FIFA chief Gianni Infantino
World.content:
New Zealand has announced that it has withdrawn its support for beleaguered FIFA President Gianni Infantino, in a break from Oceania's governing body.

 

In a statement on Friday, New Zealand Football (NZF) said: "After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within FIFA have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust."

"NZF believes this point in time represents an opportunity for all FIFA member associations to advocate for stronger governance, accountability and transparency which are fundamental in maintaining confidence of the administration of the global game," it added.

NZF also called for an independent review into the circumstances surrounding FIFA's highly controversial - and now-scrapped - private investment plan, which would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

The NZF's move puts it at odds with the Oceania Football Confederation, which issued its own statement on Friday welcoming the decision to ditch the FFE proposal and signalling its support for Infantino.

"OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under FIFA’s leadership and encourages FIFA to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary," it said.

A deepening chasm has opened up in world football over the president's position, with regional confederations and individual nations split over whether he should continue. Infantino is due to run for re-election in 2027.

European governing body UEFA, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) have all called for a change in leadership, while South America's CONMEBOL and the Confederation of African Football (CAF) have backed Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016.

New Zealand has now joined a growing list of nations to have announced their individual stances on the issue.

Wales, Finland, Serbia, and Sweden were among the first to announce that they would no longer back the FIFA president for another term. They were followed by England, Jordan, Albania, the Republic of Ireland, and Norway - the latter of which went a step further and called for Infantino to resign.

Others such as Paraguay, World Cup runners-up Argentina, and tournament cohosts Mexico have gotten behind the FIFA boss, however.

Spain players, from left, cheer alongside President Donald Trump and FIFA President Gianni Infantino at the conclusion of the World Cup championship final. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Infantino also received backing from his friend Donald Trump earlier this week.

In a post on Truth Social, the US president said the football world governing body "would be making a terrible mistake" if it decided to part ways with Infantino.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented," Trump wrote, adding: "If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again."

World.title: Poland forces Starlink U-turn over roaming price hike
World.content:
Over the past few days, Polish media have been abuzz with dissatisfaction over Starlink’s decision to exclude Poland from the international roaming list, which may double service prices for Polish users starting on August 17, 2026.

 

Polish TVP World reports that the rules taking effect this week will increase prices for Polish customers using the service outside Poland, from roughly 42 euros to 107 euros on a 100GB roaming plan.

SpaceX's role in Ukraine

Since 2022, SpaceX has become a symbol of innovation, helping Ukraine fight the Russian invasion, showing many European governments how American innovation can be helpful in times of crisis.

The Polish government, with the help of the Polish oil corporation Orlen, has proactively helped Ukraine by funding Starlink, a point emphasized by the former Ukrainian Minister of Digital Affairs and later Minister of Defense, Mykhailo Fedorov, multiple times.

Screenshots of posts on X by former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Courtesy of EU Tech Loop

Since the start of the Russian invasion in Ukraine, despite frequent political hiccups, the Ukrainian and Polish governments have been working with SpaceX and Elon Musk hand in hand to provide access to the Ukrainian military and civilians, and disable illegal Russian use of Starlink kits.

SpaceX's role in helping Ukraine has often silenced criticism of American technology in the EU, as the EU seeks to replace it with homegrown technological solutions.

Reputational risks for SpaceX

Although SpaceX is not publicly communicating the reasons for excluding Poland from the international roaming list, this decision, if not overturned, can seriously damage SpaceX's reputation in Eastern Europe, which is traditionally more welcoming to American tech innovations.

First, as European governments invest in alternative communication channels for times of crisis and the European IRIS2 alternative will only be rolled out in 2029, Starlink kits are currently the first practical solution for governments, the military, and civilians.

Second, European governments are currently discussing the Digital Networks Act (DNA) and the Space Act, which may centralize spectrum licensing management in Brussels and introduce new rules and requirements for non-European satellite providers.

If not challenged, both of these regulations may make SpaceX's operations more costly and difficult in the European Union’s market.

Lastly, the Polish feud with SpaceX may end up influencing the rest of the Eastern European flank — bad blood between the Polish government and SpaceX may damage the company's reputation and alienate policymakers, as well as limit market development among individual users in these countries.

Happy end?

As of late Thursday, the news of Starlink reinstating Poland in the European region was shared by Janusz Cieszynski, former Minister of Digitalization of Poland.

This allows Polish customers to use Starlink services outside their country at a reasonable price, without making Polish-purchased Starlink kits more expensive in Ukraine, simultaneously dispelling speculation that the previous move was targeted at Ukraine.

According to Assistant Professor Tomasz Pugacewicz at Jagiellonski University in Krakow, Poland was previously missing from the list.

This story was originally published on EU Tech Loop and has been shared on Euronews as part of a syndication agreement.

World.title: Unprotected minors and alleged illegal returns: NGOs warn of Ceuta humanitarian crisis
World.content:
Thousands of illlegal migrants who arrived Ceuta late-July are still in the autonomous Spanish enclave while reception facilities struggle to cope with an emergency that has overwhelmed their capacity.

 

Many migrants are sleeping in the open on the streets, with residents handing out food and NGO and associations cooking non-stop for almost two weeks.

The situation is one of "complete vulnerability", Halima Ahmed, spokesperson and social educator for Ceuta-based NGO Luna Blanca, tells 'Euronews'.

There are people who eat only once a day and rely on humanitarian organisations or even on neighbours cooking food in their own homes. On its first day of response, Luna Blanca distributed 3,500 food containers and since then has continued cooking every day with the help of volunteers and donations.

Within the crisis,one particularly vulnerable group is being mentioned: children.

Among those still outside the reception system are boys and girls who have yet to enter the child protection scheme. Some of them, according to organisations working in Ceuta, remain in hiding because they are afraid to go to the centres set up by the authorities.

Knowing how many there are is part of the problem.

Around 1,500 unaccompanied minors have already been identified and are within the protection system, but Save the Children estimates that more than 4,000 are still unidentified in Ceuta.

Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco sleep on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Monday 3 August 2026. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue) AP Photo

Some are hiding or remain beyond the reach of child protection services, while reception facilities are overwhelmed.

Their situation has sparked worry and another crisis, this time a political one: the question of what to do with them hangs over the Spanish government.

While Ceuta insists it does not have the capacity to take them in on its own, the transfer of minors to the Spanish mainland is dividing Spain's autonomous communities, and the possible return of some to Morocco raises questions about the safeguards that must accompany any repatriation.

At the same time, NGOs trying to meet the most immediate needs are also facing accusations of going beyond humanitarian assistance and supposedly helping migrants leave Ceuta irregularly for the mainland. 'Euronews' has spoken to five organisations to map out a crisis where humanitarian emergency, child protection, the debate over sharing responsibility and the limits of aid all intersect.

Children at risk of violence, trafficking and exploitation

Precariousness hits particularly hard for those who crossed the border alone. "Every night a boy or a girl spends on the street exposes them to serious dangers, from a risk of violence, trafficking or exploitation to psychosocial or even health risks", warns Catalina Perazzo, Director of Advocacy and Territorial Development at Save the Children.

The organisation says that, through other groups working on the ground, it has received accounts of violence and sexual assault, although it notes that it has not dealt with these cases directly.

The problem does not affect only those who remain on the streets. Facilities opened for those already inside the protection system are also stretched to the limit. "With the resources the autonomous city has, with the reception centres and the means they have, it is impossible for them to uphold the rights of children and adolescents", says Perazzo.

Unicef shares that assessment. The agency says many minors are still on the streets and that protection centres are "totally saturated". Its immediate priority is to know how many there are, who they are and where they are. "Right now not all children in Ceuta are protected, they are not safe; they are in a situation of neglect," José María Vera, executive director of Unicef Spain, tells 'Euronews'.

We cannot play games with human rights Verónica Laorden National head of CEAR's Advocacy, Research and Studies Service

The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) also warns that minors who have not yet been identified cannot fully access the protection system or care tailored to their needs, including psychological support or legal advice. "They are in situations of abandonment", says Verónica Laorden, national head of CEAR's Advocacy, Research and Studies Service.

Organisations agree that the urgent priority is to locate, identify and protect all minors. But with reception resources at breaking point, another question immediately arises: if Ceuta cannot cope on its own, who should?

The controversial question of relocation: mainland or Morocco?

While some autonomous communities have expressed reluctance to take in unaccompanied minors, the organisations consulted by 'Euronews' argue, with varying nuances, that Ceuta cannot handle the situation alone.

For Amnesty International, the debate cannot be reduced to which regions are willing – or not – to receive minors. "The state must ensure the best interests of the child, and that best interest of the child takes precedence over other statuses, such as migration status," says Amnesty International researcher Dani Canales.

Save the Children likewise believes it is necessary to speed up the transfer of minors to the mainland, where they can be taken in while the best solution for each child is assessed individually. The organisation calls for shared responsibility between Spain's regions and reminds that managing migration flows also requires a joint response at European level.

Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco gather on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Monday 3 August 2026. (AP Photo/Antonio Sempere) AP Photo

But transfer to the mainland does not have to be permanent. Also on the table is family reunification in Morocco. Unicef, Save the Children, CEAR and Amnesty all agree that any decision must be taken on a case-by-case basis, according to the best interests of the child.

Before any return, organisations insist on checking whether the child needs international protection, listening to their wishes, locating their family and determining whether this really is a safe environment. "There can be no mass returns", says Laorden.

Save the Children also points out that the two options are not mutually exclusive: a child can be temporarily moved to another region while the authorities assess whether later family reunification in Morocco is the right solution.

When help arrives before the authorities

While institutions decide how to reorganise reception, much of the immediate response has fallen to organisations and local residents. But NGOs warn they cannot permanently replace the state.

"Humanitarian assistance cannot rest solely on organisations", says Laorden. For CEAR, once the initial days of emergency are over, it is up to the state to guarantee care and rights for those left without support.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain sleep in a warehouse near the border between Spain and Morocco, in Ceuta, on 3 August 2026. AP Photo

This is where one of the paradoxes of the crisis appears: some organisations say they have staff and resources to act, but do not always have the legal powers to intervene on their own.

Save the Children says it has offered its services both to the autonomous city and to the central government, but child protection is a public responsibility and the organisation needs authorisation for certain interventions. "Our only frustration is that we need to be given permission to do it", explains Perazzo.

The battle against disinformation

Meanwhile, accusations have circulated on social media, claiming that certain humanitarian organisations are helping migrants leave Ceuta irregularly for the mainland. These include unverified messages and images linked to people carrying Red Cross bags on a ferry.

'Euronews' explicitly asked the organisations interviewed whether they knew of cases in which NGOs had irregularly facilitated such transfers. None of the sources consulted provided any cases that would support that accusation.

The Red Cross declined an interview with 'Euronews', but denied the allegations in comments to 'RTVE Verifica' .

Amnesty International says it has also tracked other episodes of disinformation linked to the crisis, including images of disturbances presented as recent and as having taken place in Ceuta which, according to the organisation, did not match either the location or the time claimed.

For Canales, disinformation ends up pushing aside debate about an emergency in which people still need assistance and protection.

"It diverts the discussion elsewhere and does so on the basis of false information in order, in some way, to instrumentalise certain messages", he says.

Amnesty sees signs of possible rights violations

In the meantime, Amnesty International continues to gather information about the conduct of the Spanish authorities during the crisis and has raised its concerns with the Interior Minister and the government's delegate in Ceuta. Among them is the possibility that returns may have taken place without the necessary safeguards.

Canales stresses that the investigation remains open and avoids presenting the possible violations reported to them as established facts. However, he says the evidence gathered so far suggests, "at this preliminary stage", that there may have been human rights violations and "summary and unlawful returns".

The issue has taken on particular importance after Spain and Morocco agreed to step up coordination in order to repatriate "as soon as possible" people who entered Ceuta irregularly. The agreement was confirmed both by Spain's Interior Ministry and by official Moroccan sources.

This is not about criminalising people. They are not numbers, they are people Halima Ahmed Spokesperson for Luna Blanca

The criticism is not directed solely at Spain. Moroccan civil society organisations have also condemned the political use of migration by Rabat and demanded accountability for the situation driving thousands of young people to try to leave the country.

For Amnesty, what has happened in Ceuta cannot be viewed in isolation. The organisation places the crisis within a broader problem of European migration policy which, in its view, has prioritised "closing borders" over establishing "safe and legal routes for migration" and for seeking asylum.

According to Amnesty, the lack of legal alternatives is pushing some people towards increasingly dangerous routes. The organisation insists that any return, regardless of how people arrived, must respect the safeguards required under international law and allow possible vulnerabilities or needs for international protection to be identified.

CEAR also stresses that the urgency of the situation cannot justify diluting legal safeguards. "We cannot play games with human rights", says Verónica Laorden.

A city torn between solidarity and exhaustion

Almost two weeks on, Luna Blanca also describes Ceuta as a city on its knees. Ahmed talks of overwhelmed neighbourhoods, dirt and a growing sense of insecurity among some residents, but rejects the idea that this frustration should be used to criminalise all those who have arrived.

"This is not about criminalising people. They are not numbers, they are people", she says.

As the debate continues over how many minors should be moved, where they should be housed and who should take responsibility for their protection, the organisations interviewed agree that there is still one unresolved question for all of them: knowing who they are, where they are and ensuring they are safe.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Dog rescued alive as 72-hour window closes
World.content:
The animal was pulled alive from the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali as Colombian rescue teams pressed on with their search for survivors following the earthquake. The animal was carefully carried away on a stretcher and examined by veterinarians at the scene, who treated injuries to one paw and scrapes across its body. It was reported to be in a stable condition.

 

The rescue took place during the crucial first 72 hours of the operation, as teams worked through collapsed structures in Cali on 13 August, focusing on areas where people could still be trapped beneath the rubble.

The dog’s survival offered a rare moment of relief during an otherwise difficult and emotionally draining rescue effort. There were no immediate details on whether the animal’s owners had been located.

World.title: Zambia suspends vote count after violence
World.content:
Zambia has halted the counting and publication of election results after violence targeting poll workers and reports of stolen ballots. The electoral commission says it will reassess the suspension within 24 hours.

Zambia's electoral commission has suspended the counting and announcement of election results nationwide with immediate effect, citing violence directed at election officials.

The commission said ballot papers had also been stolen in some cases and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours.

Why has Zambia suspended vote counting?

The Electoral Commission of Zambia said the decision followed incidents of violence targeting polling staff.

It added that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were.

The general election is a major test for President Hakainde Hichilema, whose economic reform program has been weighed against widespread frustration over the cost of living.

Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations.

Were there problems during voting?

Long queues formed before dawn at polling stations in Lusaka, with some voters gathering around makeshift fires as they waited.

Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems.

European Union observers were monitoring the election.

Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu, who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Brian Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters.

World.title: Berlin's Russian House: A hub for propaganda and espionage?
World.content:
The "Russian House" stands in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is used to spread propaganda for Putin's Russia. Now, French authorities accuse it of espionage.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin. The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters was opened in 1984.

At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings, and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

In early August 2026, it became known that French authorities are linking the Russian House to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin this week.

In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, he emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked.

"It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other.

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency "Rossotrudnichestvo," the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad, and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian."

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.

The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party, told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany."

Symbols of frienship remain on display in Berlin's Russia House Image: Dmyrto Katkov/DW

Germany fears for the Goethe-Institut in Russia

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from open conflict over the Russian House because it fears that the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.

It was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.

Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists’ associations and political, cultural and other foundations."

However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."

This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.

Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contacts provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.

This article was translated from German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in August 2026 to reflect news developments.

World.title: Why women are breaking men's endurance records
World.content:
Sophie Woods has completed the 2,000-kilometer Via Alpina faster even than the fastest-ever man. DW explains why she is not the only woman breaking men's records in extreme sports.

New Zealand runner Sophie Wood, who competes under her maiden name, Sophie Grant, recently accomplished something truly remarkable.

Running for 29 days across the Alps, from Trieste to Monaco, Woods covered around 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) while climbing a total of more than 100,000 meters (328,083 feet) – on an average of three to four hours of sleep per night.

This made her the fastest person ever to complete the Via Alpina. The 42-year-old ultra-runner finished the route more than seven days faster than the fastest man ever to do so.

"It gives me goosebumps thinking about it, to take the overall record is amazing," Woods told DW.

"I was there for the adventure. I didn't really want to be running for longer than a month, that was enough."

The longer the distance, the smaller the gender gap

Woods is not the only woman to have broken a men's record in endurance sports in recent years.

In 2026, Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250, a race covering roughly 400 kilometers in the United States, setting a new overall course record.

A year earlier, Tara Dower ran the Long Trail in Vermont. a distance of about 440 kilometers, in 3 days, 18 hours, and 29 minutes, beating the previous men's record by 2 hours and 40 minutes.

In 2019, Germany's Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race. Cycling nearly 4,000 kilometers across Europe, she finished just under eight hours ahead of the second-placed male rider. That same year, Jasmin Paris became the first woman to win the 430-kilometer Spine Race in Great Britain, shattering the previous course record by more than 12 hours.

A comprehensive analysis by RunRepeat and the International Association of Ultrarunners examined over five million results from more than 15,000 ultramarathons. The findings showed that the longer the distance, the closer women came, on average, to matching men's times.

In 2019, Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race Image: Mateusz Birecki/IMAGO

In the events analyzed, on average, the men were still 11.1% faster. At the 100-mile mark, the gap narrowed to just 0.25%. At distances exceeding 195 miles, the women were on average 0.6% faster.

'We're good at solving problems'

So why are women able to keep pace—or better—when the physical demands increase?

Certain physiological factors may play a role. On average, women possess a higher proportion of fatigue-resistant Type I muscle fibers and rely relatively more on fat as an energy source during endurance activities.

The advantages men typically enjoy—such as greater muscle mass and higher maximal oxygen uptake—may be less decisive in ultra-long events than in shorter races.

"Probably we are better at burning fat, and therefore it makes us able to go longer," Woods said – before pointing to other possible factors.

"I think we're good at putting our egos aside. And I think we're good at solving problems."

Competing in an ultramarathon is about much more than who can run the fastest. There are key decisions to be made about sleep, nutrition and physical pain. That's where her team comes in.

"I just put my life in their hands," she said.

"You kind of control everything you can and then you just throw it into chaos and see what comes out in the wash."

As little as 90 minutes of sleep, 7,000 calories a day

The extreme physical strain was evident in her sleeping patterns – towards the end, she was sleeping as little as 90 minutes a night. When she simply couldn't go any further, she would lie down right next to the trail.

"You just curl up on the side in a little mossy glen and hope that no one thinks you've died," she said.

"The sleep deprivation was one of the hardest parts of the whole thing."

Her alarm would often go off again as early as three in the morning.

Sophie Woods broke both the women's and men's records on the Via Alpina Image: Ulrich Wagner/IMAGO

At the same time, maintaining her physical energy was a huge problem, with her team estimating that she was consuming between 6,000 and 7,000 calories a day – through sports drinks, soft drinks, as burritos, falafel wraps, sandwiches, pasta, and McDonald's food. She ate much of this while on the move.

In the Dolomites, heat and pain added to the challenge.

"I bawled my eyes out in the Dolomites," she said.

"I was really hot. I was really sore. I was really swollen. I was shuffling along and I was just like: I don't know if I can do this."

Despite it all, she carried on.

Women long neglected in sports research

Despite setting the record, Woods wonders what she and other women could achieve if their bodies were studied as thoroughly as men's.

"As a woman, you need to be very careful when you read these studies to actually see who they are studying, because often it will be 10 male cyclists," Woods said.

"We have just been left behind in all of the research for decades," she said.

"As women, we are fighting for crumbs in the sporting world. We are fighting for more coverage, we are fighting for more research, we are fighting for more sponsorship."

The fact that several individual men's records have been broken by women doesn't mean that women are inherently better endurance athletes than men. Men still hold many records and are, on average, significantly faster over shorter distances.

However, in an interview with the BBC, sports physiologist Nicholas Tiller described very long endurance events as "the great equaliser."

Woods is simply not interested in who holds the advantage on paper.

"I think the bravest thing to do is to try," she said.

"Try the scary thing. It doesn't matter what happens in the end because at least you've tried."

World.title: Germany news: Wildfire forces evacuations in western woods
World.content:
08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Several people were injured Friday morning when fire broke out in a 21-story apartment complex in Berlin's Friedrichshain neighborhood, near the Ostbahnhof train station.

The blaze started on the 11th floor, say firefighters, and quickly spread to floors above.

A fire department spokesperson described the situation as "dramatic."

Witnesses say numerous residents stood at windows and balconies prepared to jump rather than be consumed by smoke and flames.

Although jump cushions were installed as a precaution below, these were not used and authorities say residents were retrieved from a stairwell with a rescue ladder.

Some 130 fire, police and emergency services personnel were in action before residents could be saved and the fire extinguished.

Smoke damage is said to have been extensive, causing at least five injuries, and leaving roughly 70 people to be cared for on site.

The cause of the fire is unclear, though police are treating it as a possible balcony fire.

World.title: Hunger stones: The history behind 'if you see me, weep'
World.content:
Centuries-old hunger stones are emerging as Europe's rivers recede. Among the most famous is the Decin hunger stone in the Elbe River with its cryptic message.

As Europe's rivers recede during periods of drought, long-hidden traces of the past have resurfaced.

Alongside Nazi-era shipwrecks, unexploded World War II bombs and prehistoric mammoth remains, some rivers reveal history literally written in stone.

One such inscription, in German, reads: "Wenn du mich siehst, dann weine" — "If you see me, weep."

These words are etched on a hunger stone in the Elbe River near Decin in Czechia, close to the German border.

The 2026 drought has revealed historical artifacts lying under Europe's rivers, like this century-old shipwreck in Croatia Image: David Jerkovic/Pixsell/IMAGO

Why 'hunger'?

Hunger stones, or "Hungersteine" in German, are riverbed boulders that usually stay underwater and hidden, but become exposed when river levels drop significantly during prolonged droughts.

Unlike a high-water mark, which records the highest water level, the hunger stone marks the lowest.

For centuries, communities carved dates or inscriptions onto these stones whenever the waters of rivers like the Elbe, Danube or Rhine receded dramatically. Some hunger stones bear lists of years, including 1616, 1746 and 1842.

The 2026 drought has seen water levels in the Danube river reach new lows Image: Cristian Cristel/Xinhua/IMAGO

In a 2019 study "Extreme Droughts and Human Responses to Them: The Czech Lands in the Pre-Instrumental Period," Czech historian and climatologist Rudolf Brazdil and his colleagues drew on chronicles, administrative records and other documentary sources to examine how drought-affected communities lived long before systematic weather measurements.

For people living along rivers such as the Elbe, low water created a host of problems. Barges carrying timber, grain and other goods struggled to navigate shallow channels, disrupting trade along one of Central Europe's vital transport routes. In severe cases, shipping had to be restricted or halted altogether.

And drought also meant crop failure, rising prices — and hunger.

Hunger stones like this one didn't just commemorate years of drought; they also attempted to mark low water levels Image: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

More than just drought memorials

While hunger stones were often treated as symbolic reminders of drought, they've proven to be more than that.

A 2020 study published in the journal Climate of the Past found that many of the dates and markings on Elbe hunger stones closely matched documented periods of exceptionally low water. The researchers concluded that many of the inscriptions were intended to record how low the river had fallen, rather than merely commemorate drought years.

The study also documented drought year markings on the Decin stone dating back to at least the 16th century, underscoring that the famous inscription "If you see me, weep" of 1904 represents only one chapter in the hunger stone's much longer history.

Hunger stones, like this one in Techlovice, often bear years and water level marks Image: Wikipedia

A doomsaying stone?

Yet, its fame lies mainly in its seemingly foreboding message. Even its sighting during the more recent European droughts of 2020 and 2022 inspired media coverage, describing its message as "chilling", "grim" or a "harbinger of hard times."

In his 2019 study "Die Botschaft der Hungersteine" (or "The Message of the Hunger Stones"), Bernd Gross drew on newspaper reports, postcards and local historical records to reconstruct the history of the Decin hunger stone and noted that its inscription may have been inspired by an older one.

Gross cited newspaper reports from the 1890s that described a hunger stone near Techlovice, upstream from Decin, that reportedly bore German inscriptions such as: "We cried — We cry — And you will cry."

The man most often associated with the Decin stone's inscription is F. Mayer, a local innkeeper and boatman and member of the Elbe shipping community.

According to Gross, Mayer had the now-famous phrase carved onto the stone during the drought of 1904, dated July 18, along with his name.

This 1904 photo featured the 'celebrity' Decin hunger stone, seen by thousands of visitors Image: Wikipedia/Public Domain

A celebrity of its time

At the time, newspapers referred to it as the Bodenbach or Tetschen hunger stone, after the neighboring towns that today form part of Decin. They reported on the exposed stone and its message, while contemporary accounts described thousands of visitors who went to see it.

Postcards featuring the hunger stone also circulated widely, spreading awareness of the site far beyond the Elbe Valley.

The Reichenberger Zeitung, in circulation from 1860 to 1938, reported on August 28, 1904: "Day after day, groups gather on the rock; everyone wants to set foot on it at least once. However, the markings carved into the sandstone are likely to lose their visibility due to this frequent trampling."

Visitors were reportedly intrigued not only by the inscription but also the earlier dates carved into the rock, recording drought years stretching back centuries.

The stone that nearly disappeared

Ironically, the drought of 1904 that put the Decin stone and its inscription on the map very nearly caused its destruction.

Local river authorities decided to remove rocks and other obstacles from the Elbe to improve navigation, and Gross' study states that there were concerns that the Decin hunger stone could be removed as well.

Following the intervention of the Tetschen Boatmen's Cooperative, which petitioned the imperial authorities, the stone was spared. News reports stated that officials agreed to route planned river works around it in order to preserve what was already regarded as a historic landmark of the Elbe.

Many hunger stones lying in the Elbe also bear later dates: this one has 1963 and 2003 on it Image: Arno Burgi/dpa/picture alliance

And while other obstacles were removed from the river, the Decin hunger stone survived.

The stone's story did not end there. When another severe drought exposed it in 1911, Mayer's famous inscription was reportedly carved again, this time more deeply. Later in 1938, a Czech inscription was added alongside the older markings.

Together, these dates and inscriptions chart centuries of the stone's history and its role as a marker of exceptionally low water levels on the Elbe.

Edited by: Oliver Mojen

World.title: UK: Nigel Farage beats a trash can in Clacton by-election
World.content:
Nigel Farage reclaimed his Clacton seat with 63% of the vote, but his main rival, Count Binface, took over a quarter, as Farage skipped the count citing security concerns.

UK right-wing populist leader Nigel Farage won Friday's by-election in Clacton, regaining the parliamentary seat he resigned a month earlier to trigger the vote.

He took about 63% of the vote, while his main challenger, comedian Jon Harvey running as trash-can-costumed "Count Binface," secured roughly 27% — his best result yet in eight election attempts. The turnout was 44%.

What triggered the Clacton by-election?

Reform UK's Farage called the special election to prove his voter support amid a parliamentary investigation into an undeclared £5 million ($6.75 million, €5.85 million) gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Britain's major parties boycotted the race, calling it a self-serving stunt. This left Farage facing 33 mostly independent and novelty candidates.

Farage skipped the official vote count, saying police warned him of an "organized campaign to disrupt" the result. Essex police disputed reports of a credible threat but said a "proportionate and robust" security operation was in place. He also canceled a planned victory speech.

Count Binface's policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using their phone on speaker mode while on public transport Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," he told supporters.

What happens next?

The win doesn't resolve Farage's political troubles. The parliamentary standards investigation, paused when he resigned, is expected to resume and could still force him from his seat. Farage says the money was a personal gift he wasn't required to declare.

Last month, ​a Survation poll put Farage's share of the vote at 73%, a figure he fell short of. It comes as Reform UK's national polling is also slipping behind a resurgent Labour Party under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Who is Count Binface?

Count Binface is the alter ego of Harvey, a British comedian, writer and producer who uses the character to satirize UK politics.

He is a self-styled "intergalactic space warrior" who campaigns wearing a trash bin on his head. While he was expected to receive a large share of the vote, the figure was not expected to exceed 20 percent.

Binface has become somewhat of a serial candidate, challenging prime ministers past and present in line with a long tradition of novelty candidates in UK politics.

The satirical political character has challenged numerous UK prime ministers in past campaigns Image: Toby Melville/REUTERS

With the other parties boycotting the election, he became Farage's default rival with a comical platform vowing to "cut your taxes, and raise everyone else's," build one affordable home and nationalize singer Adele.

"The moral victory is already mine," Harvey, aka Binface, told the AFP news agency at the counting center ahead of the final count.

Skip next section Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

An Air India Airbus A320 that suddenly lost altitude on August 4 recorded losses in all three hydraulic systems, briefly losing crucial flight controls, media reports on Friday cited an initial Airbus analysis as saying.

Air India flight AI2379 from Thailand’s Phuket to New Delhi had dropped 300 feet during cruise over the Indian state of Odisha, before recovering and landing safely in Delhi.

Twenty passengers and four crew members were injured during the incident which was classified as "serious" by Indian aviation authorities.

India’s ​Aircraft Accident Investigation ‌Bureau is probing the incident with technical assistance from Airbus and France's BEA.

What do the Airbus findings say?

Airbus shared the technical evaluation after decoding the flight data recorder in a communication to Air India in response to the Indian flag carrier’s request for an assessment .

The plane’s elevators and ailerons, which control ​its pitch and roll, were unavailable for about four ​seconds, ‌during which the aircraft pitched upward, Reuters cited Airbus as saying in its preliminary findings.

The first officer applied a full nose-down input during the timeframe but ​there was "no direct response" from the flight-control surfaces, Reuters cited the assessment as saying, adding that the hydraulic systems recovered within seconds.

The initial analysis has not established a root cause and Airbus has asked Air India to conduct checks on ​the aircraft’s systems and sensors and to provide more information about the incident.

Airbus has also asked Air India to share the recent maintenance history of hydraulic systems along with more detailed accounts from the pilots.

There was no statement from the planemaker and Air India on the assessment.

Earlier this week, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

On Thursday, an internal communication from Air India showed that the carrier would now conduct a mandatory dope test for all its pilots, expanding checks beyond regulatory requirements.

Under the current rules, airlines in India randomly test at least 10 percent of their flight crew for psychoactive substances each year.

World.title: Can childhood trauma be prevented with a drug?
World.content:
Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.

Trauma is usually treated as something you carry, manage, work through and sometimes ease. Rarely as something that could be stopped before it takes hold. That is what a group of researchers in Munich and Stockholm set out to test .

They began by making the first days of life hard. Mother mice were given far less nesting and bedding material than normal. That was enough to make mothers erratic, and the first days of life unpredictable. The mice raised in that hardship grew up looking perfectly healthy — with no obvious illness or anything visibly wrong.

Then researchers put them in groups and watched what happened. Repeatedly, these mice ended up at the bottom. Pushed into the lowest ranks of their social hierarchies, first as adolescents, then again as adults. A difficult infancy had left no visible mark — but it had set the position they would occupy for the rest of their lives.

When the researchers gave some of them a drug, the pattern disappeared.

The study, published in June, was led jointly by Mathias Schmidt at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and Juan Pablo Lopez at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm .

How does childhood trauma affect the brain and body?

Start with cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. When something stressful happens, cortisol floods the system. This is a standard, protective response.

What matters just as much is the off switch. The body needs to register that the danger has passed and wind the response back down. It does this through cortisol receptors — the parts of cells that detect the hormone and signal the system to stand down.

A protein called FKBP51 controls how sensitive those receptors are. Early hardship, the research suggests, causes the body to produce too much of it. That makes the receptors harder to trigger, so the signal to stand down never fully lands, and the stress response stays switched on far longer than it should.

Schmidt's point is that none of this is something a person can feel.

"Your cortisol response is something you don't feel," he said. "You may think you're very stress resilient, but your body is pumping out cortisol, and you don't know."

Can a drug block the effects of a difficult childhood?

The researchers used a compound called SAFit2, which blocks FKBP51. Given to the mothers during the stressful period, it reached the offspring through breast milk.

The treated mice went on to perform identically, within their social groups, to mice that had experienced no adversity at all — the social cost of a hard start erased.

The effect showed up in the brain as well as in behavior. The team screened gene activity across six stress-related regions and found that early adversity had left a broad imprint across them. The drug largely reversed it, most clearly in two: the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens, regions involved in emotional control and reward.

Can childhood trauma be reversed?

Not on this evidence.

In the Munich study, the compound was given during the stressful period itself, not after. What the study demonstrates is prevention, not repair.

Other studies have shown behavioral effects when the drug is used in adult animals, but full reversal of trauma already in place remains unproven. And prevention only works if you can identify who's at risk before the harm is done — a problem this research doesn't address.

Would this drug actually work on humans?

It's too early to say.

The study tested male mice only, so it is not yet known whether the same holds in females. And SAFit2 remains a research compound 3 effective in animals but not yet developed or safety-tested for human use. Still, Schmidt sees a realistic path toward clinical application within the next decade, noting that stress mechanisms are "very, very similar in animals and humans."

War scars and genes: Can the impacts of trauma be inherited? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is trauma treated now, and why doesn't it always work?

Existing treatments for stress-related disorders, including PTSD and trauma-linked depression, rely heavily on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These drugs target serotonin pathways. They work for many patients, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and a significant portion of patients don't respond at all.

By contrast, targeting FKBP51 would mean treating the pathology at its source. "We would actually not only be treating the symptoms, but also the cause of the disorder by acting directly [on] a stress mechanism," said Schmidt. "These types of drugs are currently not on the market."

Longer-term, Schmidt envisions a more targeted approach: identifying individuals who are genetically vulnerable to stress, whose FKBP51 expression is already elevated, and treating that group specifically after acute traumatic events.

On the other end of the spectrum are people who, through genetics or prior experience, prove remarkably resilient even under extreme conditions, and may not need medication at all. Understanding who does need it, Schmidt said, and reaching them in time, is where the research is heading next.

What are the signs of unresolved trauma?

Schmidt is careful that trauma is highly individual, psychologically and physiologically. The rough guide he offers is duration, not intensity.

A strong stress reaction immediately after a car crash or a violent event is considered normal — the body doing its job. What concerns clinicians is when the response persists well beyond that: still unable to cross a street a month later, still unable to sleep six weeks on. Those are his illustrative examples rather than diagnostic thresholds, but the principle holds. If a stress response isn't fading, it's advisable to speak to a doctor.

That remains practical guidance for now. The drug, if it ever exists, is at least a decade away — and on current evidence, it would need to come before the damage, not after.

Editor: Kaukab Shairani

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here .

World.title: El Gobierno amplía la vida de la central nuclear de Almaraz hasta 2030 por la “volatilidad de precios” originada en Oriente Próximo
World.content:
El principio del fin de la energía nuclear en España se gana una prórroga de dos años y medio mientras las guerras en Oriente Próximo y Ucrania se enquistan y no dejan de alborotar los precios energéticos mundiales. El Gobierno ha autorizado la ampliación de la vida útil de la central de Almaraz (en Cáceres), tal y como había recomendado el Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear hace un mes y habían solicitado desde el otoño pasado sus propietarias: Iberdrola, Endesa y Naturgy. Según se publica en el Boletín Oficial del Estado de este viernes, el Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico concede la renovación de la autorización de explotación de la Central Nuclear Almaraz, Unidades I y II, y prorroga “la vigencia de la autorización de explotación de ambas Unidades hasta el 8 de junio de 2030, teniendo en cuenta que la central nuclear cuenta con una Revisión Periódica de Seguridad (RPS) vigente hasta dicha fecha”. El apagado programado debía comenzar en noviembre de 2027 y no se cambia el resto de los previstos hasta 2035. Desde el Gobierno se subraya que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se pretende defender al sistema energético y a los consumidores de la volatilidad de los precios internacionales.

El Ministerio justifica la decisión por el nuevo contexto energético internacional y la volatilidad del precio del gas derivada de la crisis en Oriente Próximo, según el texto de la orden. “La crisis en Oriente Medio ha supuesto una disrupción en el contexto energético global, incrementando y añadiendo volatilidad de forma significativa a los precios de los combustibles fósiles, entre ellos el gas natural. Según indican organismos internacionales, el contexto geopolítico y los daños en infraestructura de producción y exportación de combustibles extienden el riesgo y la incertidumbre a los próximos años”, indica el texto publicado en el BOE.

Según los cálculos incluidos en la resolución, mantener Almaraz hasta 2030 tendrá un efecto “acotado y poco significativo” sobre el despliegue renovable y contribuiría a reducir la dependencia del gas. El Ministerio no quiere que la decisión se entienda como un paso atrás y deja clara cuál es su estrategia en la misma orden de prórroga de Almaraz: “La política energética aprobada y en ejecución en España, alineada con la normativa y objetivos europeos, tiene como base la apuesta por la generación renovable como forma más competitiva de producir electricidad, aprovechando asimismo las ventajas competitivas del país en términos de recurso, tecnología y capacidades. Esta apuesta ha permitido mejorar la posición de España en cuanto a costes energéticos en el contexto europeo, proteger a los consumidores ante subidas de precio, y generar un contexto inédito de atracción de proyectos industriales y de electrificación”.

Fuentes del Ministerio subrayan las “circunstancias extraordinarias derivadas del conflicto en Oriente Medio y de la continuidad de la guerra en Ucrania”. “Hay una situación energética internacional excepcional y sobrevenida que está generando un escenario de elevada volatilidad y precios altos de los combustibles fósiles, cuya duración es actualmente imposible de prever”, se subraya como punto de partida. Y como remate, se incide en que “la volatilidad y la incertidumbre son significativamente mayores a las anticipadas hace tan solo unos meses”. El cierre efectivo del estrecho de Ormuz provocado por la guerra de Irán ha ocasionado que se dispare el precio del gas en Europa.

Por lo tanto, se actúa en consecuencia: “En el contexto actual, la prórroga, coyuntural, puede contribuir a moderar la exposición de los consumidores a unos picos de precios de los combustibles fósiles no previstos anteriormente. Ello permite seguir protegiendo a la población ante la volatilidad de los precios y la incertidumbre en este periodo, mientras se sigue ampliando la respuesta estructural frente a la dependencia de los precios de combustibles fósiles: el despliegue de renovables”, explica el Gobierno.

La orden señala igualmente que la continuidad de Almaraz aporta estabilidad al sistema eléctrico, según el propio operador, aunque la prórroga no “cambia la necesidad de continuar con las actuaciones ya en curso dirigidas a fortalecer la seguridad y estabilidad del suministro”.

Una extensión “acotada”

El Ministerio insiste en que la extensión es “acotada y limitada”, y que se otorga tras comprobar el cumplimiento de las tres condiciones que siempre exigió para concederla: que fuera segura para las personas (como avala el CSN en su informe preceptivo anterior), que no comprometiera la seguridad de suministro y que no suponga ningún coste para los ciudadanos. Es decir, no hay “ningún tipo de rebaja fiscal ni contraprestación económica para las empresas eléctricas”.

“La extensión solicitada del periodo de explotación para las Unidades I y II de la Central Nuclear Almaraz se limita en torno a 31 y 19 meses respectivamente, lo cual representa una proporción reducida de la vida media prevista del parque nuclear español, no alterándose el resto del calendario ni la fecha de cese definitivo del conjunto del parque nuclear a 2035. De acuerdo con los análisis realizados, dicha extensión tiene un impacto muy limitado sobre los objetivos de política energética del país”, explica la orden del departamento dirigido por Sara Aagesen.

El protocolo firmado en 2019 entre las propietarias del parque nuclear español y la Empresa Nacional de Residuos Radiactivos (Enresa), sociedad dependiente del Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica, contemplaba el cierre ordenado del parque hasta 2035, empezando en ese año 2027 que ahora se traslada a 2030 para el recinto extremeño. Las dos unidades de Almaraz eran las primeras en echar el cierre y, pese a contar desde 2020 con el visto bueno del CSN para funcionar durante 10 años (los permisos del organismo de seguridad se dan por una década), el calendario fijaba el cierre de las plantas cacereñas en siete y ocho años, respectivamente. Esto es, ya tenían permiso para funcionar 10 años, por lo que era de esperar que el CSN no se pronunciase en contra.

Finalmente, y tras muchos meses de debate soterrado, presión social en la comarca implicada, declaraciones públicas para testar la posición de la otra parte y negociaciones sobre el alcance de la posible medida, las eléctricas decidieron pedir la ampliación de la vida de ambas unidades de Almaraz hasta 2030, por mucho que su primera intención apuntaba a una extensión de diez años. Iberdrola, con una participación del 53% y Endesa con un 36%, eran partidarias de esta mayor ampliación, si bien, Naturgy, con un 11%, se opuso, y ganó la partida toda vez que, al estar constituidas las nucleares como comunidades de bienes, las decisiones deben adoptarse por unanimidad.

Además, Endesa e Iberdrola habían venido batallando para lograr un recorte de los impuestos que gravan a estas plantas, esencialmente, el del combustible nuclear gastado, que el Gobierno de Mariano Rajoy aprobó en 2013 para hacer frente a la deuda del sistema eléctrico. Pero, a medida que se acercaba el plazo límite para solicitar la prórroga al CSN (un año antes del cierre previsto), las compañías renunciaron a los recortes fiscales que venían reclamando y que el ministerio, y el Gobierno en su conjunto en no pocas declaraciones, siempre consideró “una línea roja”. Con todo, mantienen recurrida en los tribunales la tasa de gestión de residuos de Enresa.

La decisión del Ministerio pone fin al trámite y evita que el cierre escalonado de los dos reactores se active para sus fechas previstas: el 1 de noviembre de 2027 para la Unidad I y el 31 de octubre de 2028 para la Unidad II.

En cualquier caso, y según recoge la orden ministerial de este viernes, la prórroga de funcionamiento estará subordinada al cumplimiento estricto de las condiciones e instrucciones de seguridad dictadas por el CSN. El Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear emitió ya el pasado 16 de julio un informe favorable a la renovación solicitada, condicionado al cumplimiento de los límites y exigencias de seguridad nuclear y protección radiológica recogidos ahora en la orden. El aval técnico del organismo regulador certificó y acreditó que la instalación nuclear cacereña reúne las condiciones de seguridad necesarias para operar de manera segura durante dicho periodo de prórroga. Tras este pronunciamiento del CSN, el expediente fue remitido al Gobierno, abriendo un plazo para que el Ejecutivo tomara una decisión definitiva sobre su continuidad.

La orden obliga a las empresas a mantener las dotaciones de personal de plantilla con funciones relacionadas con la seguridad previstas para los años 2028 a 2030. También señala que la prórroga “deberá facilitar la mayor implicación de las empresas propietarias en alternativas industriales y de empleo en el territorio y debe ser utilizada por las mismas para avanzar en el diálogo social para una transición justa”, aunque sin imponer condiciones explícitas al respecto.

World.title: Sumar rechaza la prórroga de la planta de Almaraz y acusa al PSOE de incumplir los acuerdos de gobierno
World.content:
No han tardado en llegar las reacciones a la prórroga de la central nuclear de Almaraz (Cáceres), autorizada por el Gobierno y publicada en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) este viernes, víspera de festivo. Sumar ha sido tajante en su rechazo a la medida, acusando al PSOE de incumplir el acuerdo del gobierno de coalición que ambos partidos firmaron en 2023. También socios del bloque de investidura como Podemos han criticado la decisión, al igual que las formaciones ecologistas. El PP, Vox, los socialistas extremeños y las plataformas locales que defendían su permanencia más allá de 2030, en cambio, han celebrado la extensión de la vida útil de la planta.

El ministro de Cultura, Ernest Urtasun, de Sumar, ha cargado directamente contra el PSOE por no respetar el acuerdo que propició la coalición: “Es un incumplimiento del acuerdo de gobierno del PSOE con Sumar y, por tanto, expresamos nuestro rechazo”. En un comunicado, ha acusado a los socialistas de haber “cedido a las presiones del oligopolio energético en detrimento de la transición ecológica”, y ha añadido que la prórroga “envía un mensaje equivocado en plena transición energética” porque “frena el despliegue de las renovables”.

Fuentes del grupo confederal de Sumar se han pronunciado en la misma línea, insistiendo en que el “mantenimiento del parque nuclear obedece a presiones corporativas y no a necesidades técnicas, medioambientales ni de competitividad económica”. Han subrayado que la prórroga, un asunto que ya había generado fuertes tensiones entre los socios de la coalición, “frena la transición energética e hipoteca a la ciudadanía”. La formación insiste en que seguir alargando la vida útil de las plantas “posterga la descarbonización real apoyada en renovables e impone a la sociedad costes y riesgos inaceptables, además de encarecer el precio de la energía”.

El PP, en cambio, ha celebrado la decisión, pero con muchas reservas. Génova ha criticado que la prórroga es insuficiente y que solo “supone un parche a una gestión ideologizada” de Pedro Sánchez, puesto que el Gobierno no ha renunciado al calendario de cierre establecido para el resto de centrales, presentando la ampliación de Almaraz como un hecho puntual motivado por la “volatilidad de precios” causada por la inestabilidad de Oriente Próximo. La formación de Alberto Núñez Feijóo, al contrario, defiende que “la energía nuclear es un recurso clave” que debe tener vocación de permanencia en el mix energético.

En esta línea se ha expresado públicamente el vicesecretario de Economía del partido, Alberto Nadal, en redes sociales. Secretario de Estado de Energía entre 2011 y 2016 con Mariano Rajoy al frente del Ejecutivo, Nadal ha calificado la autorización a Almaraz para operar hasta 2030 como una “gran noticia para Extremadura y para toda España”, pero a la vez ha criticado que la decisión se hiciera “de tapadillo el 14 de agosto y justificada por la guerra de Irán, cuando la prórroga es de tres años”.

La presidenta de la Junta de Extremadura, María Guardiola (PP), se ha mostrado por su parte satisfecha con la prórroga. “Una decisión que da certidumbre a una comarca, que protege miles de empleos y que mantiene en Extremadura una actividad que durante décadas ha sido fundamental para la vida de tantos pueblos y familias que dependen de ella”, ha escrito en X. “Hoy es un día para celebrar una buena noticia”, ha manifestado en la misma línea el secretario general del PSOE de Extremadura, Álvaro Sánchez Cotrina. “Por fin respiramos aliviados y vemos la luz al final del túnel”, ha agregado Fernando Sánchez, presidente de la plataforma Sí a Almaraz, Sí al futuro, y alcalde del municipio cacereño de Belvís de Monroy.

La Asociación de Municipios en Áreas de Centrales Nucleares y Almacenamiento de Residuos Nucleares (Amac), así como la patronal catalana Foment del Treball, también han reaccionado con satisfacción a la noticia. Ambas han expresado además su deseo de que la ampliación se extienda a las demás plantas que hay sobre el territorio.

Más apoyos a la prórroga han llegado de Vox. La decisión ha sido celebrada tanto por el vicepresidente de la Junta de Extremadura, Óscar Fernández —“Almaraz, sí gracias. ¡Nucleares, sí gracias! El primer paso está dado. Pero solo es el primero, porque el objetivo debe ser 2050″, ha escrito en las redes sociales—, como por el secretario general de la formación en el Congreso, José María Figaredo. “Es un éxito tremendo para toda España”, ha valorado en una entrevista en Antena 3.

Del lado opuesto se han posicionado los grupos ecologistas, muy críticos con la ampliación de la planta. Greenpeace considera que la prórroga no responde a criterios de seguridad ni abaratará la factura, sino que supone “una cesión vergonzosa del Gobierno” a las presiones “del oligopolio eléctrico encabezado por Iberdrola, Endesa y Naturgy”. Eva Saldaña, directora ejecutiva para España y Portugal de la ONG, ha tachado la decisión de “error histórico”, que echa por tierra toda la credibilidad del Gobierno y que además pondrá en riesgo 26.130 millones de euros en inversiones en tecnologías limpias.

La Plataforma por un Nuevo Modelo Energético también ha alertado de que la decisión, “muy lamentable”, “supone un peligroso precedente”; la Fundación Renovables ha criticado que implica “echar por tierra” toda la política y planificación energética de la última década. Según el coordinador federal de Alianza Verde, Juan López de Uralde, la prórroga es una “vergüenza”, concedida “con agosticidad y alevosía”, que !vuela por los aires los planes energéticos que impulsan las renovables. Vergüenza del Gobierno PSOE/SUMAR”, ha recalcado.

También el secretario de Organización y portavoz de Podemos, Pablo Fernández, ha calificado este viernes de “auténtica vergüenza” la medida. La líder de la formación morada, Ione Belarra, se ha pronunciado en el mismo sentido en X. “El gobierno aprueba la prórroga de la central nuclear de Almaraz hasta 2030 el 12 de agosto. Hay que tener poca vergüenza pero poco más se puede esperar de un gobierno que prometió vivienda y sólo hizo rearme. El PSOE es una máquina de alimentar a la derecha”.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.
