World.title: Medal rush for Hungary at the European Aquatics Championships as Milák, Kós and relay strike gold – VIDEO
World.content:
Hungary enjoyed a spectacular evening at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris on Thursday, with Kristóf Milák setting a European record in the men’s 100m butterfly before helping the Hungarian men’s 4x100m freestyle relay claim a historic gold medal with a national record.

The two victories capped an outstanding day for Hungarian swimming, while Olympic champion Hubert Kós also produced another strong performance, finishing fourth in the 100m butterfly with a personal best.

According to MTI, Milák won the butterfly final in 49.48 seconds, breaking the European record and finishing just 0.03 seconds outside Caeleb Dressel’s world record.

Milák delivers European record at the European Aquatics Championships

The defending European champion and Olympic champion had to fight for the victory until the closing metres.

The field remained tightly packed after the turn, with at least four swimmers still in contention for gold. Milák, however, produced a superb final ten metres, moving clear of his rivals to clock the second-fastest performance in history.

France’s Maxime Grousset took silver in 49.70 seconds, while Switzerland’s Noè Ponti finished third in 49.93.

Kós narrowly missed the podium after swimming a personal best of 50.25 seconds, good enough for fourth place.

The Hungarian pair had already demonstrated their strength during Wednesday’s programme. Kós had won the 200m backstroke with what MTI described as the fifth-fastest performance of all time, while Milák finished third in the 100m freestyle with one of the fastest times ever recorded in the event.

Despite those demanding races, both arrived at Thursday’s butterfly final in strong form.

European Aquatics Championships – Kristóf Milák with his gold medal. Photo: MTI

Men’s 100m butterfly results

Kristóf Milák (Hungary) – 49.48, European record Maxime Grousset (France) – 49.70 Noè Ponti (Switzerland) – 49.93 Hubert Kós (Hungary) – 50.25, personal best

Interesting analysis – The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget

Historic relay gold for Hungary

The medal rush continued later in the evening as Hungary won the men’s 4x100m freestyle relay for the first time in European Championships history.

The final line-up of Hubert Kós, Szebasztián Szabó, Nándor Németh and Kristóf Milák touched the wall in 3:10.03, setting a new Hungarian record and European Championships record.

Russia, competing under neutral status, finished second in 3:10.12, while Croatia claimed bronze in 3:11.08.

Hungary had qualified for the final with the fifth-fastest time in the heats, but the team was significantly strengthened for the medal race by the arrival of Olympic champions Kós and Milák.

Kós opened the relay with a personal best of 48.18 seconds, cutting almost seven-tenths from his previous best.

Szabó briefly moved Hungary into the lead before handing over in fifth place, while Németh closed the gap and sent Milák into the final leg only 0.01 seconds behind the leader.

Milák produces stunning anchor leg

Milák then delivered one of the standout relay performances of the championships.

With the advantage of a flying relay start, he split 46.29 seconds over the final 100 metres and overtook the Russian team in the closing strokes to secure gold for Hungary.

The overall winning time of 3:10.03 improved the previous Hungarian national record of 3:11.06, set by the team that finished fifth at the Tokyo Olympics.

Men’s 4x100m freestyle relay results

Hungary – 3:10.03, national and European Championships record

Hubert Kós, Szebasztián Szabó, Nándor Németh, Kristóf Milák Neutral athletes – 3:10.12

Ivan Girev, Vasily Kukushkin, Aleksandr Shchegolev, Egor Kornev Croatia – 3:11.08

If you missed it: Hungarian swimmer ranked world’s second best, says prestigious outlet

Kós adds another Hungarian gold in the 200m backstroke

Hungary’s success at the European Aquatics Championships had already begun before Milák’s record-breaking performance, with Hubert Kós claiming gold in the men’s 200m backstroke in Saint-Denis.

Kós took control of the race immediately and was inside world-record pace at the 50-metre mark. By halfway, he was around eight-tenths of a second ahead of the pace set by former world-record holder Aaron Peirsol.

Although he could not maintain that speed over the second half of the race, the Hungarian remained comfortably in front and touched the wall in 1:53.08, securing Hungary’s first gold medal in pool swimming at this year’s European Championships.

Greece’s Apostolos Siskos finished second in 1:53.81, while Italy’s Thomas Ceccon took bronze in 1:53.96.

Kós’s winning time was also historically significant: 1:53.08 is tied for the fifth-fastest performance ever recorded in the event. The Hungarian already owns another of the fastest 200m backstroke performances in history, further strengthening his position among the discipline’s leading swimmers.

Pádár reaches the 200m freestyle final

There was further positive news for Hungary in the women’s 200m freestyle. Nikolett Pádár finished third in her semi-final in 1:57.24 and qualified for the final with the seventh-fastest time overall.

A golden evening for Hungarian swimming

The two victories gave Hungary two gold medals on Thursday evening alone at the European Aquatics Championships, underlining the strength of a men’s team built around several Olympic champions and internationally established swimmers.

Milák was the central figure of the night, first coming within three hundredths of a second of the 100m butterfly world record and then producing the decisive final leg in the relay.

Kós also played a key role, adding a fourth-place finish and two personal bests to his earlier European title in the 200m backstroke.

For Hungary, Thursday’s performances represented not only another haul of medals in Paris, but also a series of national, continental and championship-level benchmarks that made it one of the strongest sessions of the tournament so far.

World.title: Government press conference: Paks nuclear power plant faces shutdown risk
World.content:
The Danube has begun falling again at Paks, increasing the threat of further restrictions or even a complete shutdown at the Paks nuclear power plant, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Thursday. The government has already begun emergency river-engineering works, while two 80-metre barges are being prepared for possible deployment if the water level drops faster than expected.

According to MTI, the water gauge at Paks stood at around minus 119-120 centimetres on Thursday afternoon. Magyar said even a few centimetres can now make a significant difference to the operation of Hungary’s only nuclear power station.

For foreign readers, the negative figures refer to the local water gauge datum and do not mean that the river itself has a negative depth.

Paks nuclear power plant approaching critical water levels

Experts expect the gauge to fall to around minus 121 centimetres on Friday morning and potentially reach minus 132 centimetres by Sunday or Monday, Magyar said.

That is a crucial threshold. If the river falls to minus 132 centimetres, one of the two turbines currently operating would again have to be shut down.

The medium-term outlook is even more concerning. According to the prime minister, the level could reach minus 136-137 centimetres within six or seven days. At minus 140 centimetres, the entire Paks nuclear power plant would have to be taken offline.

At present, only two of the plant’s eight turbines are operating, producing almost 500 megawatts of electricity.

Magyar stressed that Danube levels can be forecast with reasonable confidence only a few days in advance, rejecting claims that the exact severity of the current situation could have been predicted months ago.

The crisis is not unique to Hungary. Romania began shutting down the last operating reactor at its Cernavodă nuclear power plant on Thursday because of historically low Danube levels, after its other reactor had already been taken offline in late July.

Emergency bed sill already under construction

The government’s main intervention is the construction of a riverbed sill between Paks and Dunaszentbenedek, close to the nuclear plant’s cold-water intake channel.

The structure is intended to raise the upstream water level sufficiently to maintain the cooling-water supply required by the plant.

Around 145,000 cubic metres of rock are planned to be placed in the Danube. The first 35,000 cubic metres will form a transverse rock ridge designed to produce a meaningful rise in the water level. Another 110,000 cubic metres will later reinforce the riverbed and protect the structure against erosion caused by the Danube’s current.

The project is technically challenging. Gacsályi József, deputy technical director-general of Hungary’s National Directorate General for Water Management, said around 800 cubic metres of water per second currently pass through the river section where the structure is being built.

The sill will be constructed across a section of roughly 300 metres between the plant’s cold- and warm-water channels.

Work is taking place on both banks. Hungarian soldiers are working primarily on the left bank, which can be accessed on dry ground, while contractors and water-management specialists are operating on the deeper right-hand side.

Heavy machinery is already arriving, access roads and storage areas are being prepared, and the first quantities of rock have been delivered.

The government wants the crucial part of the structure completed within about 30 days, with construction continuing around the clock.

As we wrote today – The danger is not over: Budapest water supply under pressure again

Two barges could provide rapid emergency relief

A second, faster intervention is also being prepared.

Two approximately 80-metre barges are to be positioned downstream of the cold-water intake and secured to piles on the right bank. They would be placed at an approximately 45-degree angle rather than perpendicular to the shore.

The vessels are intended to act as temporary flow-control structures. According to modelling presented at the briefing, partially sinking the barges could immediately raise the water level by around 10-15 centimetres, while the full deployment of one barge could potentially produce an increase of about 20 centimetres.

The two barges would create a combined diversion structure roughly 160 metres long.

They are expected to be ready for testing from Friday so that they can be used rapidly if the Danube falls below the critical level earlier than forecast.

However, the government regards their use as a last-resort measure. Magyar warned that an uncontrolled barge could create serious problems if it broke free, became lodged in the river or obstructed the plant’s warm-water outlet.

As we wrote today, Danube water level falling again. Major intervention planned to protect Paks nuclear plant – pictures

Construction to continue into the autumn

Preparatory work on the left bank is scheduled to accelerate between 15 and 18 August, including clearing the route and installing geotextile material.

A pontoon structure on the right bank is planned between 17 and 21 August to allow rock to be delivered directly into the riverbed.

Rock placement will then proceed from both sides during late August and early September, with the two sections of the water-raising ridge expected to be joined by around 11 September. Additional reinforcement work is planned to continue into October.

The project is designed ultimately to guarantee a gauge level of around minus 90 centimetres at Paks, which the government says would allow the nuclear plant to operate at full capacity.

Emergency project to cost EUR 16.9 million

The government currently estimates the gross cost of the Paks-Dunaszentbenedek bed sill at HUF 6.165 billion, or approximately EUR 16.9 million at the official 13 August exchange rate.

The figure includes the reconstruction of affected road sections and rehabilitation of the riverbanks.

Funding will come from Hungary’s national emergency reserve, while the budget of the National Directorate General for Water Management will be opened to cover the project.

Magyar said spending would be closely monitored and contractors would be required to account for all expenditure.

The government has also received private-sector offers of assistance. Austria’s Strabag has offered technology, transport and materials free of charge, according to the prime minister, while Hungarian-owned KÉSZ Group has also made an offer.

Magyar criticised major companies associated with the former Fidesz government for what he described as a lack of similar offers.

Full shutdown could cost HUF 50 billion a month

The financial stakes are significantly larger than the cost of the emergency intervention.

According to Magyar, a complete loss of production at Paks would cost the state budget at least HUF 50 billion, or roughly EUR 137 million, every month. That estimate does not include the additional cost to businesses and the wider economy of replacing domestic nuclear generation with more expensive electricity imports.

The prime minister estimated that the water shortage and reduced Paks production are currently cutting around 0.1% from Hungary’s GDP, although he stressed that precise calculations are not yet available.

Maintaining Paks output is particularly important because the nuclear station normally plays a central role in Hungary’s electricity supply. Recent record-low Danube levels have already forced the plant to operate far below its usual capacity.

Nuclear safety limits the available solutions

Government officials said numerous engineering options had been considered with water-management, energy and nuclear experts.

Some were rejected because nuclear safety had to remain the overriding consideration, Magyar said. The government ultimately selected the riverbed sill and possible deployment of barges as what it considers the safest, most effective and most cost-efficient immediate combination.

The National Atomic Energy Office has been monitoring the project since the planning stage, while engineers from the Budapest University of Technology and Economics contributed to the modelling.

The Defence Administration Office is coordinating the numerous state bodies, contractors and military units involved.

Magyar described the situation as the reverse of a flood emergency: instead of protecting infrastructure from too much water, authorities are attempting to maintain sufficient water levels to protect critical infrastructure.

Environmental approvals running alongside emergency work

The accelerated construction has also raised questions about environmental permitting.

The government has classified the situation as an emergency, allowing physical works to begin before all procedures have been completed. Officials stressed, however, that this does not eliminate environmental studies or the requirement to obtain permits.

Hydrobiologists and ecologists have been involved in planning, according to the water-management authority. The environmental authorisation process must begin by the end of September and will examine effects on wildlife and the river ecosystem.

A permanent operating permit for the sill will be possible only if the structure meets the relevant requirements.

Magyar said modelling suggests that the structure would increase Danube levels by no more than around one centimetre during a future flood, and therefore should not significantly increase flood risk.

Paks II and Hungary’s longer-term cooling strategy questioned

The emergency has also revived a broader debate over how Hungary’s nuclear power system should adapt to increasingly extreme river conditions.

Magyar said the government would examine the possibility of installing cooling towers or closed-loop cooling systems. Such investments would be expensive, but he said they could eventually become necessary for the lifetime extension of the existing Paks plant, the planned Paks II expansion, or both.

He also questioned whether the existing environmental and cooling permits for Paks II adequately reflect the river conditions Hungary is now experiencing.

The government is preparing broader climate and water-management strategies, including the “Water into the Landscape” programme, while Magyar said Hungary would seek to make water management a priority during negotiations over the next EU budget.

He also argued that international agreements governing use of the Danube need to be reconsidered because many were drawn up for very different river-flow conditions.

Austria and Slovakia have complied with existing agreements, Magyar said, but the underlying hydrological situation has changed substantially.

If you missed it today: Russian Rosatom breaks silence as it builds Hungary’s newest nuclear reactors

Political dispute over responsibility for the crisis

The prime minister also used Thursday’s briefing to criticise Viktor Orbán’s former government, which governed Hungary for 16 years before Magyar took office in May 2026. Magyar accused the previous administration of failing to prepare sufficient long-term solutions for low Danube levels and of neglecting possible investments such as changes to Paks’s pumping infrastructure.

These were political allegations by the current government rather than findings presented as part of the technical assessment.

Magyar also criticised proposals circulating online, including suggestions involving dredging, blasting or large-scale pumping systems, arguing that some could endanger nuclear safety.

He separately attacked Mi Hazánk leader László Toroczkai over criticism of the decision to shut down Paks turbines, saying nuclear safety could not be compromised for the sake of maintaining electricity generation.

Low Danube levels becoming a long-term energy challenge

The government maintains that the emergency measures will prevent the Paks nuclear power plant from losing all of its generation capacity, but officials acknowledge that there is currently no clear indication of when the Danube will return to substantially higher levels.

That makes the crisis larger than an immediate engineering problem.

The government is preparing a wider energy plan covering wind power, electricity storage and greater diversification of energy sources. Magyar said Hungary needs more capacity to retain and store energy and must ensure that electricity is available from as many domestic and external sources as possible.

For Paks, meanwhile, the coming days remain decisive. The barges are being prepared for immediate use, while construction of the more permanent riverbed sill proceeds around the clock.

If the Danube continues to fall towards the minus 140-centimetre threshold before the interventions take effect, Hungary could still face the first complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant in its more than four decades of operation.

World.title: The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget
World.content:
Hungarian football finances remain heavily dependent on centrally distributed funding rather than supporters buying tickets, according to a new analysis of the country’s top-flight league. NB I clubs generated more than HUF 63 billion (around EUR 173 million) in combined revenue in 2024, yet ticket and season-ticket sales contributed only about 4% of that total.

The figures were highlighted in an analysis published by Mfor, which examined how Hungary’s 12-team first division is financed and how the structure affects clubs’ business decisions.

For international readers, NB I – officially the OTP Bank Liga – is the highest tier of Hungarian club football and includes teams such as Ferencváros, Újpest and Paks.

Hungarian football finances rely far more on central money than fans

Corporate accounts analysed by G7 showed that NB I clubs collected roughly HUF 2.54 billion (EUR 7 million) from tickets and season tickets in 2024. Against total league revenue exceeding HUF 63 billion (EUR 173 million), matchday admission therefore generated only around 4% of revenue.

The difference becomes particularly striking when compared with the money distributed centrally for the current 2026/27 season.

The Hungarian Football Federation (MLSZ) announced in July that HUF 10.5 billion (EUR 28.9 million) will be distributed among the 12 NB I clubs during the season. The money is not divided equally, as payments depend partly on sporting and player-selection criteria.

By comparison, Mfor calculated that an entire season consisting of rounds with ticket income similar to the 2024/25 opening weekend would produce a theoretical gross ticket-value equivalent of about HUF 2.8 billion (EUR 7.7 million). The publication stressed that this is an estimate rather than clubs’ actual cash income.

Public broadcaster pays billions for television rights

Central financing is built from several major contracts.

According to the MLSZ, Hungary’s public broadcaster MTVA is paying HUF 6 billion (EUR 16.5 million) for broadcasting rights for the 2026/27 season. State-owned gambling company Szerencsejáték Zrt. is paying another HUF 6 billion (EUR 16.5 million) for marketing rights and HUF 3 billion (EUR 8.2 million) for betting rights. All three agreements run for only one season.

Mfor notes that the television-rights fee has fallen by 40% from the HUF 10 billion paid under the previous agreement. However, the additional Szerencsejáték funding means the amount available for redistribution to clubs has not fallen at the same rate.

Sports economist János Kele argued in the Mfor analysis that this funding structure weakens the immediate commercial incentive for clubs to maximise paying attendance. Supporters remain crucial for atmosphere, sponsorship appeal, community links and long-term brand value, he stressed, but their direct contribution at the turnstiles is relatively small.

Financial incentives can even affect team selection

The system also has a direct sporting dimension. Under the MLSZ rules, NB I clubs are encouraged financially to field Hungarian and young players. On average, five Hungarian players should be on the pitch, including one under-21 footballer.

As much as 45% of the NB I central distribution is linked to domestic and young-player minutes. On a HUF 10.5 billion central pool, that represents as much as HUF 4.725 billion (around EUR 13 million).

The incentive has already influenced decisions on the pitch. Mfor cited Nyíregyháza’s match against Újpest, when 19-year-old goalkeeper Mátyás Molnár came on at half-time. Head coach Tamás Bódog acknowledged afterwards that complying with the youth-player requirement was a factor in the substitution.

As we wrote earlier, Dominik Szoboszlai signs a new Liverpool deal until 2031, read details here

Ferencváros operates on a different scale

The financial differences between individual Hungarian clubs are also substantial. According to the G7-based calculations cited by Mfor, Ferencváros had a budget approaching HUF 20 billion (EUR 55 million) in 2024, while smaller provincial clubs typically operated with HUF 2–3 billion (roughly EUR 5.5–8.2 million).

Paks, for example, recorded HUF 2.9 billion (EUR 8 million) in revenue while finishing third in the league and winning the Hungarian Cup. Ferencváros, meanwhile, benefits not only from a much larger budget but also from European competition, a larger stadium, a stronger commercial brand and greater visibility on the international transfer market.

Player sales brought NB I clubs HUF 9.3 billion (EUR 25.6 million) in 2024, close to 15% of overall revenue. However, Mfor notes that the MLSZ’s own strategy identifies Hungary as having the lowest share of player-sale income among the regional leagues it studied, as well as a negative net transfer balance.

Billions invested, but few international youth successes

Hungary’s record in men’s youth football offers another perspective on the sums flowing into the domestic game. Since 2010, Hungarian teams have qualified for the finals of a men’s youth European Championship through the qualifiers on only a handful of occasions. The standout period came at U17 level: Hungary reached the 2017 U17 European Championship, its first appearance at that tournament since 2006, and qualified again for the 2019 edition. UEFA records confirm both appearances. The 2019 side went one step further, earning a place at the FIFA U17 World Cup in Brazil through its performance at the European Championship, UEFA said.

Other tournament appearances during this period need some context. Hungary played at the 2014 U19 European Championship as the host nation, and its result there secured qualification for the 2015 FIFA U20 World Cup. UEFA explicitly listed Hungary as the host rather than one of the seven teams that qualified through the elite round. Similarly, Hungary participated in the 2021 U21 European Championship as co-host with Slovenia, while the 2023 U17 European Championship was also staged in Hungary, giving the home team an automatic place.

In other words, despite the considerable resources channelled into Hungarian football, 2019 remains the last time a Hungarian men’s youth national team qualified for a European Championship through the qualifying competition – and also the last time one earned a place at a youth World Cup on the pitch.

Conclusion

The figures illustrate the central question facing Hungarian football finances: whether clubs can gradually build a model based more strongly on supporters, commercial income and profitable player development, or whether their financial stability will continue to depend primarily on centrally negotiated and distributed funding. With the main broadcasting, marketing and betting agreements currently guaranteed for only the 2026/27 season, that debate is likely to remain highly relevant beyond the current campaign.

It is, however, very disheartening that in recent years the clubs have made no effort to increase attendance figures or sell their own branded merchandise, as they have essentially been receiving funding from the central budget. If, however, revenue from the fund decreases, they will have to adopt models similar to those of the major European clubs, where clubs encourage supporters to purchase season tickets and match tickets, for example.

World.title: Romania’s Presidential Administration to host summit on animal welfare
World.content:
The Presidential Administration will host the second edition of Animal Summit Romania on September 29 - 30, Diana Pungă, a state adviser for relations with civil society at the institution, announced on Friday, August 14.

The event, organized by the non-profit Sache Vet Association and Bucharest’s Animal Protection Administration ASPA, will take place at Cotroceni Palace.

Over two days, it will gather public administration representatives, veterinarians, legal and education specialists, non-governmental organizations and other experts to discuss animal protection and welfare and solutions to challenges in the field.

“Romania continues to face major challenges in the field of animal protection. Beyond the issue of abandonment and the lack of education about responsible pet ownership, civil society frequently raises concerns about the non-transparent operation of some private shelters, suspected abusive euthanasia practices and difficulties in uniformly enforcing existing legislation. In many communities, volunteers, NGOs and active citizens end up compensating for the lack of coherent institutional mechanisms by becoming directly involved in animal rescue, shelter monitoring and the promotion of responsible sterilization and adoption,” an announcement from the organizers reads.

All of these aspects point to an urgent need for clear standards and consistently implemented public policies protecting both the communities and the animals, the organizers said.

World.title: Central Romania: EBRD extends EUR 120 mln loan for PV plant, battery system near Brașov
World.content:
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Friday, August 14, that it has extended a financing package of up to EUR 120 million for the development, construction, and operation of Econergy’s Părău 2 project in Romania.

The project includes a 342 MW solar photovoltaic plant and a 150 MW/300 MWh battery storage system in Brașov, according to a statement by the lender.

The financing consists of an EBRD A loan of up to EUR 57 million and an EBRD B loan of up to EUR 63 million, which includes a EUR 3.6 million debt service guarantee provided by commercial banks Privredna banka Zagreb and NLB.

According to the EBRD, the Părău 2 project will increase renewable energy production, help improve grid flexibility, and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

The project is co-financed by BSTDB (the Black Sea Trade and Development Bank), OTP Bank, and Exim Banca Românească, as part of a debt financing package of up to EUR 229 million.

“By financing one of the country’s pioneering solar and battery storage investments, the EBRD is helping to increase the generation of renewable energy, strengthen energy security and support a more resilient and flexible electricity system. The support of the European Union through InvestEU demonstrates how public and private partners can work together to mobilize financing for the green transition,” said Georgios Gkiaouris, the EBRD’s Head of Energy Europe.

The project is backed by Romania’s Contract for Difference scheme, which was developed with EBRD technical assistance and aims to unlock 5 GW of solar and onshore wind capacity. The solar plant has secured a 125 MWac allocation in the first auction at a strike price of EUR 49.4/MWh for 15 years, while the remaining capacity will operate on a merchant basis.

The European Union supported the EBRD A/B loan through a first-loss portfolio guarantee provided by the InvestEU programme, which covers up to EUR 115 million and helps mitigate the risks associated with the project’s substantial exposure to merchant revenue.

World.title: Romanian consumer goods distributor AQUILA reports slightly higher revenues amid challenging context
World.content:
AQUILA, one of the largest players in the fast-moving consumer goods distribution sector from Romania and the region, reported revenues of RON 1.6 billion in the first half of 2026, amid an economic environment marked by declining consumption, according to a report submitted to the local stock exchange.

The figure represents a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year.

Revenue from the distribution segment increased by 6% in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, driven by the organic growth of this business line. The main contributor to this performance was the traditional retail channel, which grew by 22%, followed by the HoReCa channel with 7% growth, and the gas station channel with 1%, evolutions that offset the 19% decline recorded in the organized retail channel.

Revenue from the logistics segment increased by 6%, driven by higher operating volumes and the expansion of logistics activities across multiple temperature categories, particularly in the frozen products segment. Revenue from the transport segment increased by 13%.

The company's own brands continued to strengthen their contribution to the group’s performance, with revenues of RON 78.5 million in the first half of 2026, up 23% compared to the same period in 2025.

The results for the first half of the year were affected by a more challenging operating environment, marked by weaker consumer spending in Romania, an approximately 30% increase in fuel costs, and unfavorable foreign exchange movements, as well as by the temporary impact of the group’s market share expansion strategy and continued investments in the development of our operating platform.

In this context, EBITDA amounted to approximately RON 61 million, down 33% compared to the same period in 2025, while the net result was negative, at approximately RON 21 million.

During the first six months of the year, the group invested EUR 3 million in the development of its logistics infrastructure, process digitalization, operations automation, and equipment modernization, in line with its growth strategy and commitment to improving operational efficiency.

“Our distribution segment continued to deliver growth, supported by the expansion of the traditional retail and HoReCa channels, the consolidated contribution of our own brands, and the commercial synergies generated through the integration of the acquired companies. At the same time, we chose to prioritize strengthening commercial relationships and increasing market share, which play an essential role in supporting long-term growth and value creation,” said Cătălin Vasile, CEO of AQUILA.

The company head noted that the strategy had a temporary impact on commercial margins and profitability but created “a foundation for capitalizing on the investments made and supporting sustainable performance in the period ahead.”

World.title: Raiffeisen Bank Romania issues a new series of bonds denominated in RON
World.content:
Raiffeisen Bank, one of the largest banks in Romania, issued on August 13, 2026, a senior preferred eligible bond issue maturing in 2033, with a total value of RON 750 million.

The tranche represents the bank’s 0th series of eligible bonds, the financial institution informs through a statement sent to Economica.net.

The bond issue was addressed to institutional investors and was placed at a fixed coupon of 7.538% for the first five years, respectively 0.85% above the yield of the benchmark Romanian government bonds denominated in lei.

The bonds received a Baa1 rating from the rating agency Moody’s, two notches above Romania’s sovereign rating (Baa3).

After obtaining approval from the National Bank of Romania, the bonds are set to be included in the bank’s own funds and eligible liabilities base and listed on the Luxembourg and Bucharest stock exchanges.

In Romania, Raiffeisen Bank serves approximately 2.4 million individual and corporate customers. The bank has been active in Romania for more than 25 years.

Earlier this year, Raiffeisen bought Garanti BBVA's ​Romanian business for EUR 591 million, its ‌first significant acquisition in recent years. The deal marked a turning point for Raiffeisen, which has long been under pressure to withdraw ​from Russia due to its invasion of ​Ukraine and the imposition of Western sanctions on ⁠Moscow.

World.title: Central Romania: Winners Holding Investments, Finas Group commission 100 MWh energy storage battery after EUR 25 million investment
World.content:
Cluj-based companies Winners Holding Investments and Finas Group have commissioned the second energy storage battery in their joint portfolio, with a capacity of 100 MWh, following an investment of more than EUR 25 million.

The project, located in Glodeni, in Mureș County, comes several months after the companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding with China’s equipment producer Sieyuan Electric Co., Ltd., the companies said.

In April, the first unit in the companies’ portfolio, a 10 MWh battery located in Aghireșu, in Cluj County, was completed.

A third battery, with a capacity of 200 MWh, is scheduled for completion by November in Jibou, in Sălaj County. The project is valued at approximately EUR 45 million.

“Each battery brought online represents a concrete step toward a more stable and flexible energy infrastructure for Romania. We thank all our partners and collaborators for their professionalism and support during this challenging period for the energy market, as well as the management team, led by Tudor Strilciuc, for the rigorous implementation of these projects,” Claudiu Șugar, the representative of Winners Holding Investments and Finas Group, said.

World.title: Colliers: Rents up by 12% YoY for offices in central Bucharest amid limited supply
World.content:
The limited supply of modern, well-located space continues to put upward pressure on rents in central Bucharest, pushing them upwards by nearly 12% at the end of June 2026 compared to a year ago, according to the mid-year market update report from real estate consultant Colliers.

More than 100,000 square meters of office space were leased in Bucharest in the first half of 2026, slightly below the level recorded in the same period of 2025. Average rents in central Bucharest and other central areas rose from EUR 16 to EUR 18 per square meter, the same source said.

Across the market as a whole, average rents rose by around 3%, while new projects currently under development are quoting rents 10-15% above the levels typically seen in their respective submarkets. According to Colliers, this shows that although demand remains below historical averages, the limited availability of competitive office space is gradually strengthening the position of landlords with buildings in highly sought-after locations.

”The office market is currently sending two signals that may appear contradictory at first: leasing volumes remain modest, yet rents are rising for good-quality space. The explanation lies in limited supply, amid suboptimal leasing demand. Companies continue to look for modern, efficient and well-located buildings, while the number of genuine options meeting these criteria is shrinking in central areas,” said Victor Coșconel, Partner | Head of Leasing | Office & Industrial Agencies at Colliers.

New demand, meaning transactions that directly contribute to higher occupancy levels, recorded a slight increase in the first half of the year. Overall, however, leasing activity remains below the average of recent years and is closer to 2020-2021 levels than to those seen before the pandemic.

Nevertheless, Collier’s consultants are seeing signs that could support a gradual market recovery in the period ahead. Several companies are assessing new leases, including players entering the local market for the first time, particularly service centers from Western Europe seeking premises of several thousand square meters. The IT&C sector has also recovered slightly from recent lows, although activity remains well below pre-pandemic levels.

Another factor that could support demand is employees returning to the office more frequently. In many companies outside the IT sector, mandatory office attendance increased from one or two days per week to three days in 2025, while a growing number of employers are now discussing four days per week, a model that could become increasingly widespread.

The profile of companies driving demand is also changing. While the IT sector accounted for over half of Bucharest leasing activity in 2019, its share fell to around 20% in 2025, though it increased to 31% as of the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, financial services, the energy sector, construction companies, professional services and consumer goods companies each accounted for 8-9% of leasing demand in the first half of 2026.

Limited supply, even when considering the lackluster leading demand, remains the main factor supporting rental growth, Colliers consultants emphasized. No new office projects were delivered in Bucharest in the first half of 2026, following a 2025 with no deliveries.

However, the market is beginning to move again: just over 50,000 square meters of new office space are expected to be delivered over the full year, while projects currently under construction could add nearly 300,000 square meters of modern office space over the next few years. Even so, the volume remains low compared with peak years, when more than 200,000 square meters could be delivered in a single year.

The overall vacancy rate edged up to 12.25% in mid-2026, from 11.75% at the end of 2025, although the increase came mainly from peripheral areas. In competitive, well-located buildings, available space remains limited, with vacancies generally in single digits or even close to zero. In the Central Business District, vacancy remains at approximately 4%, while rents reach up to EUR 24 per square meter per month, compared with a high of EUR 22 at the end of last year.

The differences are also evident between submarkets. In Floreasca - Barbu Văcărescu, the vacancy rate stands at around 5%, while in Pipera it reaches 40%. This shows that Bucharest’s overall vacancies are heavily influenced by a small number of areas and buildings, while significantly less space is available in competitive projects.

This widening gap between modern, well-located buildings and the rest of the market is not unique to Bucharest. The regional ExCEEding Borders Office 2026 report, recently published by Colliers for the six main office markets in Central and Eastern Europe - Bucharest, Warsaw, Prague, Budapest, Bratislava and Sofia – shows that new office supply is at historical lows across the region, while prime rents are under upward pressure in all six capitals.

World.title: NBI ANALYSIS | Bucharest Strengthens Its Position in CEE: Competitive Pricing, Limited Supply and Convergence Potential
World.content:
News from Companies

Bucharest is entering a new stage of real estate market maturity. The pricing gap versus major Central and Eastern European capitals, a tightening residential supply pipeline and the strong performance of the hospitality sector are strengthening the investment case for Romania's capital.

Bucharest's real estate market is undergoing an accelerated process of maturation at a time when investors are placing greater emphasis on the balance between entry price, asset quality, liquidity and long-term appreciation potential. Bucharest retains a significant advantage: residential values remain competitive compared with more mature CEE markets, while new supply is becoming increasingly difficult to replicate in established locations and segments such as premium residential and hospitality continue to develop rapidly.



In 2026, the average asking price for new apartments in Bucharest reached approximately €2,636/sqm. By comparison, regional benchmarks for new residential properties indicate levels of approximately €4,330/sqm in Warsaw, €4,540/sqm in Bratislava, €5,320/sqm in Budapest and €6,400/sqm in Prague.



Even after the appreciation recorded in recent years, Bucharest therefore maintains a competitive entry price compared with major CEE capitals, alongside meaningful convergence potential as the market continues to mature.



The same trend is visible at macro level. In the first quarter of 2026, residential property prices in Romania increased by 7.8% year-on-year, above the 5.1% European Union average. While Romania is not leading the pace of appreciation in the region, the evolution confirms that the local market is participating in the broader repricing cycle across Central and Eastern Europe.

"Bucharest should increasingly be viewed within a regional context. The gap compared with capitals such as Warsaw, Prague or Budapest is not simply a pricing differential; it also indicates the convergence potential that Bucharest still has ahead. We have an increasingly sophisticated urban economy, a significant concentration of business activity, strong residential and investment demand and a growing hospitality sector, while real estate values remain competitive within the region. For investors, this creates an attractive equation, but the next cycle will not lift the entire market uniformly. Value will increasingly concentrate in well-positioned assets supported by infrastructure, efficiency, services and liquidity. The differentiator will no longer be the square metre alone, but the property's ability to generate and preserve value over time." said Vlad Musteată, CEO of North Bucharest Investments.

One of the strongest structural arguments for the market comes from the opposing trajectories of residential prices and future supply. In Bucharest, housing prices have increased by approximately 60% over the past six years, while the number of building permits has declined by around 45% over the past three years. A reduced development pipeline limits the market's ability to respond quickly to new demand cycles and increases the differentiation between standard products and assets that are difficult to replicate.



Within this equation, the scarcity of well-positioned assets is becoming a value driver in itself.



Market maturation is also redefining the premium segment. Beyond location, buyers are increasingly focused on quality, efficiency, technology, services and property liquidity. At the same time, demand is becoming more international, supported by entrepreneurs, regional executives, expatriates and the Romanian diaspora, who increasingly evaluate Bucharest against other European markets.



In 2025, Bucharest recorded a 12% increase in RevPAR, revenue per available room, the highest growth rate among the six CEE capitals analysed, outperforming Warsaw (+9.1%), Prague (+8.3%) and the regional average (+8.9%). Bucharest also ranks third within CEE-6 in terms of ADR and RevPAR levels, behind Prague and Budapest.



This performance confirms the continued development of the hospitality sector and supports the emergence of new asset categories, including aparthotels and serviced residences, driven by business travel, expatriates, bleisure and medical tourism. For investors, these segments add the potential for recurring income and professional asset management.



Bucharest's investment case is therefore not built around a single indicator, but around the convergence of several trends: a competitive entry price compared with major CEE capitals, residential value appreciation, a tightening future supply pipeline, increasingly sophisticated demand and strong hospitality performance.

"We are already seeing a shift in the way investors assess Bucharest. The question is no longer simply how much a property costs today, but what return it can generate, how liquid it will remain five or ten years from now, and how the asset compares with alternative opportunities across the region. Bucharest is increasingly being evaluated not only as a local real estate market, but as a regional destination for capital. The combination of entry pricing, market maturation and limited supply could become one of the capital's key competitive advantages over the coming years." concludes Vlad Musteată, CEO of North Bucharest Investments.

Bucharest does not need to become the next Warsaw or the next Prague. The opportunity lies in strengthening its own position within Central and Eastern Europe at a time when capital is becoming increasingly selective and the distinction between simply owning property and holding a high-performing investment asset is becoming increasingly important.



*This is a press release.

World.title: Bucharest Stock Exchange-listed Transgaz reports 40% lower net profit
World.content:
Romanian majority state-owned and BVB-listed gas transmission operator Transgaz (BVB: TGN) reduced its net profit by more than 40% in the first half of this year, from RON 519 million in the same period last year to RON 303 million, as a result of declining revenues and increasing operating expenses, according to a new report.

Revenues from operating activity recorded a decrease of 4% compared with last year, respectively a decrease of RON 61 million, while operating expenses increased by 13%.

Consolidated gross profit of the Transgaz group recorded a decrease of RON 235 million, and the consolidated net profit recorded a decrease of RON 215 million.

At the same time, revenues from the operating activity of the subsidiaries in the Republic of Moldova recorded an increase of 113%, respectively by RON 19 million. The company’s results for the first half of 2026 were mainly influenced by the revenues from the natural gas transmission activity carried out by Vestmoldtransgaz. Transgaz obtained RON 167 million in this way.

Transgaz was listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange following a primary public offering carried out in December 2007. Over the past year, the value of Transgaz stocks increased by 99.38%, from RON 48.1 per share in September 2025 to RON 95.9 on August 13.

Also this week, Transgaz announced that it had contracted an EUR 300 million loan from Banca Transilvania. The financing is intended for the development and modernization of the national natural gas transport infrastructure.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Democracy Digest: US Charges Mexican Cartel Members over Czech Weapons Deal
World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

Multiple challenges

World.title: What Our Sons Never Asked: Sarajevo Film Breaks Generational Silence About Siege
World.content:
Some of the film’s most charged moments happen in the space between a father finishing a memory and a son deciding what to do with it.

In one scene, Faruk describes risking his own safety to put out fires caused by shelling. His son’s response, a simple, unrehearsed statement of pride, visibly catches his father off-guard. In another, Ismet, who worked as a hotel driver during the siege, describes coming home one day to find his own father, and his son, Adnan, has to work through memories of his own in real time.

Nur said she was conscious of never pushing anyone past what they wanted to say. “I never want to push people to say something that they really don’t want,” she said.

There was real tension in some of these exchanges, a son signalling he wanted to keep certain memories to himself, sometimes, she suspected, to protect a father from seeing how much a story had affected him. Handing the questions to family members rather than asking them herself was, she said, “very experimental”.

A trained interviewer knows how to sit inside a silence and let it do the work; a son doing it for the first time is more likely to wonder if he’s doing it right, whether he should move on to the next question. But what came out of that unfamiliarity, in Nur’s view, was something more honest than a polished interview would have produced.

Feelings that clearly hadn’t been spoken aloud before, including the moment she calls one of her favourites in the whole film: a son telling his father, plainly, that he’s proud of him. “In a lot of families,” she said, “it’s not so much that you tell your parents you’re proud of them. You show it through actions, but maybe not through words.”

Asked how the film manages to hold the brutality of the siege, the deaths, the deprivation, alongside its lighter, almost tender moments, like an improvised birthday cake, Nur pushed back gently on the idea that these are two separate things requiring balance.

The people she interviewed brought up the lighter memories themselves, unprompted – playing football with the journalists, for one – and she came to see those moments as a form of resistance in their own right, inseparable from the horror around them.

A story that didn’t make the final cut, but stayed with her, involves Ismet smoking a cigarette in Baščaršija with a friend while hearing grenades in the distance nearby, and later describing it as the best cigarette of his life.

“It wouldn’t be the best cigarette of his life if the other things weren’t going on,” Nur said. “It’s so intertwined that, for me, it only felt natural to bring both in.” Still, she said she stayed conscious of the balance throughout editing, wary of leaning too heavily on the good stories, in case the film ended up suggesting the siege “wasn’t that bad”.

The film’s end credits list crowdfunding donors ahead of institutional backers, a reflection, Camo said, of how the project actually got made.

The original funding covered a short film. Once it became clear in the edit that the material demanded something longer, that funding no longer covered the film that existed. Additional Dutch funds proved hard to secure mid-production, and some of the feedback the team received was pointed: a strong story, but “European history”, with funders preferring projects more directly tied to the Netherlands, despite what Camo sees as an obvious, substantial connection between the Netherlands and the Bosnian war.

Crowdfunding became the last resort, and it worked. Donors included people from Bosnia, members of the Bosnian community in the Netherlands, and friends and colleagues of the filmmakers. That money went largely toward archive footage, by far the production’s biggest cost. “Without their help, it was really crucial,” Camo said.

The Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) supported the archive research for the film.

‘We don’t know this history’

World.title: North Macedonia Indicts Ex-Deputy PM Grubi Over Lottery Machines Purchase
World.content:
North Macedonia’s former First Deputy Prime Minister, Artan Grubi. Photo: vlada.mk.

Prosecutors in Skopje on Thursday charged Artan Grubi and seven others with abusing their official positions to enable the purchase of video lottery terminals that could not legally be put into operation, costing the State Lottery more than 8.2 million euros.

Grubi is accused of allegedly pushing for the move in 2023 and 2024 while serving as first deputy prime minister, despite knowing that the procedure was illegal and that the State Lottery could never use the gambling machines.

“The defendants, acting jointly during 2023 and 2024, took actions that exceeded the limits of their respective powers and duties, with the intention of causing harm to the legal entity the State Lottery,” the prosecution said in the indictment.

The gambling machines were subsequently purchased but, according to the prosecution, were never used.

Grubi has denied any wrongdoing.

The indictment came days before a house-arrest order for Grubi is due to expire. Prosecutors have asked the court to extend his house arrest, while also seeking 30 days in detention for another of the accused, the former State Lottery director Perparim Bajrami, who remains at large.

Grubi fled North Macedonia in December 2024 as authorities moved to investigate suspected wrongdoing at the State Lottery.

An international call for his arrest was issued, and he remained outside the country for more than a year. Grubi initially denied that he was on the run, saying he had travelled to Kosovo for private reasons and would return after completing his obligations there.

He eventually returned to North Macedonia in February this year and was arrested at the Blace border crossing while entering from Kosovo.

He was released from custody the same day after prosecutors asked for house arrest instead of custody, arguing that most of the evidence had already been secured and citing concerns over his personal safety in detention.

A court approved the measure, prompting widespread criticism over the relatively lenient treatment of a former senior official who had already fled the country once.

Grubi, a senior figure in the now opposition, ethnic Albanian Democratic Union for Integration, DUI party, served as first deputy prime minister and minister of political system and inter-community relations from 2020 to 2024.

In December 2024, the US State Department sanctioned him for alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Quarter-Century After Peace Deal, North Macedonia Has Yet to Fully Heal
World.content:
The anniversary comes at a time when Ohrid is again at the centre of political debate.

The Democratic Union for Integration, DUI, the main ethnic Albanian party that was formed by the former leaders of the insurgency, and has been in government for much of the time since the conflict ended – before being relegated to the opposition after the 2024 general elections – has accused the current VMRO DPMNE party-led government of undermining the agreement.

It has pointed to several developments.

These include challenges to the constitutionality of the Law on the Use of Languages, opposition to bar exams being taken in Albanian, the abolition of the so-called “Balancer” mechanism for ensuring equitable ethnic representation in public employment – and a current push to adopt an new Law on Fair and Equitable Representation, designed to replace the “Balancer” system.

Popetrevski, however, doubts a coordinated government plan to dismantle Ohrid. “I see no basis for claiming that there is a coordinated plan to dismantle the Framework Agreement,” he says.

“After 25 years, it is not only legitimate but necessary to reassess how the solutions stemming from the Framework Agreement are functioning,” he adds.

The “Balancer” system illustrates the dilemma. Introduced to help ensure equitable representation of ethnic communities in public institutions, it achieved much of its intended purpose, Popetrevski says – but also produced “absurdities”, such as cases of people changing their declared ethnic identity to obtain employment.

The language law, he adds, also should not be beyond scrutiny, particularly given the concerns raised by the Venice Commission over aspects of its implementation, including the broad use of bilingualism in court proceedings.

At the same time, Popetrevski cautions against ignoring the cumulative effect of several contentious issues being raised within a short period.

“Politics does not happen in a laboratory, in an isolated system,” Popetrevski says. If questions concerning language, equitable representation and the Badinter mechanism are raised simultaneously, this may create an impression among some Albanians “that there is a step backwards from 2001”.

That is why, he argues, any changes to the deal must come with a clear political message.

“If dysfunctional solutions are being corrected, it must be unequivocally clear that the constitutional fundamental values and principles are not being called into question,” he asserts.

At the same time, Popetrevski rejects the DUI’s claim that is the sole “guardian” of Ohrid. “The DUI has no exclusive right to interpret and defend the Framework Agreement,” he insists.

A party that spent almost two decades in government, he argues, also bears responsibility for the agreement’s shortcomings.

“If every criticism of a particular solution is declared an attack on the Framework Agreement, then the agreement is transformed from a mechanism for building cohesion into a tool for day-to-day political mobilization,” he says.

Popetrevski’s assessment is also shaped by his own recollections of 2001.

Aged 25, he was reporting for one of the country’s national television stations when the conflict erupted. Covering a war in his own country while attempting to maintain journalistic distance was one of the most difficult professional challenges of his career.

“In a conflict, nuances are very easily erased. Either you are ‘ours’ or you are ‘theirs’,” he recalls.

In an article several years ago, he wrote that those in his newsroom who managed to be “journalists first and Macedonians and Christians afterwards” were a minority. He stresses that this was not a criticism of his colleagues, but a reflection of the atmosphere of the time.

A quarter of a century later, he believes distance has made those lost nuances easier to see.

“There was genuine dissatisfaction among Albanians with their position in the state. Acknowledging that does not mean justifying the taking up of arms,” he says.

The reverse is equally true, he adds: condemning the use of weapons does not mean denying that serious problems existed before the conflict.

“Perhaps the most important thing we know today is that there was no military solution,” he assesses.

The wider international context was crucial. The United States and European Union opposed any redrawing of borders, even though partition and territorial changes were among the ideas circulating during the conflict.

Beyond simply ‘not shooting each other’

World.title: Nearly 200 People Rescued From the Sea as Fire Ravages Omiš Area
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – An utterly devastating wildfire in the Omiš area has left a trail of destruction along the Croatian coast, with nearly 200 people rescued from the sea.

Those rescued headed for the safety of the sea and boats, fleeing the flames during a dramatic overnight evacuation. The enormous fire rapidly spread across the Omiš area on Thursday night, forcing residents and visitors to seek safety wherever they could. Index reports that as the flames approached the coastline, dozens of people, including children, entered the sea or boarded vessels in an attempt to escape the fire.

A large-scale maritime rescue operation was launched after authorities received reports at around 23:40 that a significant number of people were in the sea and on boats without supervision. The National Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Rijeka coordinated the operation together with the Split Port Authority and its stations in Makarska, Milna and Hvar.

Police vessels, the Croatian Coast Guard, customs officials and the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service were also involved. Members of the public and a private passenger-boat company joined the rescue effort.

The most intensive phase of the operation took place between 12:15 a.m. and 2:45 a.m., with rescuers moving between the coastline, the sea and vessels where people had taken shelter.

According to the latest information, port authority crews rescued 194 people, mainly from the areas between Nemira and Ruskamen. Authorities noted that the final number of people rescued could be higher, as other emergency services, private citizens and companies were also involved in the operation.

The fire has also resulted in a serious number of injuries. According to KBC Split, 36 people sought medical assistance, with 14 subsequently hospitalised. Ten of those patients are being treated in intensive care, and seven are in life-threatening condition.

Most of the patients in intensive care suffered serious burns. Doctors described the treatment of burn victims as particularly complex and said that preparations were already under way to transfer some patients to hospitals in Zagreb to ensure they receive the best possible care. Among those seriously injured is a 17-year-old, according to information reported by Index. Further details about individual patients have not been released because of medical privacy.

The response to the disaster is continuing on the ground.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković has already arrived in Omiš together with several government ministers. A crisis meeting is being held with senior firefighters, local officials, Civil Protection, police and representatives of KBC Split. President Zoran Milanović is also scheduled to visit Omiš today. According to the Office of the President, he is expected to meet with the mayor of Omiš and representatives of the firefighting service before visiting areas affected by the fire. His arrival is scheduled for 14:00.

Following the overnight rescue operation, maritime authorities continued monitoring the affected coastline as the emergency response moved into a new phase. For many caught in the path of the flames, however, the night will be remembered for the extraordinary decision to escape into the Adriatic, and for the rescue crews who went out into the darkness to bring them back to safety.
