World.title: Australians are held hostage and tortured overseas – and we play roulette with them
World.content:
NationalHuman rights Opinion Australians are held hostage and tortured overseas – and we play roulette with them

Alice Edwards August 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Britain now has a senior official whose job is to bring home citizens wrongfully detained abroad. Australia decided it doesn’t need one. With states increasingly weaponising hostage diplomacy, and Australians facing heightened dangers, the government has rejected a Senate recommendation for a special envoy for wrongfully detained Australians. Hostages: Kylie Moore-Gilbert (centre), now free in Australia, and still trapped overseas (clockwise from top left) Yang Hengjun, Mo Munshi, Gordon Ng and Robert Pether. Illustration by Monique Westermann Britain appointed former Foreign Office minister Alistair Burt as its first envoy for complex consular detentions. In cases referred to him by the foreign secretary, he will provide senior strategic oversight, co-ordinate work across government, engage with families and offer ministers an independent perspective. Hostage diplomacy is coercion through deliberately inflicted suffering: the definition of torture reduced to statecraft.



Australia has chosen a different course. In its formal response to the Senate inquiry in June, the government said it “partially accepts” the recommendation. It will retain its complex case committee and appoint special envoys only when officials decide the case requires one, arguing this provides flexibility across a diverse caseload. In my four years as United Nations special rapporteur on torture and other ill-treatment, my caseload returned again and again to hostage diplomacy: individuals detained abroad not for anything they had done, but for what they were worth. I dealt with families as angry with their own governments as with the kidnappers – because they felt ignored and their demands unanswered. What they wanted was rarely complicated. They wanted to know that someone senior was responsible, and that the file would not go quiet when the official handling it moved on. Related Article Exclusive

Foreign relations Don’t shut down families of Aussies in trouble overseas, high-profile former prisoners warn This practice belongs in a torture mandate for a reason. Many former hostages report being both physically and psychologically tortured. Some are held in deplorable conditions, including in underground or dirty and windowless cells. When a person is held in solitary confinement, denied consular access and threatened with decades in prison so that their suffering – and their family’s – will force a government to pay, trade or concede, the pain is not incidental to the detention. It is the point of it. That is coercion through deliberately inflicted suffering: the definition of torture reduced to statecraft.



And it is spreading. Reliable global figures are difficult to compile, but the James W. Foley Legacy Foundation recorded at least 142 Americans wrongfully detained between 2015 and 2025, against 54 in the preceding decade – a rise of 163 per cent. Canberra’s own travel advice warns of arbitrary detention in 10 countries, including China, Iran and Russia. Australian writer Yang Hengjun remains imprisoned in China under a suspended death sentence. Another Australian citizen, Gordon Ng, is serving a sentence in Hong Kong under the territory’s national security law. Engineer Robert Pether cannot leave Iraq despite his release from prison, amid grave concerns about his health. Each case requires sustained senior advocacy across years, agencies and changes of personnel. Related Article Opinion

China relations Wong is in an exquisite predicament. She must make China fear her response Justin Bassi ASPI executive director The government deserves credit for accepting parts of the Senate’s reform program: a published framework for assessing wrongful detention, better identification and data collection, stronger family support and deterrence as a foreign-policy priority. Yet the central problem remains. Responsibility is dispersed, and some cases may never be identified as wrongful detention at all. Kylie Moore-Gilbert, who spent more than two years imprisoned in Iran on espionage charges she denied, benefited from an ad hoc Australian envoy who helped negotiate her release. Her concern is that most cases never receive comparable attention. “The vast majority of wrongful detention cases do not benefit from having an envoy appointed,” she told me.



Some remain within the complex case committee, while others “languish within the much larger pool of consular cases”, never recognised as wrongful in the first place. Australian businessman Mohammed “Mo” Munshi, released from prison in June 2024, for example, remains trapped in Mongolia under an indefinite travel ban. Former prisoner Kylie Moore-Gilbert has become an advocate for the release of Robert Pether. That identification gap can determine whether a case receives a co-ordinated diplomatic strategy or is treated as an ordinary overseas prosecution. And the structure is vulnerable. When wars or mass evacuations occur, complex-case personnel are diverted into the all-hands response; staff rotation forces repeated handovers and disrupts relationships with families already living through prolonged uncertainty. Britain’s model is modest but meaningful. Its envoy does not automatically assume every case; the foreign secretary refers them. The crucial distinction is continuity: Britain and other Australian allies, the US and Canada, have a standing senior official building expertise across a portfolio of cases. Australia creates one only occasionally, requiring a new appointment, mandate and working structure each time. The Australian approach seems to prioritise bureaucracy over speedy, life-saving responses. It underestimates the importance of consistency over time, both for families and for building relations with the other side’s negotiating team.





Alice Edwards is a writer and lawyer and, for four years until July this year, was the United Nations special rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

Victoria Police Defence lawyer Lee Ristivojevic, for Setka, told the court the prosecution’s case was “weak”. “It’s submitted that the nature of the allegations, of the charges, that if he was to be found guilty, he’s not likely to receive a term of imprisonment for the offences,” she said. “We say that it is not a serious example of the offence.” Ristivojevic said Setka had “what I’d described as a positive bail history in terms of court orders”, and that it was “not suggested he’s breached any conditions of bail”. She further submitted that a compelling reason to release Setka on bail was that he provides essential care for his elderly mother.



Related Article Updated

Building Bad Setka charged with harassing a CFMEU administrator Magistrate Nicole Spicer ultimately granted Setka’s bail application, noting that none of the alleged victims had sought personal safety intervention orders. “I do consider that the risk can be brought to an acceptable level by the imposition of conditions targeted to make clear that the particular behaviour that you have allegedly engaged in in making social media commentary of a personal and allegedly harassing nature simply cannot occur whilst you are subject to the grant of bail,” Spicer said. She imposed bail conditions that Setka “not threaten or harass any employee or representative of the CFMEU administrator, or any person named in criminal charges” against him. She further ordered him not to “make posts or comments on any social media platform which are threatening, intimidating or use obscene language directed towards or about such individuals”. Police established Operation Hawk in mid-2024, in response to this masthead’s Building Bad series, which exposed criminal behaviour and corruption in the CFMEU. World.title: Fozball hits unwanted 33-year record in bizarrely boring loss to Dolphins
World.content:
Manly 0 Dolphins 22 SportNRLNRL 2026 Fozball hits unwanted 33-year record in bizarrely boring loss to Dolphins Dan Walsh August 14, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

At various points in 2026, Manly have been one of the most exhilarating attacking sides in the NRL. The Dolphins still are, and are finals-bound for the first time in their history as a result. So at half-time in Friday’s clash at 4 Pines Park, you could only ask, what on earth had happened? Loading The same questions remained at full-time too, along with how Selwyn Cobbo defied the laws of man and nature to ground a 57th-minute try in the corner while wearing heavy contact from Clayton Faulalo and Reuben Garrick. From an 8-0 half-time lead, the Dolphins closed out the grittiest of grinding wins with 31 errors in total. But their 22-0 victory margin is really the only take-away in a contest that barely got out of first gear, and never threatened to find second or third.



Manly’s finals hopes, already circling the drain, slipped straight down it when Jamayne Isaako provided another rare highlight – latching onto an intercept and setting up an 85-metre try to NSW Origin flyer Jack Bostock. Loading The locals summed up Manly’s slide into ignominy best. When Lehi Hopoate was denied a late try for putting a hand into touch, fans made an early exit – neatly wrapping up a campaign under Kieran Foran that had once promised so much. ‘Fozball’ is officially done for the season, and Manly were held to zero on home soil for the first time since 1993. Until the Dolphins’ backline stars shone brightly enough to seal a win that keeps them in touch with the top four, this Friday night affair was most notable for nothing much happening.



A pair of sin-bins for Manly speedster Tolu Koula (28th minute) and Dolphins back-rower Connelly Lemuelu (35th minute) for professional fouls hardly opened up a 12-on-12 shoot-out. Instead, the visitors’ safety-first footy and home side’s shot confidence held firm. Manly spent much of the first 20 minutes camped on the Dolphins’ tryline. They never threatened to cross it though as passes went to ground and over the sideline. Manly lock Jake Trbojevic. Getty Images After holding firm in defence, the Dolphins offered little in attack themselves before finally crossing the Brookvale Rubicon into Manly’s half in the 25th minute. Even then, their first attacking crack at the Sea Eagles line amounted to only a penalty goal after a Jason Saab high tackle.



Related Article Live

NRL 2026 NRL LIVE updates: Rabbitohs make three try-saving tackles to lead against Bulldogs When they next came calling, Jeremy Marshall-King snuck out of dummy-half and caught Koula offside, with Kodi Nikorima finally skinning the shortened defence for the opening try. Hopes of a brighter second half were put on ice when Manly’s Jake Simpkins fumbled a ball a metre into the air from dummy-half before regathering, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow misjudged a kick take by roughly 10 metres. And as much as anything, those two bemusing moments, from two of the game’s more enterprising attacking teams, said it all.

World.title: Students held a lesson in civic participation
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Students held a lesson in civic participation August 14, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Premier Ben Carroll was wrong to say he would prefer students to be in school learning, rather than protesting (″⁣Students ditch class to protest One Nation″⁣, 14/8). We read about concerns that people are becoming disconnected from politics, yet object when tomorrow’s voters choose to connect through a few brief moments of participation. What better way to learn? As a retired teacher, I would easily run out of fingers if I counted the many hundreds of times schools required students to take part in activities that had far less relevance to any educational curriculum. Anybody who seriously believes that those protesting students were somehow retarding their education has little understanding of education. Mostly, of course, objectors are merely engaging in politically motivated naysaying.

Dennis Dodd, Shepparton Seeing dangers through young eyes

Despite Barnaby Joyce’s statement that the students protesting about Pauline Hanson were “brainwashed by Labor”, I believe that they actually understand the dangers of One Nation’s policies. How refreshing to see the younger generation recognising the dangers of what an alarming proportion of the older generation don’t.

Ken Finley, Mount Martha An exercise in engagement

Good on the students for expressing their voices against the ideologies of One Nation. Of course, there has been the predictable response and dismissal of their voices by conservative politicians (“‘Socialist’ teachers encouraging students to protest One Nation: Joyce”, 13/08). They dismiss the voices of students at their peril, and forget that in a few years many will be eligible to vote. I find it a bit hypocritical of politicians to try to silence the voices of students, yet we want them to be more engaged with the political process and with civics in general. We also tend to forget that when students take action, they are expressing lessons from school. Yes, teachers would probably prefer students to stay at school and attend their classes. But we also want our students to be engaged with the world and the issue they care about.

Jeremy de Korte, Newington



Take protest to ballot box

The students’ protest is not comparable to climate action protests, which were about everybody and a global issue. It is not comparable to protesting against a government, since that is in response to the actual actions of those in power. This is against a party seeking to gain support for its bid to exercise some power. If you don’t like it, vote against it. If you’re too young to vote – are you also too immature to understand why? This shows a misunderstanding, or rejection, of the democratic process. Educators, and perhaps some parents, should be ashamed.

Anthony Caughey, Elwood THE FORUM Private benefits

May I suggest an alternative view to opponents of government funding of non-state schools (Letters, 13/8)? Our taxes support the education of all children, regardless of school. Parents choosing to top that up with a non-government school (usually with considerable sacrifice) pay for these “state-of-the-art facilities” mentioned, often contributing to the school building fund in addition to fees.

Consider also the alleviation of strain on state schools by these parents, as well as the social and community benefits afforded by the diversity in education style.

Removing base government funding would make educational choice a privilege only of the uber-rich.

Lisa Langtree, Greensborough Celebrate the frogs

People bemoan the lack of biodiversity in this state and the state of many species. Now there is a growing second population of endangered grass frogs, in a place set aside for biodiversity (″⁣How did frogs get to Brighton? For council, it’s a $40,000 question″⁣, 14/8). Someone or something has arrested their slide into extinction. If the council had any sense, it would celebrate it, not condemn it.

Benjamin Levy, Caulfield North



Job expectations

It’s just not right that CEOs get bonuses for doing their job. Surgeons don’t get a bonus for saving a life or a pilot for landing a plane. These executives are employed (like everyone else) for the experience and knowledge they bring to their profession. Why pay them more for doing their expected job?

Linda Lewis, Watsonia Independence daze

Your correspondent’s view (Letters, 14/8) that since Wales was incorporated into England in 1536 most Welsh people haven’t accepted it may or may not be true, but it ignores the possibility that the English may not have accepted it either. It brings to mind the sentiment often expressed whenever Scotland considers a referendum to decide its ties with England; that the best way to guarantee Scottish independence is to let the English vote as well.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully Bin there, done that

I took my rubbish out for its weekly pick-up. It’s a small-sized bin and it was not even a quarter full. With both a fortnightly green waste and a recycle bin, plus container return and soft plastics recycling we have less need for rubbish disposal. With a little effort by us as consumers (including more thoughtful buying at the supermarket), a large bin-full fortnightly should be more than adequate for every household. Weekly large bin pick-up is a surefire route to laziness and a strain on our environment. Silly proposal by Jess Wilson. Bin it!

Freya Bennett, Baxter Nothing to brag about

Andrew Bragg’s suggestion that low-income Australians should accept substandard building standards in order to afford a house to live in is a low blow and not the answer to our housing problem. Living in a cold house during winter or a hot box in summer, only serves to increase energy bills and health issues for many. Or telling people to put on another sweater is akin to saying stop buying smashed avocado for breakfast. Rude.

Andrea Morrow, Northcote Our better angels

I have been undergoing cancer treatment at The Alfred for a few months. It has been an extraordinary, reflective, revelatory and surprisingly joyful experience. The care has been simply superb – from reception to nursing, technical services and senior specialists – unfailingly competent, caring, sensitive, respectful and engaging — drawn from many parts of the world. It is a reminder of all the better angels politicians should appeal to, rather than self-interest. They might heed writers like Rutger Bregman, who declare faith in the innate goodness and decency of human beings, and quote many examples of individual communities bonding and co-operating during crises.

The contrast between this and the way politics has been practised for 30 years is appalling – preoccupation with re-election, focus group analyses, marginal electorate analyses, preference deals, ″⁣wedging″⁣ opponents, regardless of the national interest. The scale and scope of necessary change is immense – if change does not occur the future looks bleak.

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne



Humourless chat

I recently tested the humanity and approachability of ChatGPT asking, “If I had $10 in one pants pocket and $10 in the other what would I have?” The answer, as we all know, is “somebody else’s trousers!“

The answer I received was “$20” with an explanatory equation ($10 + $10 = $20). How dull is that?

Neil Falconer, Castlemaine Don’t target the person

Are you personally responsible for every decision a government makes? Should you be held individually accountable for their actions? I think not. So why should we penalise a young Iranian student by preventing them studying here (″⁣Unis’ hardline ban on Iranian students labelled ‘unfair‴⁣⁣, 14/8)? This hurts one individual student and their family. It does not ″⁣send a message″⁣ to the country’s leaders. Travelling through Iran showed me that the people are the most hospitable and welcoming in the world (and I have been to more than 100 countries). Strangers thanked me for visiting and for understanding that the ordinary person is not the same as the regime. Sanctions should be applied to a country’s leaders and exporters, but not an individual seeking a better life.

Julie Christensen, Blackburn North No longer reliable ally

I find the reported comments of US officials assuring Australia that all is well with the AUKUS treaty amusing (“Pentagon ‘very clear’ over AUKUS”, 14/8). Their reassurances are worthless. When are Anthony Albanese and his cabinet going to notice that our once reliable ally has seen its institutions and its democracy dismantled by a president who wreaks havoc wherever he goes?

Does Albanese seriously think that Trump would jump to our rescue if we were invaded? Anyone who thinks he’s only there until the end of his second term is deluding themselves. He is reportedly already preparing ways to manipulate this November’s mid-term elections or even cancel them by declaring a state of emergency.

Trump will look for a way to stay in the White House. He is certainly not building his ballroom for the convenience of his successors. The Albanese government should base Australia’s security policy on the probability that the United States will for the foreseeable future be a far less predictable ally than it has been for the past 80 years.

Edmund Doogue, Crawley, WA Protest brings change

I attended secondary school in the conservative province of Alberta, Canada, in the 1960s. I and some of my female friends skipped school to attend a protest about supermarkets paying us female staff less than men for stacking the shelves – they said we were doing different jobs. This protest motivated us to gather female students back at school to confront the principal and tell him we did not agree with the school policy to make all female students take “cooking and sewing” classes but not allow us to take “woodwork or metalwork”. We got into trouble for skipping school and holding an in-school protest. But it was worth the detention we were given.

We knew things needed to change and we needed to play our part in making that happen. The catalyst for our protesting was not “socialist” teachers but young women who thought a better future would be there for everyone if changes were made.

Sandy Guest, Yarraville Macbeth reads the news

I would like to have a go at understanding Shakespeare reading the news (Letters, 14/8). It might go like this: ″⁣Life’s but a walking shadow, a poor player, that struts and frets his hour upon the stage, and then is heard no more; it is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. So let’s cross to the tennis.″⁣

Simon Thornton, Alphington



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Protests

I have great faith in the young people who have chosen to protest against the politics of hate, racism and intolerance. They clearly want Australian politicians to solve issues rather than create them.

Linelle Gibson, Williamstown I was so heartened seeing the kids turn out in protest against Pauline Hanson. They are fighting for their future, and ours.

Cate Broadbent, Yarraville Bravo to the student protesters. Their active participation, contribution and commitment to Australia’s democratic process is to be congratulated.

Julienne Gleeson, Portarlington



Frogs

Re the article ″⁣How did frogs get to Brighton?″⁣ (24/8), they’ve got class.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove You have to feel for the growling grass frogs of Brighton, unwanted and endangered. It’s not easy being green.

Paul Custance, Highett The illegal immigrant population of growling frogs in the wonderful Yakulit William Nature Reserve should be deported immediately.

Richard Druce, Mount Macedon Furthermore

We know Iranians are mistreated in their own country, so when they come here our response is to mistreat them a bit more? (“Unis’ hardline ban on Iranian students labelled ’unfair‴⁣⁣, 14/8). Surely we can be better than this.

Duncan Reid, Flemington For a moment I thought they were going to deport the PM. (‴⁣⁣Deportation on PM’s mind″⁣, 24/8) and I thought ″⁣C’mon, it was only a gaffe.″⁣

Myra Fisher, Brighton East



Anthony Albanese’s melon gaffe would pass the pub test.

Adrian Tabor, Point Lonsdale Anthony Albanese has found a new secret weapon – Andrew Bragg and his views on tax rates, superannuation and housing.

Helmut Simon, Thomson Finally

With apologies to Freud, sometimes a melon is just a melon.

Bruce McMillan, Grovedale

World.title: Man allegedly lured to Kelvin Grove under pretence of date before fatal carjacking
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCourts Man allegedly lured to Kelvin Grove under pretence of date before fatal carjacking Andrew Stafford and and Dominique Tassell Updated August 14, 2026 — 7:46pm ,first published 1:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 27-year-old was allegedly lured to Brisbane’s inner north under false pretences before a group of teenagers fatally assaulted him and stole his car. Oliver Conroy thought he was going on a date, but was instead assaulted and carjacked on Victoria Park Road in Kelvin Grove about 10.30pm on July 24. Seven teenagers have been charged with murder and remain behind bars. Loading Charges against the teens, including two girls aged 14 and 15, were upgraded after Conroy died almost two weeks after the alleged assault in Brisbane’s inner north.



They face life sentences under controversial “adult crime, adult time” laws introduced by Queensland’s LNP government. The teens are accused of assaulting Conroy and stealing his BYD Shark 6 vehicle on July 24. He was taken to hospital and died almost a fortnight later, on August 6. Oliver Conroy, 27, died after an alleged assault in Kelvin Grove on July 24. A total of nine children – six boys and three girls – were initially charged over the attack.



A week after Conroy’s death, seven teens – five boys aged from 15 to 17 and the 14 and 15-year-old girls – were each charged with an additional count of murder. It boosts the number of juveniles charged with murder under the new Queensland laws from four to 11. Police are appealing for witnesses that may have been driving along or near Victoria Park Road on July 24. Queensland Police Service It also marks the first two teenage girls to be charged with murder under the legislation. Magistrate Anne Thacker remanded in custody a 17-year-old boy who appeared by videolink in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Friday ahead of his next appearance on August 24.



Six co-accused, who did not appear, were also remanded in custody, with their matters adjourned until September 1. Police are appealing for July 24 dashcam and CCTV footage captured on Kelvin Grove’s Victoria Park Road between 9.30pm and 10.30pm and Holland Park West’s Barter Avenue between 11.30pm and 11.50pm as part of the investigation. They hope to speak to a potential witness who was driving a dark-coloured SUV on Victoria Park Road. The second potential witness was last seen driving a blue sedan at 10.16pm on Carraway Street at the intersection with Victoria Park Road. Queensland Police Service Police are also seeking witnesses and footage between 8.10pm and 8.40pm on Kelvin Grove Road, near the Musk Avenue intersection in Kelvin Grove.



Two potential witnesses have been asked to come forward after they were seen driving in the area. The first was last seen driving a dark-coloured SUV along Victoria Park Road, Blamey Street and Musk Avenue about 10.15pm. The second was last seen driving a blue sedan at 10.16pm on Carraway Street at the Victoria Park Road intersection. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Two forwards, two mindsets: The contrasting philosophies driving the Hawks and Magpies
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Two forwards, two mindsets: The contrasting philosophies driving the Hawks and Magpies Jake Niall August 14, 2026 — 7:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Hawthorn were interested in Lachie Schultz during 2023, when the then Fremantle forward was exploring a move back to Victoria, but, in-part due to Collingwood’s appeal as the premiers and the Magpies’ more aggressive pursuit, Schultz ended up in black and white. Had Schultz gone to the Hawks, who were 16th in 2023 and seemingly still mired mid-rebuild, then it’s a reasonable bet to say that Jack Ginnivan wouldn’t have been strutting the social media stage as a Hawk. Hawthorn star Jack Ginnivan and Collingwood’s Lachie Schultz. Photos: AFL Photos/Getty Images. Artwork: Matt Davidson Further, had Schultz chosen Hawthorn – and vice versa – then it’s entirely possible that Ginnivan might not have been traded from Collingwood. Schultz was due to be an unrestricted free agent in 2024. Collingwood were willing to jump early, and pay the premium, having met with Schultz in the days after their storied premiership, in which Ginnivan had been the sub and recorded only seven touches in three quarters.



When Ginnivan met with Sam Mitchell and his football lieutenant Rob McCartney at Mitchell’s home (how many players have been hosted in that abode?) following the 2023 grand final, it was evident that this would be a more suitable marriage than Ginnivan’s three-year union with Collingwood, where his profile – on social media in particular – exceeded his station as a player in the competition. Schultz, conversely, would prove a better fit for the Magpies in terms of his playing style and ethos. Not as flashy or cocky. Not one to play to the madding crowds, to rile up the opposition. “Shooter” was a cog in the machine, and a defensive desperado; as nearly every person I consulted for this piece remarked, Ginnivan and Schultz are “very different players” and people. After Ginnivan’s brilliant and, at times, stormy 2022 breakout season, when he booted 40 goals and drew constant commentary for milking frees for high contact, Craig McRae had Ginnivan playing a more straightened role in 2023. This restrained role did not see him gain as much of the ball as he would have liked. The parallel stories of Schultz and Ginnivan offer insights into the different mindsets and philosophies of Collingwood and Hawthorn.



The “Fly” Pies prize adherence to system, and while Nick Daicos is allowed greater freedom, the McRae system is less flexible than that of the Hawks, who, as one insider put it, put a fence around players, “but the fence isn’t that tight”. Schultz, after an initial adjustment period in 2024, has shown himself to be a consummate cog within the Collingwood collective. At a team that places a huge premium on pressuring the opposition, Schultz is the AFL’s No.1 player for tackles inside the forward 50-metre arc in 2026 (39 in 19 games to date). Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell addressing Ginnivan and star teammate Nick Watson. AFL Photos Schultz plays much closer to goal than Ginnivan, his scoring lifting since Jamie Elliott’s season-ending injury from one goal per game to 1.6. He is efficient rather than flamboyant – you won’t see him in mocking or edgy banter with opposition fans – a trait that Ginnivan first demonstrated in that 2022 Anzac Day game when he booted five, and which culminated in the notorious exchange with Ken Hinkley on the boundary after Hawthorn’s narrow loss to Port in that semi-final in 2024. Collingwood had recognised Ginnivan’s talents and felt he was capable of playing upfield and wasn’t merely a deep forward with goal sense. “We had a level of confidence in his draft year that he’d be able to play up the ground,” said Collingwood’s long-serving recruiting boss Derek Hine, now with the Tasmania Devils.



But Ginnivan’s missteps in 2023, not least his decision to go to the races the night before the grand final, put him in a position where Collingwood were willing to let him go. At Collingwood, he was always a headline act – more so after a two-match suspension when filmed with an illicit substance in a Torquay hotel – and he did not have the full trust of the team’s leaders. Schultz (left) is a key cog in the Magpie machine under Craig McRae and alongside superstar onballer Nick Daicos (right). Getty Images One could argue that the Magpies, as the more system-based team and club – and who offer only select individuals significant autonomy to run their own race (e.g. “the Daicii”) – would not have extracted the kind of footy from Ginnivan that the Hawks and Mitchell have harvested. Schultz’s style – high pressure, but lower profile, more structured and blue collar – fitted the McRae methodology. Ginnivan’s style – playing higher upfield, taking risks to create opportunities for teammates and hitting the scoreboard (albeit less this year) – was a match for the free-form Hawthorn DNA, as personified by Nick Watson, Ginnivan and Connor Macdonald.



Related Article AFL 2026 Why John Longmire thinks Mark McVeigh is ready to be a senior coach Ginnivan has gained only 19 per cent of his disposals inside the forward 50-metre arc this year, compared to 35 per cent in 2024 – that share was 49 in his 40-goal season of ’22. He has just 19 goals this season after 29 last year, but is averaging nearly 20 possessions per game. Where Hawthorn have fared better than the Magpies was on the question of draft price, as Fremantle pushed for – and gained – Collingwood’s future first-round choice, which was earlier than budgeted; this deprived Collingwood of a first-rounder in the deep 2024 draft, and became part of Fremantle’s exchange for the prodigiously skilled Shai Bolton. The draft cost for Ginnivan was close to net zero for Hawthorn. The way Collingwood play, as it happens, is a touch more “one for all and all for one” than the mighty freewheeling Hawks. Schultz and Ginnivan found the homes that fitted their personal traits and talents. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Firefighters responding to blaze at Gloriavale Christian Community
World.content:
Firefighters were battling a blaze at the Gloriavale Christian Community late on Friday night.

Fire and Emergency said the fire in the remote community on the South Island's West Coast was reported shortly before 9pm.

One crew arrived to find a building at the site well involved on fire.

FENZ shift manager Simon Lyford said the building was "some distance" from where the residence at Gloriavale was, and they had no concerns with people sleeping on site on Friday night.

As of 10.30pm, FENZ said they had isolated power from the building and four of the crews were dealing with the fire from inside the building.

When the fire was reported, the caller said everyone had been evacuated from the building, FENZ said. They were not aware of any injuries.

Five fire crews, four fire trucks and two tankers were on site late on Friday night.

World.title: Young child dies after dog attack in Aranui, Christchurch
World.content:
A young child has died after a dog attack in Christchurch on Friday afternoon.

Senior Sergeant Dan Overend said emergency services were called to Basingstoke Street in Aranui around 4:45pm after reports of a child sustaining serious dog bite injuries.

"Upon arrival, emergency services located a young child in a critical condition.

"Despite the immediate efforts of first responders, and a member of the household, the child sadly died at the scene."

Overend said the dog involved was known to the occupants of the address and lived at the property.

"Police remain at the address carrying out a scene examination, and enquiries into the circumstances that led to this tragic incident are ongoing.

"Occupants of the address are assisting police with enquiries."

World.title: Experts call for meth safety policy u-turn after 'huge increase' in contamination
World.content:
The debate around methamphetamine contamination in homes has reignited, with the authors of a new study calling for a policy u-turn over safe thresholds.

'The impact of New Zealand's 2018 methamphetamine policy on residential contamination' was published in the New Zealand Medical Journal on Friday.

The 2018 policy raised the threshold for what was deemed acceptable from 0.5μg of methamphetamine per 100cm2 to 15μg - higher than accepted levels in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, the report said.

In an analysis of more than 420 homes, researchers from Unitec and the University of Waikato found a "substantial" rise in meth contamination since the policy change.

The report said there could be several factors behind the trend, including a potential increase in "clandestine" meth labs that was also driving increased consumption of the drug, and the policy change leading to less vigilance about the risk.

The report noted that methamphetamine use continued to rise, according to last year's New Zealand Drug Trends Survey.

The study's lead author Dr Muhammad Irfan said people could be passively exposed to meth by living in homes where the drug had been smoked or manufactured.

Meth use in NZ breaks records - why? Afternoons Download MP3 10m

He said fears about the effect of this exposure on health - particularly in children - were what prompted testing in New Zealand in 2010.

"Children are crawling ... might be touching the surface of the carpet ... putting their hands in their mouth. Their health is .. in danger because of the meth contamination."

Irfan said the cost of methamphetamine testing and a need to house people were factors in a review of the threshold in 2018, and in May that year the new levels were adopted.

He said the "huge increase" in contamination since should trigger a tightening of restrictions again, if not to pre-2018 levels then to the 1.5μg threshold recommended by Environmental Science and Research (now known as PHF Science) in 2019.

Overseas research has found passive exposure to methamphetamine could lead to eye and respiratory infections in children as well as some psychological effects, Irfan said.

Further research on the health impact was needed to establish a contamination threshold that accurately accounted for the risk, he said. In the meantime the acceptable level should be lowered, he added.

The study's release comes after neighbours in a Lower Hutt suburb raised concerns that potential buyers of a Kāinga Ora home were left in the dark about its history as a "meth lab".

The 'for sale' sign outside the Kāinga Ora property on Naenae's Langford Street. RNZ

'Jury still out' on health effects

Speaking to RNZ earlier this week, emeritus professor of toxicology at University of Canterbury Ian Shaw said the "jury's still out" on the health effects of living in a meth-contaminated home.

While he could not comment on this particular study or its findings, he was currently part of a research team - contracted by a New Zealand company - looking into the effects of meth exposure.

"As far as I'm aware, we don't really know whether residues of methamphetamine in houses have any effect on people that might live in those houses later. So we need ... a definitive study to determine that."

Shaw said the current statutory limits for meth contamination appeared fairly arbitrary.

Professor Ian Shaw Supplied

"I don't think that we have set ... that threshold based on the knowledge that below that amount will have no effect on you and above that amount it might have an effect on you."

In his opinion, the effect on people who were living in a home where meth had been smoked was very low.

"Cutting your bread on a bread board that someone smoked meth next to ... you would get really low doses," he said.

"But at the other end of the spectrum you might have a house ... that's a meth lab ... then the amounts of methamphetamine contaminating that home could be very significantly greater."

Shaw said those homes could give people a "reasonable-sized" dose of the drug.

World.title: 'Send help': Doctor's plea to Health NZ as hospital struggles to cope with demand
World.content:
Palmerston North ED doctor puts out plea for help to Health NZ Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

A Palmerston North emergency department doctor is urging Health New Zealand to "send help" after an extraordinarily busy day.

"It's been kind of a hectic day with the waiting room. I think we have close to 20 to 30 patients," Dr Dusty Bratton told Checkpoint on Friday afternoon.

Bratton was speaking as a member of the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists (ASMS).

Patients had contacted RNZ to say they had been waiting up to 17 hours to be seen at the ED. Bratton said one patient had to wait up to 27 hours.

When he arrived at the hospital in the morning, he found 20 patients with nowhere to be examined. People were even resorting to leaving the ED because of the wait times, he said.

Bratton did not know if this was normal for Palmerston North, having moved to the area a year ago from the US.

He said Kiwis were experiencing longer wait times and more "bedblock" - time spent over-capacity - than people in the US, which could lead to "bad outcomes" for patients.

"It doesn't seem to flow quite as well."

Staff were picking up extra shifts to help combat the wait times but that was not sustainable, he said.

Healthcare workers have taken to protesting in recent years as hospitals struggle to cope with demand. Kim Baker Wilson / RNZ

"[Staff are] just trying to help out as much as they can. They're staying late, coming in early."

He had personally worked an extra three shifts in two weeks.

Bratton doubted Palmerston North would be able to reach the government's target of seeing 95 percent of patients within six hours.

"The number of patients we have are greater than the number of spaces we have."

The ED needed more beds and space to admit and see patients, he said.

There was pressure to reach discharge targets and make numbers look better on paper, but Bratton did not know if that always resulted in decisions that were in the patients' best interests.

In the last month, Palmerston North Hospital has added an extra 14 beds and an assessment room to the department.

Bratton said this had not solved "bedblock" issues, however.

Asked what his message was to Health NZ, he replied: "Send help - that's all I got."

Health NZ responds to concerns

Health NZ group director of operations at Counties Manukau Dr Vanessa Thornton admitted they were "going to have to put our thinking caps on and do more" in response to wait times during flu season.

"We are starting to think about what we're going to do next year already with respect to this," she told Checkpoint.

"I think it's a really challenging time and the staff are doing a great job.

"Just this week compared to last week we've had 1500 more presentations to EDs across the country, and most of that is related to viral load and flu, particularly influenza A," she said.

Dr Vanessa Thornton RNZ / Dan Cook

Palmerston North Hospital was one of many struggling with "unprecedented demand" due to winter illness, she said. Even her own, Middlemore Hospital, had seen patients facing eight-hour waits on Friday morning.

Most hospitals were not close to the current target of 95 percent of people being seen within six hours, she said.

She wanted to reassure the public that they would not be sent home early to help meet that target.

"All patients that are urgently needing critical care are seen as a priority, but some will wait longer to be seen for treatment," she said.

World.title: Flights cancelled as fog hits Wellington Airport
World.content:
Wellington Airport says fog has caused several flight cancellations on Friday evening.

MetService said a southerly wind had pushed a low cloud shelf into Wellington over the past few hours on Friday evening.

Passengers are being advised to check directly with their airline for the latest information before travelling to the airport.

Meteorologists earlier said as temperatures cool in the evening, a thick bank of mist could sink to surface levels.

The cloud bank was expected to last through the afternoon to the early hours of Saturday morning.

Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker earlier said the southern coast of Wellington would be most exposed - including the harbour and airport.

"So you get that sea fog when sea surface temperatures and air temperatures are very close together.

"So with a southerly the air is cooled down, the sea takes a little bit longer to cool down water - it hangs on to heat better than air essentially."

He said low visibility might impact flights, depending on how much moisture builds in the air.

"Basically, planes like to see the ground before they land."

Auckland Airport affected by fog on Friday morning

Fog restrictions were in place at Auckland Airport this morning.

By 7.20am, several domestic regional flights had been cancelled as well as some arrivals.

A number departing had been delayed as well as arriving.

Of the main trunk domestic flights, one to Christchurch had been delayed, as had an arrival from Dunedin.

World.title: Households cut health insurance, despite rising claim payouts
World.content:
New Zealanders are cutting back on their health insurance, just as the amount being paid out in health insurance claims increases.

A report commissioned by the Financial Services Council showed 9 percent of people with health insurance terminated their policies last year, up from 7 percent in 2022.

At the same time, the average health insurance claim paid per member increased from $1097 in 2021 to $1921 in 2025.

"The evidence shows insurance is already providing billions of dollars of funding, expanding access to care and protecting families from the financial consequences of illness and death. The opportunity for government is to recognise and strengthen that contribution as part of a more resilient New Zealand health system," Financial Services Council chief executive Kirk Hope said.

Health insurance premiums have risen sharply recently, up almost 75 percent in the past five years alone.

Hope said it was problematic that, as health insurance usage was increasing and treatment costs were rising, households were struggling with the cost of cover.

"Just as New Zealand needs every part of the health system working better together, people are cutting back the very cover that helps them access care sooner."

People who completely dropped their health insurance would usually need to go back through the underwriting process to take it out again, which could mean pre-existing conditions were not covered.

Kirk Hope RNZ / Richard Tindiller

About 35 percent of adults have private health insurance.

Of those, 43 percent are covered through an employer or group scheme.

Hope said the Government could help by removing fringe benefit tax from employee-funded insurance.

"It's a very effective way, it's community-rated and it's not underwritten so it's a very effective way for people to get access if the employer is providing low-cost or no-cost health insurance for them, but it's very expensive for employers because they have to incur a 50 percent to 70 percent tax on premiums."

World.title: Southland says it is missing the love when it comes to South Island infrastructure
World.content:
Southland businesses meet to hear politicians’ plans Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Business people from across the South Island have met in Christchurch for the first South Island election conference to hear from politicians about their plans for the Mainland.

They covered a range of topics from transport, productivity, infrastructure and immigration, with National announcing its election plan for the South Island.

But the head of the Southland Chamber of Commerce said she still felt her region was badly overlooked and its potential underestimated.

While other parts of the country might be struggling with high unemployment rates, the Southland Chamber Commerce said its region is grappling with how fill a bout 4000 skilled jobs.

Chief executive, Sheree Carey, said there was about 10 billion dollars in new investment and eight major projects in the pipeline, including a data centre and a mineral plant, but Southland wasn't getting it's fair share of infrastructure spending.

"We need some serious consideration from government, and all the parties really, on what can we do for Southland, because if they want to double exports and increase GDP, then Southland is the region that is well on its way. So we need that support back," said Carey.

Sheree Carey said the region could do with improvements to its roading, housing, schools and social services, but she feels there was more focus on Canterbury and Queenstown.

"If they look at all the stats we are the ones that are leading in every statistics that you can see, in growth and exports and everything, and where is the love? Southland wants some love as well," Carey said.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said National's South Island plan will build more reliable transport and regional connections and help to grow exports.

National Party members and Christopher Luxon speak to media during a stand-up in Christchurch on Friday. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

The Infrastructure Minister, Chris Bishop, said the plan showed that National was backing the south.

"The Rolleston Rail intermodal rail and freight hub, here in Christchurch, leaning into public transport in Queenstown by way of a gondola. There are three different solutions on the table there. I think we need to think creatively about Queenstown transport issues. There is a strategic network plan being developed by NZTA now, but the simple reality is we just can't keep adding lanes and lanes in Queenstown," Bishop said.

He said the plans build on other investments already underway, including the new Dunedin and Nelson hospitals, and the Brougham Street upgrade in Christchurch.

Labour's Kieran McAnulty said the biggest infrastructure mistake governments make is announcing plans, only to drop them or press pause because of politics or a lack of funding.

"The way we have approached this is first and foremost recognise that the country is sick to the gut of things stopping and starting constantly. There is too much of it. We are never going to get where we need to get if it keeps happening. And people won't have the confidence to run the businesses in the way they want to, if they don't have the confidence that things will be followed through," McAnulty said.

He said Labour wants all Crown projects to go through the Infrastructure Commission's independent assurance process to stop that happening.

The chief executive of Business Canterbury, Leeann Watson, said the two main parties have a lot in common on the issue of infrastructure.

"If there is one part of our conference today where we wanted to see alignment it is in that future investment and infrastructure. Having good bipartisan support to provide a long term plan and some certainty is really important and we saw that today," Watson said.

World.title: Fiji court rules COI report into Malimali appointment was unlawful, null and void
World.content:
The Fiji High Court has ruled that the Commission of Inquiry report into the appointment of Barbara Malimali as FICAC Commissioner, in its entirety is null and void.

Justice Dane Tuiqereqere also found that the COI report was unlawful, and that its adverse findings are irrational and have been quashed

It's also been found that President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu and Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka failed to provide the applicants with natural justice.

Malimali challenged the report with former Attorney General Graham Leung, and lawyers Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi.

Local media said the judge has determined that the President, the Prime Minister and the Commission of Inquiry, breached principles of natural justice for not giving the applicants the opportunity to respond to the adverse findings against them.

Fiji Village News said Justice Tuiqereqere ruled that the work of the Commission of Inquiry after 1st February 2025, including the report is ultra vires or unlawful.

He found that the extension of the Commission of Inquiry beyond 31st January 2025 was ineffective.

As a result, the actions of the Commissioner after that date, including the completion of his report dated 1st May 2025, were unlawful, Fiji Village News stated.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka making a case for the 20 percent salary reduction for all 55 MPs in parliament last week. 30 April 2026 Facebook / Parliament of the Republic of Fiji

Justice Tuiqereqere has also found that adverse findings and recommendations against the applicants including Malimali, former Attorney General Graham Leung and lawyers Wylie Clarke and Laurel Vaurasi were unlawful, including those relating to a meeting at the FICAC office on 5th September 2024.

'Praise God for the win'

The applicants had further challenged the decision by the President, on the advice of the Prime Minister, to release the Commission of Inquiry report publicly.

Malimali and her lawyer Tanya Waqanika are on the island of Kadavu and responded to the ruling in a Facebook post, saying justice has been served.

"Praise God for the win," Waqanika said in her post.

"It has been a hard battle fighting to clear Barbara Malimali's name from the COI taxpayer funded $4m (and counting) crocodile hunting failed expedition.

"Barbara Malimali and me are here in my village and we just received the news that we WON our HBJ No 9/26 Judicial Review case against the Fiji Government (well, all the Respondents names are Govt representatives).

The judge also said the COI Chair, David Ashton-Lewis, should have provided a draft of the adverse findings against the applicants to them and an opportunity to respond before compiling the report.

The Commission of Inquiry was the brainchild of Rabuka.

In June, the High Court rejected the Prime Minister's attempt to stall its ruling that the country's former anti-corruption chief was illegally sacked.

World.title: Live: Souths on top in tense clash with Dogs
World.content:
Manly's 'Fozball' fever dream is officially over after being held scoreless at Brookvale Oval for the first time in 33 years.

In a match that failed to reach any real heights, the Dolphins had enough strike to pull away late to win 22-0 and momentarily leapfrog Cronulla into fourth spot on the NRL ladder.

The Dolphins' win did come at some cost, with in-form second-rower Connelly Lemuelu limping from the field in the second half with a hamstring injury.

But the story of the night was the Sea Eagles, whose finals hopes are now virtually over after six straight losses.

It was against the Dolphins that the Kieran Foran coaching era began with a bang, piling 52 points on them at Redcliffe back in round five.

But on Friday night the honeymoon period died with a whimper, unable to crack the opposition line and lacking any real threat in attack.

Manly can point to any number of things for the way their season has spiralled, with the club's alarming lack of depth a key issue that needs fixing.

Luke Brooks' injury has also proven costly, with the Sea Eagles having far more attacking sets than the Dolphins but failing to cross even once.

It marked the first time since a 6-0 loss to Eastern Suburbs in 1993 that Manly failed to trouble the scoreboard at their traditional home ground.

Their best chance came at 8-0 down midway through the second half, when a Reuben Garrick pass was called forward as Jason Saab sprinted away to score.

From the next set the Dolphins effectively sealed the match, as Selwyn Cobbo did extremely well to get the ball down in the corner under intense pressure from Clayton Faulalo.

Kristian Woolf's men then went in again moments later through Jack Bostock, after Jamayne Isaako picked off a Joey Walsh pass at the other end of the field.

Usually one of the most dangerous teams in the competition, the Dolphins' attack was hardly at its best either.

Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow put Isaako over for a late try, while their only other came through Kodi Nikorima in the first half while Tolu Koula was in the sin bin.

But they will have bigger fish to fry over the next month, with Parramatta, the Sydney Roosters and Gold Coast on the run home and the top four a possibility.

For Manly, the only real positive was the return of Faulalo, who was safe at the back and pulled off a superb try-saver on a runaway Cobbo in the second half.

AAP

World.title: Boxer dies more than a decade after fight leaves him with brain injury
World.content:
Prichard Colón, a former boxer who was left with severe brain damage after a fight more than a decade ago, has died aged 33.

His father, Richard Colón, confirmed his son's death in a Facebook post on Thursday.

The post did not detail the Puerto Rican boxer's cause of death.

World Boxing Organization (WBO) president Gustavo Olivieri posted a tribute to Colón on social media.

"Today, the WBO solemnly joins his family and all those who had the privilege of knowing, supporting, and loving him in mourning his passing," Mr Olivieri said.

What happened to Prichard Colón?

Colón was injured in a boxing match against Terrel Williams in Virginia in the US in October 2015.

Born in Florida, US, Colón kicked off his boxing career in Puerto Rico, where he won five amateur titles.

He was considered a "rising star" in the lead-up to the nationally televised match, ESPN reports.

Here's how a report from Reuters described the match at the time:

"An online video of the fight showed Williams, a 31-year-old fighter from Los Angeles, punching Colón in the back of the head in the seventh round, a shot that appeared to stun Colón, who was briefly examined in his corner. "Williams was penalised for the illegal punch. "Colón was then knocked down twice in the ninth round. "He was disqualified after the ninth round. "His corner mistakenly took off his gloves, thinking it was the final round and that the fight was complete."

After the match, Colón needed assistance to walk to his dressing room after the match.

He said he felt dizzy, vomited and then "passed out", according to a report from the Washington Post.

Colón was rushed to hospital where he underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain, spending seven months in a coma.

He was 23 years old.

Prichard Colon, left, and Terrel Williams during the fight. (Getty Images via AFP: Patrick Smith)

In 2016, the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation determined there was no wrongdoing on the part of organisers of the fight, the Washington Post reported.

"No one action [or failure to act] can be identified that is so apparent or egregious to justify holding accountable any one person," the regulator said in a statement.

Signs of hope

In 2017, nearly two years after the fight, Colón was still in what doctors described as a persistent vegetative state, according to an article from ESPN.

He needed around-the-clock care.

At the time, his parents told the US broadcaster they hoped Colón would regain some brain function despite the challenges he faced.

"I do believe in miracles," his father said.

By 2019, Colón had made significant progress, according to another article by the Washington Post.

After months of therapy, he was able to communicate using facial gestures, verbal sounds and a computer that tracked his eye movements.

He could pedal on a recumbent bike, and his competitive spirit was driving him to take steps with assistance in a friendly rivalry with a fellow patient.

"He gets tired and impatient like anyone, and some of his days are better than others," Washington Post reporter Kent Babb wrote.

"What's clear is that he's made it this far, beyond where anyone thought he would, because of good coaching."

'Extraordinary fighting spirit'

News of the former boxer's death triggered an outpouring of grief in the boxing world.

"Prichard's life was defined by courage, perseverance, and an extraordinary fighting spirit," Mr Olivieri said.

"His story transcended the ring and deeply touched the boxing community, which stood by him throughout the years with respect, admiration, and hope."

The WBO paid tribute to Colón's "resilience" as well as "the unwavering love of his family".

Tributes to Prichard Colón were posted to social media after news of his death broke. (Facebook: World Boxing Organization-WBO)

ABC with Reuters

World.title: Australia's Grace Kim makes fast start at LPGA event
World.content:
Australian golfer Grace Kim has continued her hot run with a stellar opening round at the LPGA Tour's Portland Classic.

Fresh off two straight top-10 finishes, Kim is just one stroke behind Colombian leader Mariel Galdiano after the first round at the Columbia-Edgewater Country Club.

Playing an all-out attack, the major champion collected seven birdies and an eagle to finish the day in a seven-way tie for second.

The world number 38 also needed only 24 putts, the fewest of any player in the field.

Kim started with a three-birdie stretch after starting her round on the 10th hole.

"Having that three-birdie start is just a nice feeling to kick-start things," the 25-year-old said.

"A lot of us out here are pretty straight, fairways and greens.

"But in terms of holing all those putts, knowing that the greens roll quite true … it's really nice to just put a stroke on it and see where it would normally go."

Kim is in a batch at 6-under, including Augusta National women's amateur champion Maria Jose Marin, Arpichaya Yubol and Olivia Cowan.

The 20-year-old Marin landed five-straight birdies on the front nine.

"I reached a flow state that I haven't reached in a while," she said.

"After the British Open I didn't play my best golf, and I think getting that confidence back with this round is all that I needed."

One shot behind them and tied for ninth is Australian Robyn Choi (67), who sprang to life on the back nine.

After going out in even par with a birdie and bogey, Choi stormed home with four consecutive birdies beginning on the 12th. She then added another on the 17th to rocket up the field.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Fellow Australian Steph Kyriacou (72) had a solid round of even par, but will have to play well with the cut projected to be around 1-under.

American pacesetter Galdiano's opening 65 featured nine birdies.

Galdiano, a 28-year-old from Hawaii, is making her fourth LPGA Tour start of the year.

"Every start on the LPGA means a lot to me, so just enjoy the moment, really," she said.

AAP

World.title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
World.content:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

World.title: Bangladesh grinds Australia into the Darwin dirt as rookie scores sparkling ton
World.content:
Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack has been ground into the Darwin dirt, experiencing another torrid day against Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium.

Led by a sparkling maiden Test ton to rookie-opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh lost just five wickets on day two, reaching stumps on 6-351 and 153 first-innings runs ahead of their hosts.

After an opening day that saw Australia bowled out for a well below-par 198, Pat Cummins's men picked up where they left off on day two, struggling for ideas and inspiration against a disciplined Bangladeshi batting line-up.

Mitchell Starc took the only wicket in an energy-sapping morning session for Australia, while Steve Smith was uncharacteristically slow in reacting to a deflected Tanzid edge, that, if taken, would have seen the opener depart for 62.

Tanzid, playing just his second Test match, took 188 balls to reach his century, and brought it up with a push back past Nathan Lyon after a nervous period in the 90s.

Tanzid completed a sparkling maiden century on day two. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

However, the 25-year-old threw his wicket away only a matter of balls later, caught in the deep after mistiming an ill-advised slog against Lyon for 101.

That was the only wicket to fall in the second session as captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, who had shared a 93-run partnership with Tanzid, continued to take the fight to the Australians alongside 39-year-old, 103-Test veteran Mushfiqur Rahim.

Bangladesh's lead by the time the new ball was taken stood at 91, with seven wickets remaining.

Starc instantly got the new ball talking, sending the first ball swinging past the bat and stumps of Shanto to the giant left hander's complete disbelief.

But it was Hazlewood who made the breakthrough in his first over, finding the edge of Shanto to have him caught at second slip by Steve Smith for 84.

Starc got in on the act three overs later, having Litton Das caught behind, also by Smith, for a 12-ball duck.

Then Pat Cummins joined the party to find the edge of Mushfiqur, and give Smith a third consecutive catch, Australia's three great pacemen striking with fearsome force to reduce Bangladesh from 3-297 to 6-308.

That third catch put Smith level with Joe Root on 218 catches, the most ever in Test cricket by a non wicketkeeper.

But Australia once again toiled as the lacquer faded from the new ball, with six-wicket hero from day one, Hasan Mahmud (13 not out), providing able support to all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who reached stumps on 32.

Relive the action in our live blog below.

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

World.title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
World.content:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP

World.title: Brian To'o is still just the beginning for the PNG Chiefs
World.content:
After a week in the spotlight following the biggest decision of his career, Brian To'o went back to work.

His showing in the Panthers' 12-6 loss to the Roosters was typical of the To'o we've come to know.

The future Papua New Guinea Chief did not bring up his 100th try for the Panthers but did churn through 17 runs for 162 metres to go with five tackle busts and two line breaks. For some wingers that's a big night but for To'o it's the standard.

'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate Two of the NRL's most successful modern coaches weigh into the debate about the concessions afforded to the league's forthcoming PNG franchise.

The performance came in the days following confirmation of To'o's move to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs and it shouldn't have been a surprise.

There are good reasons To'o has become the premier winger of his time, and having such a high baseline is one of them.

Continued excellence on his part, for both the rest of this season and his final year with Penrith in 2027, is as close to a given as you'll find anywhere in rugby league.

He is the best player the Chiefs have signed but that may not remain so. Not since the Broncos filled their boots with Queensland-based stars for their inaugural season in 1988 has an expansion team signed so much established talent.

Zac Lomax will return to rugby league with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Brendon THorne)

Of the six players to commit to the Chiefs, four have played State of Origin in the past two years. Some clubs go decades without signing one or two players who fit such a criteria.

The other two are the greatest try-scorer the Australian game has ever known and one of England's top front-rowers.

Unless Joseph Manu was just in Port Moresby on holiday, it seems likely they'll add the Golden Boot winner from the most recent World Cup to the list before long.

They have achieved all this without really entering the cut and thrust of the transfer market in earnest. Officially, the Chiefs cannot talk to any NRL free agents for the 2028 season until November 1 this year.

Manu has been linked with an NRL return with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Each of the signings they've made within the NRL have come because a club granted permission for the player in question to negotiate early or because the player activated something in their contract that allowed them to do so.

They've done all this while the luxury compound they're building is still a hole in the ground and before they have a logo or a jersey. To'o himself hasn't even been to Papua New Guinea before.

They're yet to land any young legs but if these are the players they can sign through the activation of obscure clauses and arcane options and the like, imagine what they can do in the jungle of true free agency when they have the biggest and sharpest teeth via their mountain of government funding?

With local products like Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finlay Glare, all of whom are enjoying standout seasons with London Broncos and will eventually take up development contracts with the club, to fill out the other end of the roster, the Cheifs can keep aiming high.

The floodgates have yet to truly open but already the ripples of the league's new money-monster are clear to see.

Hudson Young, fresh off a career-changing State of Origin series, is in the Chiefs' sights and despite the Raiders offering just about everything they've got to a player who has found a home in Canberra, fans there are turning as green as their jerseys because they know there's a chance they'll be money-whipped.

Young is the latest player to come into PNG's sights. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The spectre of similar moves loom over a sport addicted to transfer gossip and sank into Thursday's top-of-the-table clash because after the start they've made, no player seems out of reach for the Chiefs.

Not Sam Walker, who turned down the Roosters first contract offer midweek and has the chance to secure untold riches over the final stages of this season, a chance he has surely enhanced after a mature performance that helped put the Tricolours on top of the ladder.

Not Liam Martin, who rattled Cody Ramsey with the best shot of the night or Spencer Leniu, who struggled to find the fire against his former club and looks like he'd benefit from a change of scenery.

Not even Nathan Cleary, who tried every trick he knew but could not break down a resolute Roosters defensive line.

As impossible as it seems to picture him playing rugby league in anything but a Penrith jersey, even he is in play.

Through their tax-free contracts and the legitimacy that comes with signing established stars, the Chiefs have the capability to tip the entire league on its head.

They can pay a battler like a prince, a prince like a king and a king like a god and given they've already shown a taste for the finer things in assembling their roster, there's little reason to expect it won't continue.

Their advantages warp the salary cap beyond recognition and each signing they make is further proof of concept that the gold rush is real.

General manager of football Michael Chammas says he wears it as a badge of honour that clubs are beginning to gripe at the advantages PNG have been given and well may he, given how those clubs, blinded by the glittering of gold, let a Chief into the henhouse.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

It is hard to begrudge any player for taking what's on offer, like it's hard to begrudge the way Chammas and the Chiefs are going about it. They're playing by the rules they've been given and they're playing by them well.

Ever since Jarome Luai was announced as their first signing, their power has become more and more real and it continues to solidify with every signing they make. Now, they are securing a firm foothold on the high side of an uneven surface.

To'o is the latest, but not the last and rugby league is only just beginning to reckon with the power of what the NRL has created with its concessions to the Chiefs and how it alters the competitive balance of the league.

They have turned the dial as far as it will go and are now waiting to see what happens next, as is their way, and it is happening hard and fast all around us.

The downpour of money is a monsoon that shows no sign of breaking, even as rival clubs get swamped.

And stars like To'o who have been swept along are still just the start. Expect plenty more to dive in.

Tech.title: Apple trained its own AI model for China with help from Alibaba
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has reportedly trained a custom AI model for the China market alongside domestic tech giant Alibaba, a rare cross-border partnership that cuts across growing tensions between Beijing and Washington.

The China-focused large language model was developed in partnership with Alibaba and trained with the company’s support, Reuters reports, citing three unnamed people familiar with the matter.

Developing a custom model of its own marks a departure from Apple’s previous strategy in the country and would give the company more control over its products in the competitive Chinese smartphone market. Historically, Apple has used domestic Chinese models to bring generative AI to its devices sold there, as the US models it uses elsewhere — like OpenAI’s ChatGPT — aren’t available.

The report comes as Apple gears up to release Apple Intelligence in China.
