Tech.title: Best Computer Monitors (2026): The Home Office Upgrade You Need
Tech.content:
This isn't the only BenQ monitor made to match with Macs. The company also has the 27-inch 4K (MA270U), which gets you similar features with fewer pixels, but costs quite a bit less.

Cheap Monitors That Are Actually Good

I consider a budget monitor to be anything under $200, and you'll find dozens and dozens of these hanging out at Amazon or Best Buy. But many are old. Many have poor colors. It's trickier to find some newer models that are actually worth the money. I wasn't surprised to see that the Dell 27 Plus ranked among the very highest in my testing. It only costs $150, but it delivers really strong 1080p performance in terms of colors and brightness.

The most surprising feature of this monitor is its 144-Hz refresh rate. The smooth motion really gives the monitor the premium feel that monitors at this price lack, and it also comes with all the same adjustability features and an integrated VESA mount on the back. Put this on your desk, and aside from the resolution, you'll never think of it as a “budget” monitor.

But maybe you want to keep things even cheaper. No problem. While a monitor under $100 is going to have some flaws, I found a decent one in the MSI Pro MP243W E14. It stands out in the thing that matters most: image quality. I measured 359 nits at its brightest, and the color coverage is surprisingly good, both in terms of saturation and accuracy. It even has a 144-Hz refresh rate, which means it can double as a cheap gaming monitor when it needs to. I also like the design, which offers thin bezels around the display and an all-white exterior. Its flaws, however, include the lack of ports and adjustments. It can only tilt slightly. It's only 24 inches, which will likely feel small for most people.

I was also really surprised by the upgraded version of this monitor, the MP273QW E14. Rather than being stuck at 1080p, this model gives you a sharper image with a resolution of 2560 x 1440. While it has the same lack of adjustment, it is a more standard 27-inch size and delivers even better overall image quality.

Faster, Smarter, and More Extreme

This monitor is one of the favorites I've tested in the past couple of years. It was among the first QD-OLED monitors designed for content creation and entertainment. While there are a couple of options out there today from companies like Asus, the Dell 32 Plus 4K opens up the brilliant image quality of OLED to an entirely new audience. One reason high-quality HDR video is scarce is the lack of affordable screens to watch and edit it on. With this monitor out in the world, though, there's no excuse. It even has a 120-Hz refresh rate and plenty of ports. The combination of OLED's fast response time and the faster refresh rate makes this a solid gaming monitor in your off hours. I haven't included gaming monitors in this guide, primarily because they're an entirely different beast. Check our recommendations of the Best Gaming Monitors for some recommendations on that front.

But if you're really serious about creating professional, HDR video, there's still nothing else on the market quite like the Studio Display XDR. We all waited a long time for Apple to revisit the Studio Display, and while the monitor we eventually got was a bit less ambitious in scope than we all hoped, this 27-inch 5K Mini-LED monitor is the new king in HDR performance. It has 2,304 dimming zones, and according to my testing, it could do 1,905 peak HDR brightness in a 25-percent window. Compare that to, for example, the Dell 32 Plus 4K, which tops out at 946 nits in just a one-percent window. The difference in perceived brightness, detail, and contrast is huge, which is useful first and foremost for content creation. However, because it's been dropped from 32 inches to 27 inches, it's left a gap in the market for larger displays that don't lose sharpness. That's where the LG UltraFine Evo 6K monitor comes into play.

It just so happens to deliver a pixel density of 224 pixels per inch, making it the sharpest big-screen display I've ever tested. What I love about this LG monitor is that it's far more than just a bunch of pixels. It's one of the most beautiful monitors I've tested, sporting a gorgeous stand and base that definitely shares some resemblance with the Apple Studio Display. And like that monitor, the UltraFine 6K has a monster pair of built-in speakers that are crystal clear.

Unlike most monitors on this list, you won't need to buy a set of computer speakers. It's not a perfect monitor, though. The ports are in a hard-to-reach location, and while the stand is fun to admire, it has a couple of limitations. The lack of cable management is an eyesore, and it doesn't have as much height adjustment as I'd like. The monitor is also limited to just a 60-Hz refresh rate.

There's also the issue of price. It originally retailed at $2,000, which was painful, especially compared to the Asus ProArt 6K (PA32QCV), which is the only other 6K monitor on the market right now. These days, the price difference is down to just a couple hundred bucks. These monitors go toe-to-toe in image quality, though I prefer the LG model for its design, better speakers, and more powerful ports, while the ProArt 6K offers a longer, three-year warranty at a lower price. Regardless of which you choose, you're getting the sharpest 32-inch monitor possible. Beyond that, though, these are both solid options.

Lastly, I really enjoyed dipping my toe into the world of smart monitors. If you want a monitor that can just as easily double as a television, Samsung and LG both lead the way. I've tested out two Samsung smart monitors recently that have successfully expanded my idea of what monitors can do. My favorite of the bunch is the Samsung 32 M9 Smart Monitor. It's an OLED 4K monitor that is a rare display that's equally good for working, gaming, and watching movies. It's controlled with a remote, and Samsung throws in tons of goodies like free live TV channels to sweeten the deal. It can also be used with a gaming console, thanks to the HDMI 2.1 port. All that flexibility is great, but what really sets the M9 model apart is the OLED screen. Thanks to the fantastic image quality, it finally feels like a smart monitor that doesn't compromise that full TV experience.

For a bit of extra fun, I even tested out the non-OLED version of this monitor with Samsung's Movingstyle Rolling Monitor Stand. It's incredibly niche, but for the right home, being able to roll out a proper TV when you need it is handy. I love the idea of having a TV that is mobile rather than a permanent piece of hardware, and the Movingstyle rolling stand is a pretty compelling solution.

Tech.title: Her Brain Was Broken. It Was Fixed With Sound—Not a Scalpel
Tech.content:
Erin McNulty had been missing for weeks when her mother, Linda, sat down on a chair in her living room, exhausted. Linda had put in her usual seven-day workweek at the antiques shop she runs near Burlington, Vermont. She’d spent her free evenings driving around, trying to track down her daughter. Erin, 45 at the time, had been using methamphetamine for years.

Her substance use started in high school—first alcohol, then marijuana, and eventually heroin. Erin’s brother used heroin, too. When Linda found out, she started driving her kids to a methadone clinic three hours away in Massachusetts. The methadone helped, but it made Erin feel tired all the time, so she started using cocaine to stay awake. There were stretches of sobriety—she had her daughter during one of them, in 2008. The family took trips to the Great Escape waterpark in New York and Hampton Beach in New Hampshire. There were also several overdoses and attempts at rehab. Eventually, Erin switched to suboxone and stopped using heroin. But when a friend introduced her to meth, Linda says, “Erin was gone.”

Linda turned on the TV and was flipping through the channels when a 60 Minutes segment caught her attention. It was early 2024, and the show focused on a procedure that might help people with substance use disorders. Linda immediately thought of her daughter. The procedure involved beaming ultrasound through the skull to treat the brain. Researchers at West Virginia University were testing it on people with Alzheimer’s disease and addiction.

Galaxy Brain Your mind is a prediction machine. Feed it these stories for optimal results.

The neurosurgeon behind the procedure, Ali Rezai, was a pioneer in the field of deep brain stimulation, which involves cutting into the skull to implant electrodes that can reach neurons deep in the brain. He was excited by the ability of ultrasound—the imaging tool best known for observing fetal development during pregnancy—to reach into the same brain structures without breaking the skin. There would be no drilling into the skull, no poking or prodding the brain’s delicate tissue. The ultrasound could be delivered in 20 minutes, and patients could go home the same day.

Linda couldn’t believe what she was seeing on TV. She yelled out to her teenage granddaughter, Erin’s child, to come watch. “Look at this doctor,” she said. “They’re fixing people!” It didn’t matter that the trial was happening more than 600 miles away. She was going to get Erin to West Virginia. But first she had to find her.

Rezai, who was born in Iran, grew up in Los Angeles, and completed his neurosurgical training in New York, never expected to end up in West Virginia. “My colleagues said, ‘You’re committing academic suicide,’” he says. But Rezai saw an opportunity to pursue new treatments at the epicenter of the US addiction crisis. Almost 45 million Americans meet the criteria for a substance use disorder, and although drug overdose deaths in the US have been declining for the past three years, there were nearly 70,000 such deaths in 2025. West Virginia has the highest rate of overdose deaths in the country by population, more than double the national average.

Tech.title: This Art Project Slows Down Citi Bikes to Make NYC’s Rent Crisis Feel Real
Tech.content:
Justin Blinder lost his job two weeks before the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020. To pay his rent, he turned to delivery services, riding his bicycle across New York City to deliver food. As he went, he noticed the disparities in where the food items went. Which order of Nomé sushi went where and how much people tipped.

“The city started to feel much more economically and psychologically disparate,” Blinder tells WIRED. “It really changed so much on a block-by-block level. These inequalities and demographic differences were happening in such close proximity.”

That experience has morphed into an art-project gadget called Ground Truth that Blinder hopes will raise awareness about the housing affordability crisis in New York City and beyond by making a Citi Bike—one of the ever-present ebike rental options across the city—harder to ride through places where it’s harder to live.

Blinder, a Brooklyn artist and contractor at Meta, received a $10,000 grant for the project from a Brooklyn arts organization called Idle Hands.

A Ground Truth device attached to an ebike. Photograph: Justin Blinder

Ground Truth is a box that will trigger the brakes on the Lyft-owned bicycle, adding more resistance to the pedals when riding through rent-burdened neighborhoods, where people living in those areas spend more than 30 percent of their income on rent. Ride past an economically well-off block, and the bike is easier to pedal. Going past a block where rent takes the bulk of the households’ incomes can slow the bike down to a crawl.

There are two versions, one that can work on a regular bicycle and one built specifically for Citi Bikes.

The box mounts on the bike’s fork and is then attached to the front brake line. A battery-powered GPS component tracks the bike’s location. As it moves, the location is cross-referenced with household economic data from the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, stored on the device. When the bike passes a block the dataset says has a higher percentage of rent insecurity, the microcontroller triggers a small motor that applies the brake to add resistance, and the bike gets physically harder to pedal.

Tech.title: Dell XPS 13 Review: Move Over, Neo
Tech.content:
It’s hard to talk about the new Dell XPS 13 without mentioning the MacBook Neo. To say it takes inspiration from the choices of its rival would be an understatement—whether that’s the type of processor, the quality of the display, or the amount of memory.

But don’t think that’s a bad thing. The Dell XPS 13 feels different from other Windows laptops you can buy for $700 (or $900 for the better configuration), and a lot of that is for the better. I have some beef with this laptop's starting configuration, but I also can’t deny what makes it so compelling and unique, even among the very best laptops you can buy.

Incredible Value

Photograph: Luke Larsen

The MacBook Neo did one thing very well: translate what people love about MacBooks into a $700 package (or $600 at the time it was announced). In terms of the things you can touch and feel, the MacBook Neo is every bit as premium-feeling as a MacBook Air. The materials used in the chassis, the quality of the keyboard and trackpad, and the caliber of the display—none of it has the “budget device” stink. There's more to the story of the MacBook Neo than that, but you can tell it’s how Apple made decisions on which features to cut or compromise on.

Tech.title: Ninja Just Launched Its First Water Filter. Here’s What It Does That Others Don’t
Tech.content:
Water filtration is a booming category, and at-home units come in a range of formats: under-sink attachments, whole-house systems, water filter pitchers and countertop dispensers.

Ever the innovator, Ninja has jumped into the category with the launch of HydraSense, a slim countertop water filter that removes more than 80 contaminants (including forever chemicals, lead, microplastics and pharmaceuticals) and does a few things its competitors don’t.

The Best Countertop Water Filters, Lab-Tested by CNET See at CNET

I got a firsthand look at the HydraSense at Ninja’s New York headquarters, where the product team walked me through its unique features and showed off the filter’s pure power by running a batch of Kool-Aid through it.

Here’s what it does.

Filters out the bad stuff but leaves the good

Red Kool-Aid run through the HydraSense came out crystal clear. David Watsky/CNET

Reverse osmosis filters are the best for pure filtering power. The knock is that they strip water of minerals, which can leave water tasting bland. HydraSense’s oversized and especially dense activated carbon filter preserves naturally occurring minerals, including calcium, magnesium and potassium, for better-tasting water.

I sipped some fresh from the spout, and it tasted as crisp and clean as any I’ve had from the many filters I’ve tested.

In a demo, the product team filtered a batch of freshly made red Kool-Aid through the HydraSense. What emerged was perfectly clear liquid that tasted like clean water with no residual fruit punch flavor.

Filters 80+ contaminants, with certifications to prove it

The HydraSense activated carbon filter [left] is bigger and denser than a standard Brita filter.

If you’re wondering how well the filter works, you don’t have to take Ninja’s word for it. The HydraSense is certified by the National Sanitation Foundation, the most rigorous water filter testing body, to remove chlorine, chloramine, lead, volatile organic compounds, PFAS (forever chemicals) and microplastics.

Loads of filters on the market claim to reduce or eliminate these contaminants via in-house or third-party testing, but regulatory certifications leave nothing in question.

Lets you know when the filter needs changing

Many filtration systems require you to guess when the filter needs changing, but not this model. David Watsky/CNET

The bulk of the water filters I’ve tested have no system to let you know when the filter needs changing. It becomes a guessing game, and keeping track of how much water you’ve put through the machine is pretty much impossible.

HydraSense has a built-in monitor that lets you know when the filter is nearing the end of its life so you don’t end up changing it too soon or not soon enough. A single filter is good for 120 gallons, and replacements cost $40.

Filters fast. Like, really fast

When testing countertop water filters for CNET, one downside for most of the machines was slow filtering time — sometimes as much as an hour or more to filter a gallon. The HydraSense uses a unique pressure system to push water through the filter so it dispenses immediately. The feature is especially handy for power hydrators and families that burn through drinking water fast.

I’m a fan of the Rorra gravity filter, but it takes far longer than Ninja’s to strip water of contaminants. David Watsky

While water comes out fast, there’s a handy slow pour setting so you can fill ice trays without making a mess. You can also set the machine to dispense water in any ounce pour you want (up to 18 ounces).

Adjustable pour settings allow you to start dispensing and walk away.

The price is right, too

At $200 — currently discounted to $160 for launch — the HydraSense represents one of the best-value water filters I’ve seen. Reverse osmosis systems like the AquaTru Carafe cost nearly twice as much. Gravity filters such as the Rorra and Boroux, which work well but slowly, typically start at around $300 and go up from there.

Ninja’s newly launched HydraSense has a slim build and features you won’t find on most water filters. David Watsky/CNET

It’s closest competitor is the $120 Brita Hub. It too is certified to filter roughly 80 contaminants and does so quickly using a similar pressure system. But there’s no filter life monitor or slow pour settings, and the plastic build is notably cheaper.

The HydraSense is available now on Ninja’s website.

Tech.title: Google’s New Pixel 11 Phones Get Higher Starting Prices — Blame the RAM Shortage
Tech.content:
A slew of new phones and gadgets were revealed at the Made by Google event on Wednesday, including new Pixel phones, a foldable, a smartwatch and a personal item tracker. Following industry trends, most of these are pricier than their predecessors.

Like every other corner of the broader tech industry, phone makers have had to grapple with the RAM shortage and subsequent increased prices for memory and other components. Google acknowledged the shortage, noting that its pricing reflects that current reality. For the record, Samsung said much the same, citing the RAM shortage to justify the price increase for its foldables that launched last month.

The Pixel 11 fronts Google’s new phone lineup and starts at $899, a $100 bump over last year’s Pixel 10 — though it also comes with 256GB of storage, which is twice the minimum of its predecessor. In short, Google scrubbed the 128GB option and is forcing everyone to buy a higher tier as the new entry point. That will probably dim the chances of Google’s latest baseline flagship from living up to being a “feature-packed value monster,” as CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland described the Pixel 10.

While the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro more or less kept their predecessors’ prices the same, the Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold both got flat $100 price hikes across all their storage options.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

But another sign of the shortage’s increased toll is a reduction in RAM. Last year’s Pixel 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL both came with 16GB of memory, which you’ll still get in the 512GB and 1TB versions of the new Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL — but the starting 256GB versions come with only 12GB of RAM. In a briefing ahead of the event, Google said that its 2026 Pro phones are faster and smoother than last year’s thanks to optimizations in silicon and software. We’ll have to wait for our full reviews to test that claim.

All four phones can be preordered now, with a full release on Aug. 20. We’ve assembled a list of preorder offers from different retailers and carriers, or you can click below to secure one directly from Google.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Rene Ramos/CNET

Prices for the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for 256GB of storage, which is the new entry point. While there’s no 128GB option, there is a higher 512GB option that’s new for this year, priced at $1,019, over $100 more.

The Pixel 11 Pro also got rid of its 128GB option, but kept the others at mostly the same prices as on the 10 Pro. The phone starts at $1,099 for 256GB, goes up to $1,219 for 512GB and tops out at $1,499 for 1TB ($50 higher than its predecessor).

The Pixel 11 Pro XL, Google’s priciest flat phone, suffered a $100 price bump across the board even though its storage options didn’t change. The phone now starts at $1,299 for 256GB, goes to $1,419 for 512GB and maxes out at $1,649 for 1TB.

Similarly, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold got a $100 price hike across all its storage options. The foldable starts at $1,899 for 256GB, rises to $2,019 for 512GB and peaks at $2,249 for 1TB.

Let’s be clear, $2,249 is still a lot of money to spend on a device. But it’s far cheaper than the maximum 1TB storage option for the rival Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which Samsung priced at an astonishing $2,700.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Colors for the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 comes in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian (black).

The Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold come in four colors as well: canyon, fog, olive and obsidian (matte black). Last year’s Pixel Buds Pro 2 got a new olive hue to match.

Tech.title: We Spotted So Many Workarounds for Flock’s New Rules on Police Camera Surveillance
Tech.content:
Following dozens of reported cases of police abuse, including the arrest of three Georgia deputies on Monday and the investigation of a Massachusetts officer, Flock Safety announced new policies for the use of its AI surveillance cameras on Thursday.

Flock Safety cameras can track license plates, car features and, on the right models, humans as well. They can also listen for disturbances such as gunshots. These camera networks have drawn scrutiny over their potential to enable casual surveillance of communities, as well as documented abuses, including police using the systems to monitor former partners or inventing pretexts for searches that result in information being shared with agencies such as ICE, as I detail in my full guide here. That’s led to protests, Flock contract cancellations and in some cases, cities blocking cameras by wrapping them in trash bags because Flock won’t take them down.

This is Flock’s largest response to these issues that I’ve seen to date, with a series of changes governing how police can use its surveillance systems. Most of these changes won’t be required until the end of the year, and some won’t affect existing contracts. Flock has also created exceptions to the new rules, leaving police and sheriff’s departments responsible for enforcing them while giving them mechanisms to continue using the cameras as they see fit.

According to a statement from the American Civil Liberties Union, Flock operates more than 120,000 automatic license plate readers in at least 6,000 cities.

“Flock has attempted this before, and the security measure failed because police were easily able to circumvent the system’s requirement that they input the purpose of their search,” the ACLU says. It encourages Flock to use an independent evaluator to oversee its regulations.

Representatives from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Loopholes abound for Flock’s new regulations

Flock is putting more responsibility on law enforcement, which is problematic. Justin Sullivan/Staff/Getty

Every new Flock rule announced seems to come with a caveat. One of the biggest changes is a reduction in the length of time Flock retains camera data — and, consequently, how long that data can be used for searches — from 30 days to seven. But Flock also says that “Existing customers will keep their current, democratically approved retention periods,” meaning most users won’t see the change for some time.

There’s also a new evidence mode that ignores the new retention period, allowing police to hold data indefinitely while pursuing active investigations of their choice.

Flock is also adding a feature called “offense filtering,” which can limit the specific Flock camera information that outside agencies have access to. This doesn’t change much because police departments can set their own limits when sharing data. As previously reported, police departments have already violated state laws by sharing information with ICE, the FBI and other agencies.

Another change makes Flock’s new audit assistance feature mandatory by 2027. Audit assistance flags suspicious camera use, such as repeatedly searching for the same license plate. It’s unclear how the system could differentiate between tracking a stolen car for a period of time and stalking someone. When it flags suspicious behavior, the audit assistance tool locks the user out of the system and requires an administrator review.

Another change requires users to enter a case code for every law enforcement search, in addition to the existing option to provide a reason for the search. There is an exception for emergency searches, which can still be conducted without that information but are flagged for administrator review.

So who will conduct these reviews? I asked Flock, but have not yet received a response. Based on the company’s documentation, the administrator appears to be the person designated under the agency’s contract with Flock — potentially a sheriff or police chief, including officials in positions where Flock cameras have previously been misused. That raises questions about whether the new safeguards provide meaningful independent oversight or simply place accountability back with the same agencies responsible for using the systems.

Changes like these place greater responsibility on departments to police their own use of the technology, while potentially limiting Flock Safety’s responsibility for how its surveillance systems are used. At the same time, Flock has built in several exceptions that allow departments to bypass the new requirements, with the conditions for those exceptions appearing to depend largely on individual agency policies rather than clear, uniform standards.

These rules apply only to law enforcement. Cities, neighborhoods and businesses that contract with Flock don’t need to follow the new regulations. Recent research has also found error rates ranging from 30% to 70% in Flock camera systems, raising broader questions about the reliability of this increasingly widespread surveillance technology.

Tech.title: WhatsApp Fights Back Against Scammers With New AI Alert Tool
Tech.content:
Meta announced on Wednesday that it’s rolling out a new tool, Scam Alert, to thwart con artists on WhatsApp. The optional feature, currently in beta testing, will run an on-device machine learning model to flag scam messages without giving WhatsApp, Meta or any other entity access to your private conversations.

To take part in the feature, you must turn on the Scam Alert tool in WhatsApp’s settings menu. From there, the AI tool will be automatically downloaded to your phone. You can disable the feature at any time.

Scam Alert operates in the background by classifying incoming text messages from unknown senders. It looks at communication patterns associated with scams on the app, such as requests for personal information, an urgent tone and deliberate trust-building tactics used in romance-baiting scams, in which scammers create a fake emotional bond before asking for financial assistance.

WhatsApp will display a banner warning of a potential scam in a message that only the recipient will see. To move forward, you can either block the sender, report the conversation, ignore the warning or trust the unknown sender. That last option removes the warning flag and stops future alerts for that conversation.

Since this is an AI tool we’re talking about, it’s constantly learning, which means you can choose to share the last five messages from a trusted sender directly with WhatsApp to help keep the model accurate. This part of the feature doesn’t happen on its own; You must opt in to share this data.

Scam Alert is currently in limited beta, and Meta hasn’t yet announced the feature’s full public launch timeline.

A Meta spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

WhatsApp is the most popular messaging app in the world, with over 3 billion people using it daily. The Federal Trade Commission reported that, in 2025 alone, consumers lost $2.1 billion to social media scams. On WhatsApp specifically that year, Americans lost $425 million.

Tech.title: Pets Left in a Ruff Spot After Automatic Feeders Go Down
Tech.content:
Petlibro, the California-based pet-technology company, is in the doghouse with customers after a service outage that left some of its products inoperable.

In a post on its website, the company said functions were restored and the issue fully resolved Wednesday after apps that connect to its smart devices, such as pet feeders and fountains, were unavailable starting on Tuesday.

“Our team will continue reviewing the incident over the coming days to better understand the cause and identify improvements to help prevent similar disruptions in the future,” the company said in the post.

But customers on the Petlibro subreddit, some of whom have been using the devices to care for their pets remotely while traveling, say they’re still experiencing problems even after contacting the company. That’s concerning for owners who depend on automatic feeders, including models with built-in cameras, to feed and monitor their pets from afar.

“They suggested I troubleshoot the connection, completely ignoring what I told them about being away from home on vacation,” wrote one Reddit poster.

A representative for Petlibro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The first service alert from Petlibro was at 8 a.m. ET on Aug. 11 and read, “We began investigating a service disruption affecting the Petlibro app. Some users experienced difficulty accessing the app or controlling devices remotely. Existing settings and schedules stored locally on devices continued to operate as programmed.”

As the outage continued, some users reported that even devices already set up for feeding were not dispensing food as usual, regardless of communication with the Petlibro app.

A screenshot posted by the owner of a pet named Ralphie appears to show Petlibro’s network malfunctioning the morning of Aug. 13.

The company’s CEO, York Wu, told the website The Verge that the outage was related to the Petlibro app and its online servers, not the hardware products themselves. He told the website that feedings “are programmed directly onto the device and should continue to run as scheduled without an internet command,” and that the company was investigating reports contradicting that information.

In addition to feeders and fountains, the company also makes automated litter boxes and pet cameras. Issues with those products, which use the same app for remote functions, have also been reported on the Petlibro subreddit.

Tech.title: Pixel Watch 5 vs. Galaxy Watch 9: Comparing Google and Samsung’s New Watches
Tech.content:
While the Pixel 11 series received the spotlight at this week’s Made by Google event, the company also unveiled the Pixel Watch 5, its latest smartwatch. Though it looks similar to its predecessor, the Watch 5 does add a number of new health and fitness features, such as custom strength workouts and tracking vitals like blood pressure and insulin resistance.

Seeing as Samsung also just announced its latest Galaxy Watch 9 recently, it makes sense to compare the two major Android smartwatches. The Galaxy Watch 9 also has a number of health and safety features, some of which are the same as the Pixel Watch 5 and some that set it apart from the competition.

Here’s how the two major Android smartwatches compare.

Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Pricing

The Galaxy Watch 9 starts at $380 for its 40mm size and $410 for its slightly larger 44mm size. The Pixel Watch 5 costs slightly higher at $400 for its 41mm size and $430 for its 45mm size.

If you want cellular connectivity, you’ll have to pay more; the LTE versions of the Galaxy Watch 9 cost $50 more each, while the LTE versions of the Pixel Watch 5 cost around $100 more each.

The 40mm Watch 9 ships in cream and graphite, while the 44mm ships in silver and graphite. The Pixel Watch 5 comes in matte black, polished silver and a new satin pyrite that’s a gold-and-silver blend. The 41mm Pixel Watch 5 also comes in an additional champagne gold finish.

Those in the US also have the option of getting a special Stephen Curry edition Pixel Watch 5, which comes in the satin pyrite finish plus a “rye” silver-and-orange loop for $580.

Design and display

Like its predecessor, the Pixel Watch 5 has a classic round design reminiscent of traditional wristwatches. There’s a seamless curved display with no visible frame that makes it look quite elegant on the wrist. The Galaxy Watch 9, on the other hand, is a bit chunkier, as it features a circular display that sits inside a rounded-square base.

As mentioned earlier, both watches come in two different sizes; the Pixel Watch 5 ships in 41mm and 45mm, while the Galaxy Watch 9 is available in 40mm and 44mm. Both watches feature a Super AMOLED display with 3,000 nits of peak brightness. They’re both also IP68-rated for dust and water resistance.

The 45mm Google Pixel Watch 5. Carly Marsh/CNET

Health and safety features

Both watches offer activity and sleep tracking as well as a bevy of sensors such as an electrical heart sensor, a gyro sensor, a geomagnetic sensor, an infrared temperature sensor and more. The Pixel Watch 5, however, doesn’t have the Galaxy Watch’s bioelectrical impedance analysis sensor that can track body composition. Another feature that the Galaxy Watch has that the Pixel Watch doesn’t is a skin analyzer that can track carotenoids (antioxidants in the skin) via different color LEDs.

The Pixel Watch 5 can, however, track your blood pressure and insulin resistance trends over time to help you identify if you have elevated risks for hypertension and diabetes. The features currently don’t have FDA clearance and are therefore not available at launch, however. The Galaxy Watch 9 can monitor blood pressure as well, though it requires you to use your own blood pressure cuff for calibration.

With the Pixel Watch 5, Google is also introducing Health Guardian, which expands upon existing emergency safety features. For example, there’s now Breathing Emergency Detection, which will contact emergency services if there’s a life-threatening drop in oxygen saturation, even in the case of incidents like choking or drug toxicity.

Though both the Pixel Watch 5 and the Galaxy Watch 9 offer fitness features like smart coaching and custom workouts, they have slightly different ways to access them. With the Galaxy Watch 9, if you already have a compatible Galaxy smartphone, you don’t have to pay extra for those features. The Pixel Watch 5, however, keeps certain features behind a Google Health Premium subscription for $10 per month (or $100 per year).

Side by side look of the two new Galaxy Watches: Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Battery and processor

The 40mm version of the Pixel Watch 5 comes with a 332-mAh battery, while the 45mm version has a 465-mAh battery. According to Google, both have up to 30 hours of battery life with an always-on display. Comparatively, the Galaxy Watch 9’s 40mm variant has a 390-mAh battery white the 44mm version has a 445-mAh battery. Samsung also says that the Watch 9 lasts up to 30 hours on a single charge with the always-on display mode enabled.

The Pixel Watch 5 still uses the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor, though it’s an “Accelerated” version of what was in the Pixel Watch 4. Samsung’s Galaxy Watch 9, however, uses the updated Qualcomm Snapdragon Wear Elite processor.

Check out the below chart for more comparisons between the Pixel Watch 5 and the Galaxy Watch 9.

Google Pixel Watch 5 vs. Samsung Galaxy Watch 9

Tech.title: Using AI Shopping Carts Could Lead You to Spend More Money, Study Says
Tech.content:
When you make a grocery run to the supermarket in the future, your shopping cart might talk to you, offering tips on recipes and directions for navigating the store. But using “smart” shopping carts equipped with AI devices may also cause you to spend more money at the store, according to new research from Bayes Business School at City St. George’s, University of London.

The researchers found that shoppers who used the AI-equipped carts spent 32% more on average than those who just used regular shopping carts. People using the smart shopping carts bought 25% more items and spent 23% more time shopping in the store.

However helpful the technology might be for shoppers, the findings suggested it could also lead to significant revenue gains for retailers if done right. Shoppers, meanwhile, should be wary of relying too heavily on technology that could create new advertising platforms and steer them toward specific promotions and products, the researchers said.

“Smart cart users in our data spent more, bought more, and stayed longer than non-users,” lead author Sabrina Gottschalk of Bayes Business School told CNET via email.

Know your customer

Large supermarkets have been using AI algorithms to figure out supply chains and predict customers’ demands for years now. Using algorithms in shopping-cart smart screens is still rare in US grocery stores, but that might be changing soon.

Online grocery delivery company Instacart and Pennsylvania supermarket chain Weis Markets announced in June that they were starting to roll out AI-driven “caper carts” to select stores and planned to bring them to more stores this year.

Smart shopping carts could make buying groceries easier or faster for millions of Americans, but e-commerce isn’t always set up to benefit the consumer.

If grocery stores begin to introduce people to digital shopping experiences through screens on shopping carts, consumers may also face issues that plague shopping online, like digital nudging and dark patterns, which are sophisticated techniques in software design used to manipulate people into buying products or giving up their privacy.

Examples of these design patterns would be making the “buy” button bigger than the “cancel” button in an online store or making it hard to check out and purchase items unless you share personal information with the company for marketing purposes.

Shop till you drop

The research team gathered data for the Bayes Business School study from a German supermarket chain. They tracked 12,418 shopping visits over a month. People could decide if they wanted to rely on the screen or just use the cart the traditional way. Shoppers chose to interact with AI-equipped carts in 9,422 instances.

“Having access to detailed data on thousands of real shopping trips allowed us to observe patterns of smart cart use and shopping behaviors that are difficult to study in more traditional research settings,” Gottschalk said.

The team tracked the number of items purchased, money spent and shopping time across all visits. They also tracked screen interactions for those using the smart carts, including number of interactions as well interaction type, like product recommendations, store navigation and digital shopping lists.

“Super users,” or people who interacted with the screen more than 20 times, bought significantly more items and stuck around the store longer. But they didn’t spend any more money than the average shopper did.

The study’s authors say this may indicate that the people who most enjoy using the AI-equipped shopping carts are “hedonic shoppers” who just liked being at the supermarket and playing with the screen on the cart while shopping.

These same super users actually began spending less and purchasing fewer items when their screen interactions peaked. The authors say this suggests using the shopping carts for entertainment could produce “unwanted consequences for retailers.”

While the study found that people using the smart screens on the carts spent more than those who didn’t, Gottschalk doesn’t claim that smart carts are the cause of people spending more on groceries.

“One important point is that, although we find these patterns consistently in the data, we cannot establish causation,” she said. “Shoppers who choose to use a smart cart may simply be different from those who do not.”

Tech.title: Pixel Watch 5 Will Call Emergency Services if It Detects a Breathing Emergency
Tech.content:
A new feature on the Pixel Watch 5 isn’t designed to give users additional routine health data. Instead, it’s intended to help them when they’re unable to help themselves.

Google’s newly announced breathing emergency detection feature uses AI to analyze signals from the watch’s heart rate, motion and altitude sensors to detect signs of a breathing emergency. If it detects one, the wearer has 30 seconds to cancel the alert before the watch automatically calls emergency services and alerts their emergency contacts.

Google says the feature could provide life-saving assistance during incidents such as severe pneumonia, an accidental drug overdose, or choking. In addition to the Pixel Watch 5, the feature will also be available on the Pixel Watch 4 when the feature rolls out.

But Americans will have to wait. The feature has not yet been cleared or evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration and is currently only available in some European countries. A US release date has not yet been announced.

How the breathing emergency detection works

The feature combines data from sensors in the watch and an AI-based algorithm.

“The optical sensor uses green, red and infrared light to estimate blood oxygen levels and identify severe, persistent drops,” Pramod Rudrapatna, Google senior product manager for health, told CNET in an email. “The accelerometer looks for prolonged low movement, while the barometer helps account for environmental factors such as high altitude, where oxygen saturation can naturally be lower. These signals are analyzed together by on-device machine learning models to determine whether they are consistent with a potential breathing emergency while minimizing false alerts.”

To reduce false positives, Google says the feature will also ensure the wearer hasn’t been asleep for more than 30 minutes during the detected incident so that conditions such as sleep apnea won’t interfere with the readings.

“That combination is a smart way to cut down false alarms,” says Dr. Lindsey Rosman, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine. She adds that photoplethysmography (or PPG, the light sensors often found in wearables) has known limitations that can affect readings, but “requiring stillness alongside the oxygen drop likely helps reduce these issues [and] improves reliability.”

Rosman, who also studies the psychological impacts of cardiac wearables, warns that alerting people to a life-threatening event they can’t independently verify is a double-edged sword.

“It can save lives, but it may also drive real health anxiety and hypervigilance, even when the alert is a false positive,” she said.

If users don’t want to use this feature, they can turn it off in their settings.

Breathing emergency detection is one of four new features that come under the Pixel’s Health Guardian umbrella. The other three monitor trends for insulin resistance, blood pressure, and sleep breathing quality.

In 2025, Google rolled out a feature called loss of pulse detection on the Pixel 3 Watch in the US. That feature tracks the wearer’s pulse, while breathing emergency detection focuses on blood oxygen levels and patterns. However, if they work as promised, both features could work together to detect the same type of health emergency, such as an accidental overdose. Loss of pulse detection has been cleared by the FDA and is available now.

The Pixel Watch 5 is available for pre-order.
